Dear Colleague,
It may be useful if ‘students  of fleas' regularly  received  a list of
recently publaebed  literature  on the subject. At the same time a news
sheet could be used by anyone wanting to circulate  among colleagues  certain
Notes or Observations  (these should be concise).
With the sanction  of the authorities  of the British Museum (Natural
History) I would like $6 distribute  a Flea News several times a year.
For reasons of economy this news sheet will be kept as concise as
possible  and will only be sent to those who are seriously  interested  in the
study of fleas. Please inform me if you have no use for Flea News.
Any comments or suggestions  will be appreciated,  also notifications  of
omissions  in the literature  lists.
The opportunity  is taken to give some of my own remarks below.
Yours sincerely, |
F.G.A.M.  Smit.
NOTES AND OBSERVATIONS
Due to a complete  reorganisation  of Tring Museum (which is now occupied  by
the entire bird section of the Department  of Zoology, BM(NH) and to the
stipulation  in N.C. Rothschild's  Deed of Gift of 1913 (which became
effective  in 1923) that his collection  should be housed in the "Natural
History Museum at South Kensington",  the combined  Rothschild  and British
Museum collections  of Siphonaptera  (and documentation)  were removed from
the Tring Museum in May 1972 and are now in the Department  of Entomology,
British Museum (Natural  History),  South Kensington,  London SW7 5BD. All
communications  concerning  these collections  should be sent to this London
address. - Tring no longer means Fleas.

Talking about descriptions:  it would be most helpful if the coordinates
were more ofteri given for localities  mentioned; many of us surely have to
spend too much time tracing  obscure localities.
A new fashion (but not widespread):  giving the length of whole fleas in
hundredths  of mm, such as 2.67 mm or 3.49 mm, is of no practical  use
(because  of the telescopic  nature of the abdomen,  apart from considerable
individual  variation  in size) - 2.7 and 3.5 mm would be accurate  enough.
* * *
Slide preparations:  these often leave much to be desired. Specimens  are
often either in too’ much mounting  medium, too squashed  (perhaps  the worst
offence),  or not lying on their right-hand  side. It is also still not
generally  realized  that Canada  balsam is the most suitable  of all
mounting  media (for fleas): If another  medium  ‘has been used, this should
be stated on a slide label (to prevent  possible  frustration  when trying  to
soak off specimens).

ECTOPARASITES  - In a note appending  the enclosed  Jordan & Rothschild
bibliography  I remark that Ectoparasites  “is a scarce publication  as
only 250 copies were printed." Actually,  that figure is unfortunately
due to a 'slip of my finger': only 200 (two hundred) copies were printed
of each of the six numbers published.  - Quite a rare volume, indeed.

Dear Colleague,
The organisers  have been particularly  delighted  with the
number of papers promised.  A provisional  programme  has been made and it
is proposed  to have papers read from 8.30 a.m. to 12.30 p.m. on Wednesday,
Thursday,  Friday and Saturday. Afternoons  and evenings  will be left free
-apart from the excursions-  for the delegates  to organise  informal  dis-
cussions  and meetings  between  themselves  if they wish to do so.
Papers have been provisionally  divided  into four categories:
Medical  and Veterinary
Physiology  and Morphology
Evolution  and Zoogeography
Taxonomy  and Ecology
Lectures  will be limited  to about 15 minutes  each, with extra time
for discussion.
The International  Journal  for Parasitology  has agreed to publish
a synopsis  of the proceedings  of the Flea Conference.  As indicated
in Flea News (8), the Organising  Committee  will prepare  this synopsis
based on the new information  abstracted  by the authors  from their own
papers. The synopsis  will not take up more than two or three pages of
printed text. In addition,  the International  Journal  for Parasitology
is willing  to consider  papers for publication  but they will have to be
refereed  in the usual manner. If they are handed in to the secretariat
at the Conference,  suitably  prepared  for the Int. J. Parasit.,  they
will be sent en bloc to the editors and there will then be a possi  -
bility  of them all being published  in the same number of the
journal (if accepted  by the referees).
Contributors  are reminded  that we wish to have type-written  abstracts
‘ of the papers to be delivered by the beginning of June, if possible,
so that they can be duplicated  and circulated  before the Conference.
On Thursday,  23rd June, there will be a cocktail  party on the
village green from about 6.30 p.m. onwards and delegates  are cordially
invited to ask any friend in the U.K. -not necessarily  participating
in the Conference-  to attend this party.
Apart from the excursions,  the cocktail  party on Thursday,  June 23rd,
and the party on Saturday,  June 25th, a tennis court, squash racquets
court and swimming  pool will be available  for delegates  and their
families  throughout  the meeting.
The Organising  Committee

* * *
INTERNATIONAL  CONFERENCE  ON FLEAS - The enclosed  concise  report is merely
a factual one, listing  participants  and events. It is worth mentioning  here
that a large room in the house was entirely  devoted to a splendid  display  of
the following  items:
- colour photomicrographs  illustrating  histology  of fleas (M. Rothschild)
- drawings of internal  morphology,  including  nervous system (J. Schlein)
- electron  photomicrographs  of internal  organs with Rickettsiae  (S. Ito)
- photomicrographs  of micro-organisms  in fleas (H. &. Krampitz)
- photographs  illustrating  morphology  of Ceratophyllid  fleas (R. Traub)
- stereoscan  photomicrographs  of external  structures  (M. T. Greenwood)
- various stereoscan  photomicrographs  (F. G. A. M. Smit)
- distribution  and host data of New Zealand fleas (R. L. C. Pilgrim)
- distribution  maps of British fleas (R. S. George) —
- a flea-jump  counter(S.  Sternberg)
- new microscopes  and equipment  (Carl Zeiss)
- two historical  fleas from the Rothschild  collection  (F. G. A. M. Smit)
* * *
For the first conference  on fleas, two years ago in Lund, Sweden, most of
the work was shouldered  by two ladies - Mrs Gunvor Brinck-Lindroth  and Miss
Gunilla Lindqvist. This time, too, two ladies have done all the hard work,
namely Dr Miriam Rothschild  and Miss José Beer. After the final lecture on
Saturday  June 25th, Professor  Brinck - on behalf of all delegates  - was
therefore  pleased to hand Dr Rothschild,  the generous  hostess of the Confe-
rence, a memento in the form of an engraved  goblet while Mr Smit presented
Miss Beer with a framed old map of Northamptonshire  (on which Ashton)
surrounded  by signatures  of the delegates. ’
Those who were fortunate  enough to participate  must have memories of
a fruitful and delightful  week - a unique experience  not easily forgotten.
One colleague  summed the meeting up very succinctly  when she wrote:
"The Conference  was great, just ereahe :
Here are two personal observations  (not meant to be criticisms)  of a
general nature - they would apply to any lecture-meeting: :
- Good (in both quality and quantity) projected  illustrations  illuminate  the
dullest or most brilliant  text, especially  before an international  audience.
However, it seems rather useless to project complicated  tables or graphs
(for which there appears to be a certain fondness) as these can seldom be
digested, or even read, during the short time that they are on the screen.
- In any lecture hall there should be notices "Please try not to smoke".
Smokers (I have been one myself) do not realize how extremely  unpleasant
it can be for non-smokers  to have to breathe in the foul air which addicts
rather selfishly  polluted.

Smit & Wright, in their "Notes on the Wagner ccllection of Siphonaptera in the 
Zoologisches Museum, Hamburg" (1965, Mitt. hamb. zool. Mus. Inst. 62: 1-54) 
remark (p. 4) that "During the war years [2nd world war] Wagner wrote a new 
classification of the fleas of the world. It must have been a tremendous 
tragedy for the old man that he had to leave his large and important manuscript, 
as well as his entire library, behind in Beograd in the great hurry to get 
away [in the autumn of 1944]."" We were unable to find out how fate had ‘dealt 
with the manuscript but now I understand that it will be the MS in the Zoolo- 
gical Institute, Leningrad, as referred to by Vysotskaya & Kir'yakova in their 
1970 "'"Metody sbora i izucheniya blokh i ikh lichinok" [Methods of collecting 
and studying fleas and their larvae]. These authors provide the following 
interesting information (p. 14): "Julius Wagner prepared a manuscript for 
“The fauna of the U.S.S.R. and adjacent countries. Fleas (Suctoria)" of 775 
pages, beautifully illustrated with more than 400 drawings. Unforcunately, 
this manuscript, which deals with about 40 genera and more than 200 species 
of fleas, was kept for about 20 [ ? ] years in the Parasitological Laboratory 
of the Stavropol' Antiplague Research Institute and not published. It was 
eventually returned to the Zoological Institute, Leningrad, in 1956. The Yue N. 
Yagner manuscript was of enormous importance for information about systematics 
and feunisties of fleas and during those years it served as the basis for the 
compilation of keys.for the fleas of our country."

PERSONALIA - We were much saddened  by the news, earlier this year,of
the death of Professor  Valentina  Aleksandrovna  Bibikova,  who was in the
prime of her life and possibly  at the zenith of her work on the biolo-
gical interrelationships  between host-insect  and pathogens. Those of us
who had the privilege  of mecting her during the First Conference  on Fleas
at Lund, Sweden, in 1975, will remember  her as a very friendly  and charming
lady, full of zest. - During those. few days she acquired  several genuine
friends; their great concern about her subsequent  ill-health  and their
regular contact by correspondence  must have been a soothing  comfort to
Valentina  Aleksandrovna  during the time of her illness. Ina way, such
chance developments  of real friendship  are perhaps of greater, if diffe-
rent, value than all lectures of a conference  put together. aa

REQUEST FOR FLEA LARVAE - Professor  R. L. C. Pilgrim will be spending
about 8 months (danuary - August 1979) at the British Museum (Natural
History) to study the comparative  morphology  of flea larvae. His aim is
to examine the present status of the higher classification  of the Order
from the larval standpoint  and he would therefore  much appreciate  receiving
specimens of larvae for use in this study. He has a fair representation  of
species from New Zealand put as the native flea fauna there is very limited,
he would like to obtain specimens of genera and families not occurring  in
his own country. specially  valuable will be identified  larvae obtained  ~
from laboratory  cultures. However, as relatively  few species have been |
reared, material taken from nests, lairs, etc. of k nhown hosts will
be gladly accepted. Please send specimens - to reach London before July
1979 - with appropriate  data and an indication  of the nature of their
identification  (whether bred from identified  adults or derived from named
hosts) to: Prof. R. L. C. Pilgrim, c/o Mr F, G. A. M. Smit,
British Museum (Natural  History)  ,
South Kensington, London SW7 5BD, England.

It is with the deepest  regret that the death is recorded  of a highly
esteemed  colleague  and friend,  Professor  Dr Fritz Peus.

which IT had read during the war years, was one of the stimulants  which
aroused my own interest  in these insects. I was therefore  much pleased
and excited  when, in 1947, at Dr Karl Jordan's  suggestion,  Professor  Peus
wrote to inform me of his continuing  interest  in the study of fleas.

shortly before his death. During that long period  ali had thrice the

volans, among them another  member of Anomiopsyllinae,  namely Conorhinopsylla
stanfordi  Stewart.

Dear Mr Rothschild  - I was very pleased to receive your request for me to
collect for you parasites  off mammals and birds and I was greatly flattered
by the price stated which would induce anyone to willingly  accede to your
I thought that I could easily collect them during my journey torequest.

Unfortunately,  however, this summer proved to be very unsatisfactory,  firstly
because there was a terrible  revolution  in China, through  fear of which my
permanent  assistant  declined  to accompany  me on this journey  and my brother
did not at that time have the pleasure  of going to Urumtsi  as the Government
had prohibited  travelling  there, and secondly  because owing to the complete
absence of rain there was a terrible  drought  in the localities  I visited,
for which reason I was unable to remain this summer in one spot for several
days and in order to satisfy  my permanent  customer  on whose behalf chiefly
I went to Aksu, I frequently  had to move from one ground to another  - each

with the collection  of birds' nests from which to remove the parasites  you
want. . . s « » Owing to the drought,  through  which I lost two horses in the
middle of July, I was obliged  to move from the southern  slopes of the Tyan!
Shan' to its northern  slope. Meanwhile  I succeeded  in killing  three antelopes,
one wild boar, several  hares and over 100 birds, but on these I only found
lice, ticks and some other parasites  - probably  Mallophaga.  As for fleas and
bugs there was not a single specimen,  and I very much regretted  that I had
not the time to collect  them by staying  for several  days in one spot. ...

Kuldja to find employment,  perished. On the summit they were overtaken  by a
severe snowstorm  which continued  for nearly a whole month. Owing to this
snowstorm  we were compelled  to stay at the foot of the mountain  for eight
days without being able to do anything.  During these eight days our supplies
of provisions  became exhausted  and the horses also were nearly starving.
Consequently,  we had to choose a direction  to Narankol (towards the village
of Okhotnitchye)  and to obtain fresh supplies  of bread, tea and sugar, as
well as oats for the horses, thus losing five more days, so that we were not
doing anything  for thirteen  days. During the whole time the blizzard  continued
to rage, and we were forced to stay two more days at the foot of the mountain.
Only then did the blizzard  cease, and we were able to go on our journey, but
we had hardly left the forest zone behind us when we encountered  new diffi-
culties:  the horses began to.sink  into the snow and were unable to carry our
luggage consisting  of two large and two small boxes in sacks thrown over the
backs of the animals. The boxes contained  many heavy articles  and at some
places we ourselves  had to carry them on our own shoulders,  we often being
waist deep, or even deeper, in the snow. Notwithstanding  these great diffi-
culties  we managed  to climb up the mountain  hoping to reach the summit where,
as we thought,  the snow would be firmer. However,  the snow which fell during
the last few days appeared  to be very moist and this, in its turn, had made
the lower layers of snow, which had remained  there since the winter, quite soft,
something  like pap, and we could only get over this on foot leading  our horses
by the bridle.  During this journey  we were knee-deep  in water and our wellington
boots were often filled up with same. We could empty our boots only after having
reached  places where the snow was firmer,  and for this purpose  we not only.
had to take off our boots but also our socks and leg-wrappers  in order to
Squeeze  out the water. After having done so, we had to use the same socks and
leg-wrappers  again. After many difficulties  we reached  the glacier  on the
summit of the mountain  range, but the way there was still worse, being in many
places intersected  by ravines,  and as there was not a piece of wood to be had,
the ravines  were crossed  with much danger and we had often to roll large stones
and blocks of ice into the ravines  so as to form a kind of bridge over which
both we and our horses had to pass. We did our utmost to bring our horses over:
the ravines  but in a short time we only had one horse left which we used for
carrying  down our luggage  from the glacier. The greater  part of our luggage,
including  Chinese  coins and bank-notes,  which we had taken with us for covering
our expenses  during  the journey,  fell into the gulf, together  with our horses
when they tried to leap over the ravine and after having  reached  the other side
rolled on the ice down the abyss, _In the meantime  the weather  again became
dull and before very long the snow and rain again began to fall. To remain at
this place for the purpose  of saving our luggage  and money would mean to bury
ourselves  in an icy grave. We remained  a whole night out in the open. The next
day rain was still falling  when we undertook  a journey  on foot to that place
where we lost our horses,  but none of us had the courage  to go down the pre-
cipice for fear of catching  a serious  malady,  as water was flowing  from all
sides into the abyss and anyone going down would have to stay in the icy water
for a considerable  time. Happily,  on the summit there were two young sarts
[natives]  who had been sent out by the Chinese  Government  to repair the roads,
they heard our shouting  and came to our rescue.  For a considerable  remuneration
they were willing  to assist us to regain our luggage  and money which had
stuck in the crevices,  and as the luggage  was quite wet, it was with the
greatest  difficulty  that we succeeded  in carrying  it to the place where we
left our horse. All the glass articles  were broken, among them being two
bottles of spirit, only the glass tubes remaining  unbroken.  The saddles were
damaged  and the leathern  belts were cut, some of our belongings,  among thembeing.a kettle for cooking food and boiling the water, nppesbed  te be in such
deep places in the ravine so that they could not be reached  at all. As to the
bread we had taken with us, it had become soaked  with water and it was a long
way to the next village. After having  dried the articles  as far as. possible
I selected  only those which were required  for the collection  of butterflies,

Later on we had frost owing to which the snow became so hard that is was quite
impossible  to search for mammals, and even such mammals as the hare and the cat
did not leave footprints  on the snow, and therefore  we had to set traps at the
first burrows we had discovered,  without knowing  whether there were any animals
at all. We often found mammals in the traps set at random, but nearly every time
when I inspected  the traps early in the morning  I discovered  that the animals
caught in them were dead and, because of the cold, stiff as stone. This may be
explained  by the fact that small mammals cannot bear frost. It is very difficult
to look after the traps at night-time,  especially  if one does not know whether
there are animals  at all in the burrows. In addition  to this I had to reckon
with the fact that in our country  there is a shortage  of spirit in which the
fleas have to be preserved.  Owing to the war the sale of spirit and vodka has
been prohibited  by the Government,  and alcohol  is now being sold only by chemists
in very small quantities  when prescribed  by medical  men, provided  there isa
patient  in the family of the buyer. iets eiiaiee

Right Honourable  Rothschild  - Yesterday  I forwarded  you, by registered  post,a
letter informing  you that I intended  sending  you fleas [mostly  collected  in 1914;
not recorded  in print by anyone, therefore  presumably  lost] the same day and
I was very glad of this opportunity,  but you can imagine  my disappointment  when
I was told at the Post Office at Djarkent  that the parcel  which had to be insured
for two hundred  roubles  could not be accepted  owing to the present  circumstances
arising  from the war. I was told by the Post Office officials  that the British
Post Offices  do not hold themselves  responsible  for any losses which may occur
in connection  with insured  parcels  as same may become destroyed  by mines etc.
I was advised  to send the parcel  uninsured  but I decided  to postpone  the des-
patching  of the parcel until a more suitable  time. ..... I am much afraid
that necessity  may induce me to offer fleas to Russian  scientists  while I would

In 1949 the entire collection  of flea-literature  present in the Flea Room
of Tring Museum fitted a one--metre  shelf. There was no index to any lite-.
rature; Dr Jordan had most of the important  titles in his head.

flea literature  as was possible and a card-index  now totals nearly 41.000
titles. It will be realized that completeness  is a rather evasive target
which is seldom reached - we certainly  have not reached it (and now never
will do so). - Apart from a general index, there is also an annual one
(as a handlist up to 1950, from 1949 onwards as a card-index).

FIRST EUROPEAN CONFERENCE  ON FLEAS
(preliminary  notification)
Most students  of fleas are in agreement  about the potential  value of
a general  meeting  to discuss  various  aspects  of our subject  of study.
It is gratifying,  therefore,  to announce  that The Zoological  Institute
of the University,  Lund, Sweden -at the instigation  of its director,
Professor  Per Brinck- will be organizing  the first such conference  to
be held in Europe. This conference,  supported  by a grant from the
Swedish  Natural  Science  Research  Council,  will last three or four days
during the first half of June, 1975; it is intended  to be of a rather
informal  nature and will take place in the Zoological  Institute,  Lund,
and/or at its Stensoffa  Field Station  (near Lund).
The Zoological  Institute  of the University,  Lund, is honoured  and
privileged  to invite anyone who is seriously  interested  in the study of
fleas to attend the conference.  As the venue is in Europe, it should
be realized  that European/Palaearctic  themes (apart from general ones)
may dominate  lectures  and discussions.
Those who have access to funds will no doubt apply for a grant to
cover the cost of travelling  and boarding. Grants to cover the basic
expenses  connected  with the stay in Lund will be available  for partici-
pants from eastern.  Europe.
Accommodation:  by choice either at the Stensoffa  Field Station
(about 20 beds) in hostel conditions  # 10 Sw.Kr. a night (add for meals
at least 25 Sw.Kr. a day) or at an hotel in Lund (more expensive,  more
comfort).
The organizing  committee  consists  of Mrs G. Brinck-Lindroth,
Mr L. Lundqvist  (both of The Zoological  Institute,  Lund) and
Mr F.G.A.M.Smit  (British  Museum (Natural  History)).
If you would like to attend the conference,  please inform (without
much delay) Mrs G. Brinck-Lindroth,  Department  of Animal Ecology,
University  of Lund, Ecology Building,  S 225 62 Lund, Sweden; applicants
from eastern Europe, please state at the same time whether or not you
require a subsistence  grant.
Details about the meeting will be circulated  in due time.

THE - GHOST OF TR NG MUSEUM
In my imagination  I can still hear them. . . the heavy footsteps, a dozen
or so. « « the occasional  strange, sometimes eerie noises, always totally
maccounted for. Indeed, ghostly sounds they were; never was there any evi-
dence of a person or other object that could have caused them.
Way back in 1949, on January 2na to be precise, I arrived in Tring from
ny native country, The Netherlands,  carrying 4 microscope,  # violin and a
suitcase. I had been offered a job as temporary assistant in the Flea Room
and, being mad-keen on fleas, grasped the chance of a lifetime with alacrity.
A boarding-house  opposite the museum provided frugal but adequate lodging.
Uninhibited as my interest in these insects: was, I greatly and gratefully
enjoyed the wonderful Rothschitdian  atmosphere  which in those days still
pervaded Tring Museum. One could work with unfettered  enthusiasm  for as
many hours a day as one wanted. Tring town peing as dead as a dodo: Cand
even nicknamed 'Dedo Town' in those days) and true homely comforts out of
reach,:I used to work © - well, be: in the museum, if you like - till AN or
12 o'clock at night, including Saturdays and Sundays [in these early years
I could not quite understand  why it was thought unusual for me to go to the
museum for some hours on Christmas Day]. For the first year or so my place
of work in the museum was at one end of one of the two large Lepidoptera
Halls (demolished  in 1970; they used to house some 24 million specimens) ,
near the entrance to the two Flea Rooms (likewise demolished), one of which
was still occupied by Freddie Cox (who retired, after 50 years of assistance-
ship in the Flea Room, in 1951), the obtes noom by Dr Karl Jordan who was
then 88 years old. and still going strong (he only was stone-deaf). Quite
often Dr Jordan used to come in, after a day's work, between 8 and 9 in the
evening, also staying till about midnight (and then after arriving home -
a 15 minutes’ walk away 7 he would often make himself comfortable in his
easy chair, pick up the detective story he was reading and finally go to bed
between one and two o'clock. in the morning - to rise again at 6 a.m).
One evening, sitting as usual in the large dark hall with only a lamp
shining over TMy table, I heard footsteps not far behind me. Being flea-drunk,
I took no notices Not long after, another evening at about the same tame =
around 9 o'clock — #£ once again heard heavy footsteps but somehow thought
that Dr Jordan had come in. A little later I noticed that no lights had been
switched on in his room and indeed Dr Jordan had not arrived. Once again .
BE aia not awell upon the sounds. However, when a few days later the loud
about a dozen of them, were one evening again heard behind me,
I listened more attentively  but I failed to associate the sounds with any
person} I switched lights on, made a tour of inspection  but saw nobody -
The. caretaker used to do his round at about 11 pem. and one could hear him
far, pass and go off again. The sounds of the building itselffootsteps  s
coming from #n familiar; the wooden floors and the numerous cabinets did emitool
The footsteps  phenomenon  continued  at a rate of
once every few weéks and between 9 and 11 p.m. I had grown quite used to
them and they did not bother me. When later in my first year I happened to
mention the odd sounds to the old librarian  she looked startled and said
"So you have heard’ them.too ? They are Lord Walter Rothschild's  footsteps."
She then told me that one evening; not long after his lordship's  death, she
worked till a rather late hour and heard his footsteps  in the Bird Room
(having worked with him for many years she was very familiar with the foot-
steps of the heavy. man) - she never again  worked late hours in Tring Museum.
Subsequently  I also learned from colleagues  at Tring Museum that during the
years of the second world war members of the staff who had to be on night-
duty for*muséum=safety  reasons (a few incendiary  bombs did fall on Tring town
but the museum came through unscathed)  and for whom a bed was provided  ina
corner of the large Flea Room, soon became familiar  with the inexplicable
sound of footsteps  and it was apparently  common knowledge  then that Lord
Rothschild  regularly-revisited  his beloved  museum.
Occasionally  there were other sounds which defied explanation  and I well
remember  one evening  at around ten when at the other end of the large halla
tumultuous  banging  noise broke out which lasted for about half a minute - that
I did not like. A little later I switched  the lights on in the hall and went
down to, investigate;  no sign of, anything  that could have been playing  up.
After some years, officialdom  began to get a firmer grip on the liberal |
atmosphere  of Tring Museum  and I was instructed  to leavé the sanctuary  at
eight o'clock  each day but Saturday  and Sunday  at five. Too early to hear
the ‘ghost: and indeed for me it was the end of the footsteps.  Once, though,
I did have a most  disagreeable  experience.  The route out of the museum was
Flea Room, Dr Jordan's.  room, the room.which  Lord Rothschild  had used for his
entomological  studies,  a lobby, a corridor,  the large L-shaped  Bird Room: and
the workshop. It was winter and I never bothered  to switch on any lights
during  my way out as I could find my way blindfolded.  Well,. that evening  the
moment I entered  Lord Rothschild's  room I felt, for no obvious  reason,  at once
terribly  cold and extremely  scared,  my hair actually  rising  in fear. Nothing
unusual  was seen or heard, but I still find it difficult  to believe  that I
managed  ‘to ‘pass through  that room. - A week or so later, at around  20 hrs,
I found Dr Jordan  being violently  sick in that very room. Coincidence,  perhaps.
A’ ghostly  apparition  was never seen; not in Tring Museum. I did see a
ghost once. In February  1952 a friend and I decided  to do some trapping  just
outside  Tring. _It was a cold dark winter evening. We had placed about two-
dozen traps in an extensive  piece of jungle-like  woodland.  At 23.30 hrs we
went out there  to inspect  and bag the catches. When finally  we came to the
last few traps, which were placed around a small clearing,  deep in the jungle;
I shone the torch on the traps and informed  my friend in elated voice that
there was a fine bankvole.  He did not react. When I turned to him, expecting
him to have the bag open to receive  the catch, I saw him standing  and staring.When I looked in the same direction:  lo and behold,  only a few yards away
- in the torchlight  - was the figure of a headless  man in a long dark coat,
hands in the coat pockets,  silently  gliding  over the rough ground and gradually
disappearing  into nothingness.  We then looked at one another:  did you see that?
It certainly  was no physical  body; who, in any case, would be wandering  about
at midnight  in the cold in woodland  so dense and dark that one could not find
one's way out without  a torch ? ;
_ Ah, those were the days ! The days of good old Rothschildian  Tring Museumwhich flourished  on trust and where, for instance,  one could - day or night -freely walk into the superb library  and enjoy Audubon's  elephant-folio  volumes,
the beautifully  bound volumes  with Keulemans'  originals,  the various  editions
of Ortus Sanitatis,  Curtis’ originals  or the numerous  old books of travel and
adventure. Just how good it was to be there in those days is obvious from what
the late Dr Karl Jordan  wrote to me on 17.XII.1947:  "I spent my birthday  [86th]
in the Museum,  the greatest  pleasure  I have at my age. I am very fortunate  that
oe have such a great interest  which occupies  my thoughts  and prevents  me from
dwelling  too often and too long on the affairs  of mankind,"regular cracking  sounds.

When it became obvious  that, because of my retirement,  I could not possibly
produce any further issues of Flea News (after No. 20), I did not approach
anyone with a suggestion  to consider  taking over the chore; simply because
the preparation  of FN is a chore. Nevertheless,  I had faint hopes that
someone might like to volunteer  to carry on the compilation  of that news
sheet. I was therefore  truly delighted  to learn from Dr R. E. Lewis that
he, with the invaluable  aid of his wife Joanne, would be prepared  to attempt
a revival of Flea News. Meanwhile,  many colleagues  expressed  great dis-
appointment  and indicated  that without  FN they are quite lost. Actually,
being isolated  now myself, I no longer have an idea what is going on in
the flea world or what is being published.
The Lewis team, and the Iowa State University  of Science and Technology,
deserve our profound  gratitude  for continuing  the task of keeping  all
pulicologists  well informed. This is no sinecure. Let all who are
favoured  as recipients  of Flea News (which continues  to be a free service)
assist Bob and Joanne Lewis by providing  them with any information  which
will be of use im their compilation  work and which consequently  will
benefit all those who are privileged  enough to study the jolliest  of insects.

We plan to continue  Flea News using much the same format as that set up by
Frans Smit. It will be difficult,  if not impossible,  to match his fine example.
We will endeavor  to do so but, to make Flea News as informative  and complete  as
possible,  we need your cooperation.
We hope you will send us reprints  of your publications  promptly. We parti-
cularly  need your cooperation  in sending  us copies of your work in Conference
Proceedings  and small or newly established  journals  which are not likely to be
widely distributed  in American  libraties.  This is especially  important  when
descriptions  of new taxa are involved. In the event reprints  cannot be sent,
please provide  us with a complete  citation  of the work.
On our part, we will attempt  to search the available  literature  for cita-
tions pertaining  to fleas. To assist us, we are using several  computer  search
services  to broaden  coverage  of current  literature  not in the Iowa State Univer-
sity library. Each of these services  scans literature  in certain  broad disci-
plines (e.g., agriculture).  Our data base coverage  includes  Commonwealth
Agricultural  Bureau (CAB), U.S. National  Agriculture  Library  (AGRICOLA),  U.S.
government  documents  (NTIS), ISI Science  Citation  Index (SCI) and Iowa State
University  library  new books (OCLC).
When the computer  gives us a citation,  it will be verified  against  the
original,  if the original  is in our library. When the source is not in our
library,  the citation  often can still be verified  in one of several  indexes.
If the citation  cannot be checked  in any way, we then will decide whether  or not
to include  it in Flea News. When the title indicates  any possibility  that
information  on fleas is included  in the publication,  we will list it. An
asterisk  (*) preceding  a citation  will indicate  to you that we have seen neither
the original  nor verified  it in another  source.
Whenever  possible,  titles will be given in the language  of publication
(exceptions:  Russian  and Chinese  titles, following  Mr. Smit's precedent).
Computer  translations  will be used in most other cases.
One quirk of our computer  is that only the first 9 letters  of authors’
names are printed  out. When we cannot verify  a citation,  one or more of the
authors'  names therefore  may be incomplete  but certainly  enough letters  will be
present  for you to locate the citation  should the source be available  to you.
In addition  to the computer  searches,  periodically  we will scan journals
not thus covered,  first those in which flea papers have appeared  most frequently
in the past 8 years, then others as time permits.
We encourage  you to send us newsworthy  notes or observations  for inclusion
in Flea News, and we will try to present  some items not bibliographic  on occasion.

In the six months since we sent out Flea News 21 last December,  a number of
colleagues  have written  expressing  their enthusiasm  that the newsletter  was to be
continued.  Your letters  were most appreciated  and we urge you all to inform  us
of your current  researches  and future plans in order that the recipients  of Flea
News may be kept informed.
* * *
Dr. Robert E. Elbel, an authority  on the larvae of fleas, has recently  com-
pleted a chapter  on this subject  for a volume tentatively  titled "An introduction
to immature  insects  of North America", This is to be an update of the two-volume
classic  by Alvah Peterson  entitled  "Larvae  of insects;  an introduction  to Nearctic
species". It is to be published  by the Kendall/Hall  Publishing  Co. of Dubuque,
Iowa, hopefully  in late 1982.
x * *
Dr. George P. Holland  recently  informed  me that he had finished  the illustra-
tions for the revision  of his 1949 monograph,  "The Siphonaptera  of Canada". He
hopes that the revised  volume will be out this year.
* * *
I am aware of the existence  of two bound copies of the rare Jordan & Roths-
child 1915-1924  volume entitled  "Ectoparasites".  Both are for sale and interested
parties  sould contact  me for further  details. According  to Smit, in Flea News 10
(1977), the last complete  sets of this series were sold 30 years ago.
* * *
A REQUEST  - The editor of the highly authoritative  "Handbuch  der Zoologie"
wishes to hear from anyone interested  in writing  a volume on Siphonaptera  for that
serial publication  (it should cover every aspect of the study of fleas). Will
those who are interested  in, and capable  of, undertaking  such an important  task
please contact  Dr. M. Fischer,  Naturhistorisches  Museum  Wien, Postfach  417,
Burgring  7, A-1014 Wien, Austria.  --F.S.

Twenty years in the writing,  this beautifully  printed  and lavishly  illustrated
volume certainly  represents  one of the most ambitious  projects  ever undertaken  by
a single author. As the world-renowned  ornithologist,  Dean Amadon, says in his
forward,  "Nothing,  it seems, has been omitted  that would be of particular  interest
to readers,  and many subjects  have been included  that most of us in making such a
compilation  would have overlooked."'  It is arranged  alphabetically  from "abdomen"
to "zygote". In addition  to the general family treatments,  each species is dis-
cussed, including  description,  food and feeding  habits, nest, eggs and incubation,
other names, age, flight speed, hybrids,  weights  and range, where such information
is available.  The volume contains  a veritable  wealth of information  and is a must
for every naturalist's  library.  --R.E.L.

JUST PUBLISHED.  Anillustrated  catalogue  of the Rothschild  collection
of fleas (Siphonaptera)  in the British  Museum (Natural  History).  Volume  VI.
Pygiopsyllidae  by D. K. Mardon,  1981, viii + 298 pp., 748 figures,  £50.00.

ogy; Synonymies;  Listing  the material;  Type specimens  of species  and sub-
species;  List of institutions  in which types are deposited;  List of collectors'
names; Host names; Supplementary  glossary;  Acknowledgements;  Key to the genera
of Pygiopsyllidae;  Subfamily  Lycopsyllinae;  Subfamily  Pygiopsyllinae;  Subfamily
Stivaliinae;  Index to genera, species  and subspecies  of Pygiopsyllidae;
References;  Captions  to figures. This and earlier  volumes  may be obtained  from:
Publications  Sales, British  Museum (Natural  History),  Cromwell  Road, London SW7
SBD, England. Payment  with order requested.

PROFESSOR  J.-C. Beaucournu,  Rennes,  has indicated  that he is interested  in
obtaining  unpublished  records  of the flea fauna of the western  Mediterranean
region. This includes  Spain, Portugal,  France, Italy, Algeria,  Tunisia,  and

Following  is a short article  which appeared  in the Iowa State UniversityComputation  Center Newsletter  15(7): 6-7, July, 1981. It describes  a dataretrieval  system  currently  being developed  at Iowa State University  with theassistance  of Mrs. Nancee Nilsen.
MY FLEAS HAVE FILES!
A SPIRES Application
One of the "newer"  systems  available  to patrons  of the Computation  Centeris the Stanford  Public Information  REtrieval  System (SPIRES). This system  isa generalized  data base management  system  developed  at Stanford  University.SPIRES permits  a definition  of custom  data bases which incorporates  sophisti-cated input and editing  of data, element  and record retrieval,  and file manage-ment statistics,  all without  the formidable  investment  in developing  time-sharing  data base management  programs.
SPIRES data sets are kept in files which allow efficient  retrieval  andupdate. Even a major change to an application  data base, such as adding thatunforeseen  element  or a new index, can generally  be done with relative  ease tothe data base owner. Several  common SPIRES application  examples,  catalogs,mailing  lists, bibliographic  citations,  etc., are available  at the ComputationCenter.
A recent application  utilizing  SPIRES is presently  in use by the Departmentof Entomology.  Developing  this application  required  classification  of specimensand cross-referencing  synonyms  of these classifications.  It also requiredbibliographic  data which represents  an extensive  collection  of information  aboutthe insect order Siphonaptera  (you guessed  it, fleas).
Accessible  by six indices,  the Siphonaptera  data base is comprised  of twomajor subfiles: classification  data and bibliographic  data. The bibliographicdata can be accessed  using indices  which identify  author, species  identificationcode, subject  keywords  (including  life stages),  Siphonapteran  genus and/orspecies,  host genus and/or species,  or a Synonymy  scan. The classification  datacan be accessed  by identification  code or Siphonapteran  genus and/or species.
In order to get automatic  synonymy  cross-referencing,  the classificationsubfile  is self-indexed  on a senior synonym  code. This feature  enables  the datapreparer  to indicate  a synonymous  relationship  for a particular  entry. All sub-sequent  cross-referencing  will be formed  by SPIRES indexing  routines.
The classification  data is based on a chronological  identification  code andsynonymy  relationships  carefully  recorded  by Dr. Robert  Lewis. Over 2,300classifications  have been entered  which index bibliographic  information.  Biblio-graphic  data is eventually  expected  to include  over 11,000 citations.  Thesecitations  are an international  collection  maintained  by a continuous  literaturereview  based on computer  and manual searches  as well as personal  correspondence.
Data retrieval  is open to the public,  but data base security  is provided  toprevent  action  that would change  or remove  any data, except  by the file owner.
One input and three output formats  were prepared  for each of the subfiles.The output formats  include  a short format,  which yields only the most pertinent
information  in the fewest lines possible,  a standard  format which yields in-
formation  most commonly  required  by investigators,  and the full format which
yields all input elements  of each file.
The formats  utilize  sub-goal  processing  to capture  information  from both
subfiles. The input format enables  the data preparer  to enter information  for
new records  using prompting  techniques.  Updates  and merges utilize  the standard
SPIRES transfer  methods.
SPIRES protocols  are used to find all citations  related  to a specific  name
or specific  species. Access is provided  to both files using information  from
the classification  file to access the bibliographic  file. For example,  if a
species  appears  in the literature  under more than one name, all citations  con-
cerning  that species  can be retrieved  and viewed by accessing  any one description.
Additionally,  this request  can be very specific  and may include  only the primary
descriptions  of the species  contained  in the bibliographic  file.
A sample retrieval  session  may include  the following:
-> ..FIND. SYNONYMY
:PLEASE  ENTER ID TO BE SCANNED>>  190201
* SYNONYMS  FOUND WERE 190201 OR 190325 OR 189002 *
:DO YOU WANT TO SEE JUST THE PRIMARY  CITATIONS?  (Y/N) N
-RESULT: 5 CITATION(S)

OBITUARY
Dr. ALFREDO RARRERA VAZQUEZ MARIN 11 May 1928 - 7 December 1980
Dr. Alfredo Barrera V. Marin, Professor  on the Faculty of Sciences  of
the National  Autonomous  University  of Mexico, died at the age of 54, on
7 December  1980, in the city of Merida, Yucatan,  Mexico.
A specialist  in ectoparasitic  insects, principally  the Siphonaptera,
he taught and directed  research  for over thirty years in several institu-
tions in Mexico. During this period he published  more than eighty articles
on various subjects.
He studied at the National School of Biological  Sciences of the National
Polytechnic  Institute  (IPN). Later he traveled  to several foreign univer-
sities including:  the University  of Texas, Austin, TX in 1963; the National
Pedagogic  Institute,  Paris, France, in 1963; and the University  of Maryland,
Baltimore,  MD during 1964 and 1965.
During his academic life he received several distinctions.  In 1958 and
1959 he was Vice President  of the Natural History Society of Mexico. In 1961
he was Vice President  of the Entomological  Society of Mexico. During 1964
and 1965 he was President  of the Natural History Society of Mexico. From 1969
to 1970 he was Vice President  of the Scientific  Research  Academy and in 1970
to 1971, President  of the same. From 1973 he was a Correspondent  Member of
the Natural Sciences Institute  of Ecuador. From 1978 to 1980 he was a member
of the Review Commission  of the Science Faculty. He was also a member of the
Postgraduate  Study Council of the same institution.
For ten years (1965-1974)  he was the Director  of the Natural History
Museum of Mexico City.
He was a professor  and researcher  in several institutions  in Mexico,
among them: Secretary  of Health and Assistance,  Secretary  of Agriculture  and
Livestock,  the National  Polytechnic  Institute  and the National  Autonomous
University  of Mexico.
The merit he enjoyed as a scholar and a teacher was. great, his teachings
being of inestimable  value to his students.

RECENTLY  PUBLISHED  - The Ecology of Ectoparasitic  Insects by Adrian G.
Marshall,  1981 (ISBN 0-12-474080-4),  Academic  Press Inc. (London) Ltd., i-xvi,
459 pp., £33.00/$69.50.
This book is required  reading for anyone interested  in ectoparasitic  insects.
In the first 11 chapters  the author deals with specific  aspects of the ectopara-—
sitic mode of life from a comparative  point of view. Chapter 1 discusses  ecto-
parasitism  in its various forms as it occurs in the Hexapoda,  and includes 11
tables dealing with the classification  of ectoparasites  and their avian and mam—
malian hosts. Chapter 2 contains  a brief treatment  of the environment  in which
ectoparasites  spend their lives and from which they derive their food. Chapter
3 treats field and laboratory  methods, including  sampling  techniques,  marking for
vecapture,  preservation,  and laboratory  maintenance.  Chapter 4 is a detailed
discussion  of the life cycles in ectoparasitic  insects, treating  such topics as
mating and oviposition,  immature  and adult stages, and causes of parasite  mor-
tality. Chapter 5 discusses  food and feeding activity,  modifications  in mouth-
parts, food consumption,  and the effects of differing  diets. Chapter 6 deals
with how ectoparasites  locate their hosts, and both active and passive transfer
between hosts. Chapter 7 summarizes  what is known about host associations
among ectoparasites,  and treats host specificity,  host resistance,  and how
ectoparasites  have been used to deduce host phylogeny. Chapter 8 discusses  the
morphological  and behavioural  adaptations  which allow the ectoparasite  to remain
on or near the host. Chapter 9 considers  the interrelationships  of ectopara-
sites with other organisms  including  their own parasites,  competition  among
themselves,  and other aspects contributing  to their survival. Chapter 10 treats
the population  dynamics  of ectoparasites,  and Chapter 11 their effect upon the
health of their host. Chapter 12 contains a brief summary of the author's
conclusions.  In addition  to the list of species mentioned  in the text and an
index, there are 53 pages of bibliography.
To write a book of this type was an ambitious  undertaking  and the results
are truly impressive,  both in quantity  and in quality. The format is pleasing
to the eye and the illustrations  are appropriate  and well executed. In the
3
words of Miriam Rothschild  who wrote the forward, "One word occurred  to me when
I finished  reading the book: indispensible".  ---R.E.L.

RECENTLY  PUBLISHED  - Biology  of Insect Eggs by Howard E. Hinton, 1981
(ISBN 0-08-021539-4)  Pergamon  Press Ltd., Vol. I, i-xxiv, 1-473; Vol. II, i-
xviii, 475-778;  Vol. III, i-xvii, 779-1125. U.S. $400.00.
The publication  of this long-awaited  opus adds a new dimension  to the study
of insects. Fleas are only mentioned  briefly  on pages 10 (Aphaniptera),  26
(Siphonaptera,  Pulicidae,  Pulex irritans),  and 176 (Xenopsylla),  but the wealth
of information  concerning  the other orders of insects  makes these volumes  an
exceedingly  valuable  addition  to the entomological  literature.  A detailed  re-
view of these volumes is beyond the purview  of this newsletter,  but following  is
a brief discussion  of their content.
Volume I begins with an Introductory  Note by Colin Mapes who was ultimately
responsible  for publication  of the work, followed  by an appreciation  of the late
H. E. Hinton by T. R. E. Southwood.  Following  these are an introduction  and 11
chapters  dealing  with the following  subjects:  Number of Eggs, Oviposition,
Respiratory  Systems,  Respiratory  Efficiency  of Egg Plastrons,  Hydropyles  and
Water Relations,  Colleterial  Glands, O¥thecal  and Shell Proteins,  Enemies of
Eggs, Defensive  Devices,  Parental  Care and Techniques.  This volume also contains
155 photomicrographs  of insect eggs, mostly taken on a scanning  electron  micro-
scope.
Volume II contains  a systematic  treatment  of the hexapod  orders, dealing
with such matters as parthenogenesis,  oviposition,  chorionic  structure,  micro-
pyles, egg-bursters,  diapause,  and hatching. Where appropriate,  other subjects
are discussed  and, in a few groups, keys to the eggs are provided. The volume
concludes  with an addendum  listing  papers on reproductive  systems and micropylar
apparatus,  and a taxonomic  list of species illustrated  in volumes I and II.
Volume III contains  an exhaustive  bibliography  of 220 pages, and indexes to
species, authors, and subjects. It terminates  with a bibliography  of Hinton's
publications  from 1930 to 1977.
No doubt this work will remain the standard  reference  for decades to come.
and although  the price is prohibitive  for individuals,  it is a must for
institutional  libraries. =--R.E.L.

NOMENCLATURAL  COMMENTS  - In 1980 a number of papers dealing  with Siphon-
aptera were published  in Acta Academiae  Medicinae  Guiyang  5(2). Through  the
kindness  of Dr. Li Kuei-chen  we are informed  that these papers were published
in December  of that year. Some of the names mentioned  in these papers are
listed as in press. We have not yet seen descriptions  so are unaware  of their
actual year of publication.  However,  there are a few nomenclatural  problems
which have been cleared  up with Dr. Li's assistance.  All of the papers have
been listed in the 1980 section  of Flea News 23 and will not be completely  cited
again here.
In the Li paper on Macrostylophora,  the species luchunensis  is variously
cited as luchuensis  Huang (in press), Iuchuensis  Huang (in press), and
Luchunensis  Huang (in press). The actual description  of this taxon appears in
a later paper in this series and the name is spelled  luchunensis.  The descrip-
tion was republished  in another  journal  in 1981 but the name should be cited as:
Macrostylophora  luchunensis  Huang, 1980.
In the paper by Li and Huang, Neopsylla  Guizhowensis  Liao, 1974 should read:
Neopsylla  kweichowensis  Liao, 1974.
Also in this paper Ctenophthalmus  eothenomus  sp.n., C. brevijiciens  sp.n.,
and Typhlomyopsyllus  n.gen. cavaticus  n.sp. were described,  as well as mention
being made of Paraceras  laxisinus  He, Hsieh & Li in press. All but the latter
name were listed in the English  portion  of the paper, and their descriptions
subsequently  republished  in another  journal in 1981. The status of these names
is as follows:
1. Ctenophthalmus  eothenomus  Li & Huang, 1980
2. Ctenophthalmus  brevijiciens
Although  this name is cited both at the beginning  of the description
and in the caption  of figure 3, it is listed as C. breviprojiciens  sp.
nov. in the English  portion  of the paper and three times in the subse-
quent republication.  Since the original  name does not appear to be
based on any word of classical  origin but the latter name does, it is
suggested  that the proper citation  be Ctenophthalmus  breviprojiciens  Li
& Huang, 1980.
3. Typhlomyopsyllus  cavaticus  Li & Huang, 1980
This name was spelied as shown above in the Chinese  portion  of the
paper, but spelled Typhlomyopsylla  in the English summary. In the 1981
republication,  the authors reverted  to the original  spelling. The name
should be cited as listed above.
4, Paraceras  laxisinus  He, Hsieh & Li sp.nov.
This species was described  in a later paper in this series written
by a different  combination  of authors. It should be cited: Paraceras
laxisinus  Xie, He & Li, 1980 (mec He, Hsieh & Li, 1980).
The status of some other names mentioned  in this series is still unresolved
and it is hoped that receipt  of additional  reprints  will clarify  their positions.

RECENTLY PUBLISHED ~- The Rodents of Southern Africa by G. De Graaff, 1981
(ISBN 0 409 09829 0) Butterworth  & Co. (SA) (PTY) Ltd., 152-154 Gale Street,|
Durban 4001, S.A. i-xviii, 1-267, 12 colour plates, 111 figures, 73 maps.
U.S. $42.53.
While the large mammals of Africa traditionally  have attracted attention
from sportsmen and scientists alike, the same cannot be said for the small
mammals. Indeed, many faunal elements are extremely poorly known and additional
new taxa still are being described annually. Although the identification  manual
edited by Meester and Setzer (1971) gave stability to the nomenclature,  there
has long been a need for an in-depth treatment of the African fauna which could
be used by the non-specialist. The Rodents of Southern Africa is such a book.
As stated in the Preface, the book is not intended to be a systematic
treatise, but rather a book that can be used in teaching classes dealing with
mammals and as a reference work for the layman or field worker who wishes to
learn something about interesting  adaptations  and ways of life of a very import-
ant order of mammals. While subspecies are mentioned occasionally  in the text,
the basic taxonomic unit is the species. Though the author assumes that the
reader will be familiar with the basic principles of general zoology and its
related terminology,  the introduction  includes considerations  of such topics as
dental formulae, zoogeographic  realms, skeletal features and terminology,  organ
systems, etc. This is followed by a comparison of the Wood (1955) and Anderson
(1967) systems of rodent classification  and a checklist of southern African
rodents.
The bulk of the text consists  of the species  accounts,  in which the informa-—
tion is arranged  in a uniform  format for each taxon. Following  the generic  and
specific  names (including  the author and date of description)  are the common
names in English  and Afrikaans.  A brief outline  of the synonymic  history  comes
next, followed  by a tabular  display  of the body measurements  for both sexes. The
remainder  of the account  is divided  by the following  headings:  identification,
skull and dentition  (including  photographs  of the skull in dorsal,  ventral,  and
lateral  view, and an enlargement  of the cheekteeth),  distribution,  habitat,  diet,
habits,  predators,  reproduction,  parasites  (both internal  and external),  rela-
tions with man, prehistory  and taxonomy. Each account is also furnished  with a
distribution  map, and sometimes  line drawings. Twelve attractive  coloured  plates
depicting  the species  in their normal habitat  are included. The book concludes
with a glossary,  a list of references,  and an index.
One attractive  innovation  to be found in this volume involves  the keys.
Each of these is accented  by being printed  over a light gray background,  as are
the tables and line drawings. The result is pleasing  to the eye and greatly
facilitates  locating  the keys in the various  sections.
The text is remarkably  free of mechanical  flaws, printed  in a pleasing  format,
and well reflects  the obvious  affection  of the author for his subject  matter. In
these days of inflated  book prices, the cost is modest for a tome of this quality.

RECENTLY  PUBLISHED  - Mammal Species  of the World: aTaxonomic  and Geographic
Reference  edited by J. H. Humacki,  K. E. Kinman and J. W. Koeppl, 1982 (ISBN
0 942924 00 2). Published  as a joint venture  of The Allen Press, Inc. and The
Association  of Systematics  Collections  (JVA-Mammals,  P.O. Box 368, Lawrence,
Kansas 66044, USA). 694 pp. U.S. $55.00.
While no mention  is made in this publication  of mammal parasites,  the volume
is an invaluable  reference  to parasitologists  in general. It embodies  the con-
tributions  of 189 specialists  in mammalian  taxonomy  from 23 countries  and treats
4,170 currently  recognized  species.
The editors  frequently  refer to this volume as a checklist  in their intro-
duction,  but it more accurately  fulfills  the definition  of a catalogue  of the
mammalian  fauna of the world. The taxonomic  arrangement  follows  that of Corbet
and Hill (1980, A World List of Mammalian  Species)  with a few minor modifications.
Entries  are listed phylogenetically  by order and family, and alphabetically  by
genus and species. A typical  species  treatment  includes  the following  informa-
tion: current  generic  and specific  name, author,  date and citation  of original
description,  names of reviewers,  type locality,  and known distribution.  This
information  frequently  is followed  by a comments  section  which includes  informa-
tion on synonymic  history  and treatment  by other specialists.  Most treatments
conclude  with the International  Species  Inventory  System number. Those species
governed  by the regulations  of the U.S. Endangered  Species  Act and those listed
in the appendices  of the Convention  on International  Trade in Endangered  Species
of Wild Fauna and Flora are also annotated  under a Protected  Status heading.
The index includes  all taxonomic  names included  in the volume, including  synonyms,
nomina nuda, nomina oblita,  and other invalid  names. There are also 15 pages of
bibliography  and literature  cited.
While this volume does little toward sorting  out the ‘subspecies  confusion
so typical  of mammalian  taxonomy,  it certainly  provides  a major resource  to those
who concern  themselves  with mammalian  associates.  The editors,  contributors,
and reviewers  are to be congratulated  for their perseverance.  --RiE. Ls

In the Spring of 1982, pulicology  sprang from the laboratory  into the lime-
light for a few months. It all began when Mr. Robert Hullihan  published  in the
Des Moines [Iowa] REGISTER  a series of interviews  with a number of Iowa citizens
which he entitled  "Focus on a Foremost  Authority".*  One of these interviews  was
with Prof. Robert Lewis and discussed  his work on fleas, publication  of FLEA
NEWS, and Prof. Lewis's  aspirations  to build a data bank of Siphonaptera  informa-
tion with computer  resources.  The ink on the newsprint  was scarcely  dry when a
reporter  from the WALL STREET JOURNAL,  a prestigious  financial  newspaper  with
national  circulation,  telephoned  to request  an interview.  Ms Sue Shellenbarger
arrived  on April 1, and the fruits of her pen appeared  May 13 on page 1 of the
WALL STREET JOUNAL. The article  is reprinted  in this issue of FLEA NEWS. Ms
Shellenbarger  also consulted  with leading  authorities  R. Traub, M. Rothschild,
and W. L. Jellison. In addition  to those mentioned  in the article,  we under-
stand she also consulted  with C. Hopla and N. Gratz. Her article  succeeded  very
well in presenting  the state of the science  in pulicology.
Immediately  upon publication  of the article,  Prof. Lewis was flooded  with
telephone  calls from friends,  radio stations,  and people with flea problems  all
across the United States. The letters  began coming a few days later. If ever
anyone doubted  the problems  fleas cause for pets and their owners,  he has only
to view the stack of correspondence  from persons  seeking  advice for eradicating,
or even holding  at bay, this pesky insect.
One of those who telephoned  Prof. Lewis was a representative  from the
TONIGHT  show, an NBC-TV production  starring  Johnny Carson. The TONIGHT  show is
a late-night,  talk show entertainment  featuring  Carson and a variety  of guest
personalities.  After a telephone  interview,  Prof. Lewis was invited  to appear
on the show. Once news of this became public, there ensued another series of
interviews  for local home-town  newspapers,  and a local TV station.
Lewis flew to Los Angeles,  California,  where, on June 18, he appeared  with
Johnny Carson on the TONIGHT  show in approximately  12-15 minutes  of conversation
on fleas. As might be expected,  emphasis  was on the lighter side of the profes-
sion.
When asked about his reaction  to all the publicity,  Prof. Lewis admits to
a certain  amount of personal  satisfaction  from the attention  but, more than that,
he is pleased  that through  him entomology  and pulicology  received  the national
recognition  they deserve  - for however  brief a moment. ——JcHel «

series on his speciality  of ticks.

Like Fleabag  Hotels,
World’s  Flea Experts
Have Image  Problem
. * 7 *
And Pulicologist  Robert  Lewis
Has Bugs in a Computer;
The Rothschild  Collection
By Sug SHELLENBARGER
Staff Reporter  of THe WALL STREET  JOURNAL
AMES,  Iowa—Not  far from the bell tower
on the green, rolling campus  of Iowa State
University  is a hotbed  of sciertific  research.
In his tiny laboratory  in a university
science building,  Robert E. Lewis is sur-
rounded  by that scourge  of dog and man—
fleas. Files of 50,000 dead fleas line walls
adorned  by pictures  of fleas. Fleas arrive in
the mail. Thousands  of scholarly  articles  de-
voted to fleas fill the library. In fact, Mr.
Lewis personally  has identified  about 50 of
the 2,250-odd  flea-species  known  to man, pri-
marily by examining  the genitalia  of male
fleas.
Those achievements  make Mr. Lewis, an
amiable  52-year-old  professor  of entomology
whose graying mustache  curls into neatly
waxed tips, one of the world’s leading ex-
perts on fleas. And his laboratory  has be-
come a clearinghouse  for research  by the
world’s flea buffs—all  150 of them. “Not
very many people work on this particular  in-
sect on a world-wide  basis, and no one to the
extent that we do,” he says.
Still, Mr. Lewis and an assistant,  ‘his
wife, Joanne, keep up with research  on the
pesky flea and publish lists of new work in
Flea News, a scholarly  semiannual  newspa-
per for pulicologists—flea  experts. The un-
pretentious,  stapled bulletin  is sent free of
charge  to 150 loyal readers  in 39 natiens..
Fleas’ Diseases
Flea News subscribers  take the publica-
tion seriously,  for where else can they find
bibliographic  listings of such scholarly  arti-
cles as ‘Characteristics  of the Ectoparasite
Fauna of the Mouse-like  Water Rodents  of
Water-oak  Stands in the Central  Part of the
Byelorussian  Polyes’ya’’?
“There aren't many of us nuts working
‘on these kinds of things, so we have to talk
to one another,”  says Robert Traub, a mi-
crobiology  professor at the University  of
Maryland  and a leading  expert on fleas and
the diseases  they transmit.But Mr. Lewis, a trim man in bifocals,
also exploits what he calls “the opportuni-
ties for levity’ that his profession  affords.  A
Mark Twain quote, ‘Fleas can be taught to
do nearly everything  that a Congressman
can,” embellishes  Flea News 21. Sand-
wiched  between  scholarly  listings in a bibli-
ography  in the same issue is the following
citation: ‘‘Anonymous—Flea  pulls 200,000
times its own weight. Natl. Enquirer 55
(14) :32-33 (11 Nov.) (color picture).’’  The
photograph  cited shows the star of a Euro-
pean flea circus harnessed  to a 1%-ounce
toy locomotive  and struggling across a
man’s fingernail..
Certainly,  research  shows that the flea
can do wondrous  things. Consider  a 1973 ar-
ticle in Scientific  American  by noted British
flea expert Miriam Rothschild  and others.
The oriental rat flea, best known for its cen-
tral role in killing one of every three Euro-
peans during the 14th Century  by transmit-
ting bubonic plague from rats to humans,
also is a marathon  hopper,  the article says.
If stimulated  by the society of other fleas, it
will jump as much as 100 times its length 10
times a minute for 72 hours without pause.
Some fleas have been seen jumping  about on
Alpine snows. Others can survive  for months
frozen under the ice of Antarctica,  accord-
ing to the article. Although  fleas spin and
somersault  as they leap into the air, they
land on their feet 78% of the time, appar-
ently by spreading  their legs as they de-
scend. (Pity the research  scientist  who had
to calculate  that statistic.) “If we were as
strong as a flea, we could jump over the
Empire State Building in one leap,’ ob-
serves Mr. Traub.
Protective  Helmets?
Fleas’ remarkable  saltatorial  ability may
spring from body parts once devoted to
flight. The bodies of fleas are so cluttered
with tiny and complex  structures  as to force
scientists  intent on classifying  them to write
descriptions  several pages long. Some fleas,
for example,  have helmets—probably  not, as
it may seem, to protect  their little heads the
22% of the time they don’t land on their feet,
but rather to use in clinging  to the hairs of
their hosts. (Helmeted  fleas have been found
only in Australia  and South America,  flea
experts  point out, which supports  the theory
of continental  drift—the idea that South
America  and Australia  were once part of a
much larger  combined  land mass.)
One noted flea scholar even suggested
that fleas can sing. In an article entitled in
part ‘‘The Song of the Flea,"’ Dutch entomol-
ogist Franciscanus  G.A.M. Smit wrote that
the musical ability of fleas with certain
types of back legs should be explored.  TheWALL STREET JOURNAL
insects may produce  sound. by rubbinz  leg
parts against  body parts. But it would seem
not to matter  to the fleas. ‘Fleas  don’t have
ears,"’ Mr. Lewis explains.  They still may
perceive  sound; there's  a debate  about that.
Mr. Lewis's studies have taken a morepractical  turn. After earning  his doctorate
from the University  of Illinois  with a disser-
tation on the thoracic  muscles  of the flea, heand Mrs. Lewis—better  known as Mike—set
out to classify  the fleas of the Middle Kastand to identify their hosts. During  a stint
with American  University  at Beirut, Leba-
non, and in trips financed  by the National
Institutes  of Health, the Office of Naval Re-search, and an oil company,  Mr. Lewis has
trotted  the globe, from the ancient  capital  ofBalkh in Afghanistan  to the Syrian city ofPalmyra,  once an outpost of the Roman
Empire.
“I'm not much for ruins, but they’re  goodplaces to catch rats’ and their fleas, Mr.Lewis says.
In the field, the host animal  is trapped  orshot and popped into a bag. Then the fleapopulace  is quickly chloroformed  and pre-served  in alcohol  or slapped  between  labora-
tory slides. Such expeditions  have led to the
classification  of more than 2,000 new flea
Species in this century.  To keep them all
straight,  Mr. Lewis has arranged  to pro-gram the university  computer  to answer
flea questions  with data from his library.
For example,  a student might ask howmany different  types of fleas inhabit themountain  beaver, a small rodent in theWestern U.S. The answer: four unusually
large ones. The system still is being pro-grammed,  Mr. Lewis says. “We're  trying towork the bugs out. And I don’t mean the
fleas.”
Mr. Lewis plans to applyto a grantingagency  to finance  the project.  Alas, for him,
classifying  and documenting  fleas increas-
ingly is taking a back seat in financing  and
prestige  to curing  cancer  and splicing  genes.
In fact, ‘‘ribbing  from your friends”  is an
occupational  hazard of pulicology,  Mr.
Lewis says. Flea experts,  like flea markets
and fleabag  hotels, aren't among  the elite of
their realm. There is also the actual risk of
getting flea-bitten.  Mr. Lewis has escaped
the bites of his prey, despite his luxuriant
gray beard, but Mrs. Lewis has been inhab-
ited by unwanted  guests in a Turkish hotel
and in a Syrian market.  The couple’s  dogs
came down with a bad case of cat fleas last
summer.  ‘‘It was quite an embarrassment,”
Mr. Lewis says, neglecting  to mention
whether  he means  for him or the dogs.
Indeed, dog and cat fleas are the ones
most familiar  to most people.  The cat flea is
the more adaptable  and widespread  of the
two, and it is the type found most often,
even on dogs. The pests are most populous
in warm climates  because they can breedyear-round,  indoors  and out. In cold regions,
the larval stages die in winter unless thefleas can breed indoors.  Thus, Southern  Cal-
ifornia, Florida and the South are most af-fected.
Sometimes,  fleas do infest people. “If
there's  not a pet for them to jump on, when
they're hungry they'll bite human  beings,”
Mr. Lewis says. In California,  many peoplehave taken to spraying  their lawns with in-
Secticides  to rid them of fleas. The insects
can transmit  tapeworm  to human beings,
but that doesn't occur often. One must eat
the flea for that to happen.
Serious flea research  has come a longway in the past century.  Naturalist  Nathan-
iel Charles  Rothschild  of the British  bankingfamily, was the first to describe  the type ofrat flea that was the major transmitter  ofplague  to humans.  When he died in 1923, heleft the world’s largest  collection  of fleas tothe British Museum.  His daughter,  Miriam,carried  on the family  interest  in fleas.
In 1914, scientists  demonstrated  how fleas
transmit  plague to human beings, and the
disease,  thanks to antibiotics,  is now largelyunder  control.  It afflicts  roughly  2,000 peoplein the world each year. Plague remains  asensitive  political topic, however. (Egypt,mistaking  a city for a nation, quarantined“the country  of Denver”  for a day in 1968after a case of Plague  was reported  in Colo-rado.) Public-health  officials  insist that re-Search  on fleas and the variety  of afflictionsthey transmit,  including  tularemia  and tape-worm,  is still important.
Nevertheless,  Pulicologists’  numbers  aredwindling.  “People  are getting involved  inmore spectacular  stuff like molecular  biol-_ogy,” says Maryland  professor  Traub. ‘‘Icould fly to the moon taxonomically  and noone would care.” Flea experts who retireare seldom  replaced.
Still, new flea frontiers  remain to be ex-plored. Mr. Lewis is itching  to document  the
fleas of South America, but “those guysdown there are too wrapped  up in politics”
to support the proper flea research,  he la-
ments. ‘‘What we really need is a good out-break of bubonic plague,”  he jokes, ‘“‘andeverybody  will start paying attention  to usagain.”
William L. Jellison, a retired Hamilton,
Mont., scientist who did flea research for
the government,  couldn’t agree more. He
has amassed  a great collection  of fleas from
animals ranging from dead grizzlies and
mountain  lions to skunks  and squirrels.  But
after 20 years of trying,  Mr. Jellison,  a FleaNews subscriber,  hasn’t been able to unloadhis collection  to museums  or universities,  “I
Still have 2,000 fleas here,” he Says, “It's achallenge  to get rid of this stuff.”

WALL STREET JOURNAL  article,  the following  poem was received.
by William  J. Brown, M.D., of Wellesley  Hills, Massachusetts,  and he has kindly
granted  permission  to reprint  it in FLEA NEWS.
FLEAS
To study pulicology
You first must find a willing  flea,
But fleas don't willingly  enlist
To aid a pulicologist.
Devising  flea taxonomy
Requires  attention  to detail;
The crucial  factor seems to be
The sex equipment  of the male.
There must be dire necessity
To prompt such curious  travail.
Such tactics  used on you or me
Would seem a bit beyond the pale.
To undergo  such scrutiny
Is really not my cup of tea.
When probings  such as these prevail
I'm glad I'm me and not a flea.
The flea inhabits  many lands.
He's found, in varied size and form,
From snowy peaks to desert sands,
But favors places where it's warm.
He has no wings with which to fly
And when he walks he barely creeps.
Important  moves are chiefly by
Prodigious  catapulting  leaps.
He rolls and tumbles  through  the air;
He's apt to land most any place.
And where he lands he doesn't  care;
He sometimes  lands upon his face.
He jumps again, and after that
He jumps again with all his might
Until he finds a dog or cat
Of whom he takes a juicy bite.
The flea in shrouded  mystery
Has spread the dread bubonic  plague
And changed  the course of history
As much as Kissinger  or Haig.It was written
They say a few of them can sing;
But then, of course, they have no ears.
It seems a quite preposterous  thing!
What good is music no one hears?
This singing  business  lacks the ring
Of truth. To me it all appears
Some overzealous  ding-a-ling
Has soaked up one too many beers.
If you need fleas identified
I hope you'll use this little guide.
If I were you, however,  I'd
Employ a strong insecticide.

RECENTLY PUBLISHED ~ Mammalian Biology ain South America edited by M. A.
Mares and H. H. Genoways, 1982. (ISBN 0-931796-06-7) Contributions  at a
Symposium held at the Pymatuning  Laboratory of Ecology, May 10-14, 1981.
Volume 6. Special Publication  Series, Pymantuning  Laboratory of Ecology,
Linesville,  PA 16424 USA. 539 pp- U.S. $30.00.
To review each of the 27 contributions  published in this attractive volume
would be impractical since each deals with a separate subject. The first 10
articles treat the reader to a review of mammalogical  research in South America
and include reviews of mammalian biology during the last decade, current status
of South American mammalogy, and a series of papers on ecology, geography,
biogeography,  and faunal origins and affinities. All of the remaining papers
put the last two deal with such diverse subjects as the biogeography  of South
American  bats, evolution  of marsupials,  diversity  and adaptation  in hystrico-
gnath rodents,  biology  of Neotropical  primates  and camelids,  population  biol-
ogy, physiological  ecology,  behavioral  research,  and conservation.
The final two sections  are roundtables  wherein  a number of contributors
address  the issues of conservation  in South American  mammals  and research  pri-
orities in South America. Not surprisingly,  the latter statements  emphasize
education,  conservation,  and faunal research  as being foremost  among many pri-
orities. Massive  habitat  destruction  in recent times has brought  many species
to the brink of extinction,  and for some of these the time may have passed when
conservation  measures  would be effective.
While there is no mention  of parasites  in any of the presentations,  the
volume as a whole contains  a wealth of information  about a fascinating  part of
the world. Of particular  value to the pulicologist  are the articles  dealing
with classification  and biogeography.  The book is printed  in an attractive
format on high quality  paper, is well bound and remarkably  free of mechanical
flaws. For a publication  of this quality  the price is astoundingly  low. -R.E.L.

TRAUB HONORED - A SYMPOSIUM  entitled  "Topics in the Natural History  of
Some Vector-Borne  Infections"  was held at the University  of Maryland  School
of Medicine,  Baltimore,  on Saturday,  19 November  1983, in honor of Professor
ROBERT TRAUB. The program  was moderated  by Dr. C. L. Wisseman,  Jr., Chairman
of the Department  of Microbiology,  University  of Maryland,  and included  the
following  presentations:
"Comparison  of the prevalence  of murine typhus and Hantaan  virus in
Egyptian  rodents"  by Harry Hoogstraal
"Pheromones  and the biology  of disease transmitting  ticks" by Daniel
E. Sonenshine
"Spiroplasmas,  vectors and history"  by Karl Maramorosch
"Biotic relationships  among the southern  landmasses"  by R. E. Lewis
"Distributional  patterns  of the rodents of Africa"  by Duane A. Schlitter
The symposium  was followed  by a social hour and banquet attended  by
approximately  80 friends and family. Several of Prof. Traub's colleagues
recalled  incidents  and accomplishments  from the days when they had worked with
him on one or mote of his projects. Prof. Traub was presented  with a book of
letters from many of his friends and coworkers. The Honourable  Miriam Roth-
schild presented  him with the first bound copy of their joint work on cerato-
phyllid fleas, due to be released  officially  on 20 December  1983. A review of
this study is planned  for FLEA NEWS 28.
Although  Prof. Traub is retiring  from his administrative  duties at the
University  of Maryland,  he plans to continue  his research  activities  there and
at the National  Museum of Natural  History. FLEA NEWS is proud to have partici-
pated in this celebration  of Prof. Traub, and joins his other friends  in wishing
him many productive  years of research  in the future. ---R.E.L.  & J.H.L.

Istvan Szabd is 70 years old
Istvan $zab6 was born in Budapest on the 13th of June, 1913. He worked in
business administration  until 1957, when he joined the Department  of Zoology
of the Hungarian  Natural History Museum. His early scientific  papers dealt
with amphibians  and reptiles, but later on almost exclusively  with fleas. Lt
was Mr. $zab6 who established  the Parasitological  Collection  of the Department
of Zoology of the Hungarian  Natural History Museum, where he worked as curator
until his retirement  in 1975. He has continued  his studies since retirement.
We wish to congratulate  Mr. Szabo on the occasion of his 70th birthday!
