RECENTLY  PUBLISHED  - Walker's  Mammals  of the Worid, 4th Edition  by R. M.
Nowak and J. L. Paradiso,  1983. (ISBN 0-8018-2525-3)  The Johns Hopkins  Univer-
sity Press (Baltimore  and London),  Vol. I, i-xliv, 1-568 (xlvii-lxi);  Vol. II,
i-vii, 569-1362  (xi-xxv). US$65.00  (2 volume set).
Very often, the appearance  of a new edition  of a text involves  little more
than a different  binding,  an additional  preface,  and an increase  in price. Not
so with this monumental  revision  of Ernest P. Walker's  classic,  Mammals  of the
World, which first appeared  in 1964 with subsequent  editions  in 1968 and 1975.
This new edition  incorporates  major changes  in format and content. While the
overall  length of the text has been expanded  by almost 50 per cent, the physical
size of the volumes  remains  approximately  the same. About 90 per cent of the
generic  accounts  have been substantively  altered  and many have been completely
rewritten.
In this edition,  the authors  have broken with the tradition  of treating  each
genus on a single page and have expanded  accounts  of the genera where more data
were available.  Sections  covering  the physical  description  of the genera remain
the same as in earlier  editions  but the remaining  text has been transmogrified.
Accounts  of the orders and families  precede  the generic  accounts  and include
information  applicable  to all members  of the group. Where possible,  generic
accounts  include: scientific  and common name, number and distribution  of the
species,  measurements,  physical  description,  habitat,  locomotion,  daily and
seasonal  activity,  diet, population  dynamics,  home range, social life, repro-
duction,  longevity,  and interactions  with humans. No emphasis  has been placed
on internal  anatomy,  physiology,  genetics,  laboratory  experimentation,  parasit-
ology, pathology,  or paleontology.  The World Distribution  Charts at the begin-
ning of Volume I have been revised  to reflect  changes  in taxonomy  and distribu-
tional information.  Approximately  350 new photographs  are included,  either to
replace  or supplement  earlier  illustrations,  and approximately  100 additional
genera have been illustrated.
An innovation  over earlier  editions  is the inclusion  of species  lists.
Where possible,  these are arranged  in systematic  order, including  subgenera
where designated.  Where this information  was lacking,  the species  are listed
alphabetically.
The total number of taxonomic  categories  accepted  in this edition  are: 19
orders, 134 families,  1018 genera, and 4154 species. The authors  consider
coverage  of descriptions  of new species  and major taxonomic  revisions  complete
to the end of 1979, but much information  published  through  late 1981 is included.
---continued  next page
The volumes  are attractively  printed  on an excellent  grade of paper which
greatly  improves  the quality  of the photographic  reproduction.  The end papers
contain  comparisons  of U.S. and metric measurements,  but only metric units are
used in the text. The type size has been greatly  reduced  to accommodate  for the
expanded  text, but this certainly  does not detract  from the attractiveness  of
the printed  page.
It is evident  that the authors  were devoted  to the task of revising  this
monumental  work, and in doing so have greatly  improved  its usefulness,  especi-
ally to the nonspecialist.  While the price might at first seem high, close
examination  of these two volumes  should convince  the reader that they would be
a bargain  at twice the price. ---R.E.L.

OBITUARY
C. Andresen  Hubbard
10-XII-1897 30-IV-1984
It was with considerable  sadness  that we were informed  by Mrs. C. A. Hub-
bard of the death of her husband.
Dr. Hubbard  was born at Davenport,  Iowa, and christened  Clarence  Albert.
In 1904 his family moved to Portland,  Oregon,  where he graduated  from the
public school system in 1917. The same year he enrolled  in the University  of
Washington,  Seattle,  receiving  his Bachelor  of Education  degree in 1920 with
a minor in Zoology. From 1920 to 1922 he was a teaching  fellow at the Univer-
sity of Washington.  In 1922 he assumed  the position  of Head of the Biology
Department,  Pacific  University,  Forest Grove, Oregon, functioning  in this
capacity  until 1942. During this period he continued  his graduate  education
and, in 1932, earned a double Masters degree in Education  and Zoology  from
the University  of Washington.  In 1937 he was awarded  the degree of Doctor of
Science  by Pacific University  for his dissertation  entitled  "Fleas of Western
North America",  which formed the basis for his book of the same title published
by the Iowa State College  Press in 1947. He was a biologist  with Vanport  Col-
lege (now known as Portland  State University),  Portland,  Oregon, from 1943 to
1946 and in 1944 became Head of the Department  of Biology  at Warner Pacific
College,  Portland,  occupying  this position  until 1962. During this period he
received  a Fulbright  grant to study fleas and plague in Iraq (1953) and subse-
quently  a National  Science  Foundation  grant to study the fleas of northern
California  and East Africa. On another  Fulbright  grant in 1962 he went to the
Malaria  Institute  at Amani, Tanga, Tanzania,  where he initiated  studies  on

fleas and plague in that area. These studies were further supported  from 1962
to 1967 by another grant from the National Science Foundation. In July 1967,
he entered retirement  at Tigard, a suburb of Portland,  Oregon.
During his professional  career Dr. Hubbard published  61 papers, 51 of
which dealt with fleas or related subjects (see Flea News 26 for bibliography) .
He also described  76 new flea taxa on the species level, 15 of which are cur-
rently considered  to be junior synonyms. He erected 3 genera, Augustonius,
Corypsylloides  and Foxelloides,  all of which are currently  considered  to be
synonyms.
In his later years Dr. Hubbard, or simply Hubbard, as he signed his let-
ters, always insisted that fleas were secondary to him and that his main inter-
ests resided in their mammalian  hosts. In spite of this, the bulk of his pub-
lications  dealt with the flea fauna of the western United States, and his is
the only comprehensive  review of this fauna that has ever been published.
Hubbard was an excellent  field mammalogist,  returning to collecting  local-
ities often to add additional  records of the rarer species. He was occasionally
mildly criticized  by some of his colleagues  for his use of the vernacular  in
his writings, but they have stood the test of time and have yet to be replaced
by superior  works.
In the wordsof a colleague  who knew him personally,  "Hubbard was a great
old gentleman  and I will miss him and his interesting  letters".

RECENTLY  PUBLISHED  - The Rothschild  Collection  of Fleas. The Ceratophyl-
lidae: Key to the genera and host relationships.  With notes on their evolution,
zoogeography  and medical importance  by R. Traub, M. Rothschild  and J. F. Haddow,
1983. (ISBN 0-12-697680-5)  Cambridge  University  Press/Academic  Press (Cam-
bridge and London), i-xv, 288 pp. + 90 pls., 205 figs., 175 maps (X 60.00,
$99.00)
It has generally  been assumed  that the last volumes  of the monumental
Catalogue  of the Rothschild  Collection  of Fleas by G.H.E. Hopkins  and M. Roth-
schild would treat the complex  family Ceratophyllidae.  It has also been as~-
sumed that at least two and, more likely, three volumes  would be required  to
cover the entire family. Early works by Jordan (1933), Wagner (1934) and loff
(1936) began the process  of bringing  order to the family, but these authors suf-
fered from lack of material  and knowledge  of the world fauna as we know it
today. For example,  Ioff stated that he examined  only 69 species. Since 1936
over 400 additional  ceratophyllid  species  have been described.  For these and
other reasons,  the authors of the volume reviewed  here deemed it impractical  to
follow the Catalogue  format established  in the preceding  six volumes  and this is
not to be considered  as part of the Catalogue  series. The result is an assem-
blage of articles  by various  authors,  or combinations  thereof,  which seems
likely to confound  pulicologists  and bibliographers  alike for generations  to
come. Although  of somewhat  smaller dimensions  than the Catalogue  volumes,  the
title is very similar and the binding identical  in both substance  and color.
Beyond these minor criticisms,  the book contains  a wealth of information
and certainly  represents  the best synthesis  of information  for any family of
the order Siphonaptera.  Due to the varied nature of the different  sections,
it seems appropriate  to review them separately.  After a brief Introduction
describing  the scope of the volume, data arrangement,  explanation  of maps and
map captions,  data limitations  and notes on the higher classification  of the
order, are Acknowledgements  and the following  sections.
SMIT, F.G.A.M. 1983
Key to the genera and subgenera  of Ceratophyllidae.  pp. 1-36. 250 figs. 90 pls.
This section  begins with a brief characterization  of the family and a com-
parison of it with the Leptopsyllidae.  Following  this are notes on the morph-
ology of members of the family, beginning  with the cranium  and concluding  with
the modified  abdominal  segments  in both sexes. Then come descriptions  of the
7 new genera and 8 new subgenera  erected  here, and a key to the genera and sub-
genera currently  recognized  as belonging  to the family. After each genus are
listed all of the valid species,  with the generitype  or subgeneritype  indicated
by an asterisk  (*). The 250 figures are grouped at the end of the key. After
these come 90 plates, each containing  5-6 superbly  retouched  photographs  of a
representative  species of each genus and subgenus,  arranged  in alphabetic  order.
Those familiar  with recent illustrated  works by Traub are well aware of the
effectiveness  of such illustrations,  and presumably  these were contributed  by
Dr. Traub for use in this volume.
TRAUB, R., M. ROTHSCHILD  & J. F. HADDOW 1983
Definition  of zoogeographical  areas. pp. 37-41
In this section the authors follow the classical  arrangement  of zoogeo-
graphical  regions put forward by Bartholomew,  Eagle Clarke and Grimshaw (1911)
in their Atlas of Zoogeography,  with the addition  of a Wallacean  Region for
Celebes,  Timor, Flores, Sumba, Halmahere,  Ceram and Buru. . Only some of the
-125-
subregions  from this source are recognized  and these, along with a number of new
subdivisions,  are designated  as "sectors".
HADDOW, J. F., R. TRAUB & M. ROTHSCHILD 1983
Distribution  of ceratophyllid  fleas and notes on their hosts. Material  in the
collection,  with additional  notes and maps of the genera. pp. 42-163 + 151 maps
This section treats geographic  and host-distribution,  arranged  alphabeti-
cally by genus and species. Each generic account is accompanied  by a small,
unnumbered  map showing the general distribution  of the genus. Species accounts
include the following  information:  name; authority;  date; generic,  specific  and
subspecific  abbreviation  (in cases where the species is the generitype  this is
indicated);  map reference  number; number of specimens  mounted and if alcoholic
material  is present in the collection.  Under this are listed the major host(s),
general geographic  distribution,  ecological  associations  and host records. Under
the latter heading,  hosts are indicated  as major(M),  specific(S),  occasional(0),
or accidental(A).  Also in this category,  distinction  is made between those
host records based on material  in the British  Museum (N.C. Rothschild)  collection
and those drawn from the literature.
The 151 maps at the end of this section are printed in light blue. Many of
the maps show the ranges of various  hosts with collection  records of their fleas
superimposed  in black symbols of different  shapes. Where the ranges of more than
2 host species overlap, the combination  of blue ink and reduction  causes the maps
to be extremely  difficult  to interpret.
TRAUB, R. 1983
The hosts of ceratophyllid  fleas. pp. 164-187 with 9 tables in text.
This section is an exhaustive  treatment  of the origins, distribution  and
host preferences  of both the Ceratophyllidae  and the Leptopsyllidae.  Both are
mainly limited to the northern  hemisphere  and this treatment  presents  impressive
evidence  supporting  the thesis that ceratophyllids  evolved in the Nearctic
Region as parasites  of squirrels  and their relatives,  while leptopsyllids
evolved in the Palaearctic  Region and now mainly parasitize  cricetine  and
microtine  rodents.
TRAUB, R. & M. ROTHSCHILD 1983
Evolution  of the Ceratophyllidae.  pp. 188-201
Many of the points which were made in the preceding  section are reempha-
sized in this section with particular  attention  being directed  to ceratophyllid
morphology,  taxonomy  and phylogeny,  physiology  and behavior,  and geological  age.
The authors conclude that the family is of Nearctic  origin and originated  in the
early Oligocene  (38-40 million years ago), co-evolved  with squirrels,  and only
later did some become parasites  of cricetid  rodents and birds.
TRAUB, R. 1983
Medical importance  of the Ceratophyllidae.  pp. 202-228 with 2 tables in text.
After a brief introduction,  the author sets down 23 factors affecting
epidemiology  as concerning  outbreaks  of epidemics  or epizootics.  These are
followed  by a consideration  of the effects of these epidemiological  factors.
The various types of infectious  agents (i.e. bacterial,  rickettsial  and viral)
are then reviewed  and discussed. It is concluded  that ceratophyllid  fleas are
of little importance in the transmission  of disease to humans, but that they
play their most important  role in maintaining  cycles of infection  in the
reservoir  hosts, particularly  rodents. .
The volume ends with 5 appendices.  Presumably  all 3 authors  participated
in these compilations,  except for number 4 which was written  solely  by M.Rothschild.  Their titles are self-explanatory.
1. Species  described  since 1975. p. 229
2. Classification  of hosts treated  in text. pp. 230-232
3. Alphabetical  lists of hosts cited, showing  their major ceratophyl-
lid fleas (if any). pp. 233-252
4. Distribution  of British  Ceratophyllidae.  Pp. 253, plus maps 152-175
5. List of taxa of Ceratophyllidae  treated  in this volume. pp- 254-268
Index to fleas cited. pp. 269-288
Workers  accustomed  to the standardized  format of the Catalogue  volumes  mayfind this volume difficult  to use until they become familiar  with its organiza-
tion. However,  in addition  to the obvious  usefulness  of the generic  key andthe species  accounts,  there is a wealth of information  contained  in the othersections  unparalleled  in any other volume dealing  with the order. The authorsshould be congratulated  for their persistence  and dedication  to the production

Limited,  6 All Saints Street,  London  Nl 9RL, U.K. 237 pp. (Distributed  in theUnited States and Canada  by The D.H. Wilson  Company,  950 University  Avenue,

A frequent  frustration  among specialists  is the difficulty  of locating
peripheral  information  relating  to one's specialty.  Entomology,  being the
broad discipline  that it is, is particularly  productive  of such frustration.
At last, in one relatively  small volume,  is a wealth of information  on such
diverse  subjects  as insects  in art, literature  and gastronomy;  nomenclators
and catalogues;  dictionaries  and glossaries;  laboratory  culture  and mass rearing;
sources  of illustrative  materials;  books and review  articles;  computerized
information  retrieval;  newsletters  and conference  calendars  (Ms Gilbert  is on
the FN mailing  list); learned  societies  and professional  organizations;  trans-
lation services  and guides, and many other topics. As stated in the Preface
",...the  work is intended  to be an introduction  and source book for entomology
by subject...",  and this goal as been admirably  attained. The contents  are
arranged  in 8 chapters:  1. Introduction;  2. Naming and identification  of
insects;  3. Specimens  and collections;  4. The literature  of entomology;
5. Searching  and locating  the literature;  6. Keeping  up with current  events;
7. Entomologists  and their organizations;  and 8. Miscellaneous  services.
Each chapter  or subdivision  contains  a brief introductory  statement  followed
by consecutively  numbered  listings  including  annotations.  Addresses  are
included  for all organizations,  a practice  seldom followed  in similar  publica-
tions of this type.
The authors  are to be congratulated  for their devotion  to the field of
Entomology  and their demonstrated  good taste in including  an illustration  of
a flea (Spilopsyllus  cuniculi)  on the cover. ---R.E.L.

NEW JOURNAL  - Acta Zoologica  Mexicana  is a new series begun by the Instituto
de Ecologia,  Mexico,  D.F. It will include  papers dealing  with behavior,  ecology,
systematics  and zoogeography  of the North American  fauna. Submissions  may be in
Spanish,  Portuguese,  English  or French, and should include  a summary  in either
Spanish  or English. The Instituto  expects  to produce  a minimum  of six issues
per year. Manuscripts  will be reviewed  by an international  editorial  committee.

CONGRATULATIONS  - Wolfgang  Dorow has been awarded the Diploma  of Biology
from the University  of Frankfurt,  West Germany,  for his work about Siphonaptera
and Protocalliphora  in the nests of the Great and Blue Tits (Parus major, Parus
caeruleus).  His work deals with abiotic and biotic factors affecting  the flea
population  in a bird's nest, with the influence  of the parasites  on the host.
Also, methods of sampling  fleas out of birds' nests, sex-ratio  and strategies
of host-finding  and parasite-avoidance  are discussed.
* * *
Prof. J. C. Beaucournu  has reported  the successful  completion  of the
doctorate  degree from the University  of Rennes by his student,  JEAN DEUNFF, in
May of this year. Prof. Beaucournu  kindly presented  us with a copy of Dr.
Deunff's  dissertation  entitled  "Parasites  de Siphonaptéres",  pp. 406. Our
congratulations  to Dr. Deunff and our thanks for this addition  to our library.

The 35th International  Science  Fair took place at Ohio State University,
Columbus,  May 7-13, 1984. There were 585 entries, 17 of which were entomological
in nature. The Entomological  Society  of America  made three cash awards, one of
which was won by Julie Blake, 14, Suwanee High School, Live Oak, Florida, for
her project Controlling  the Common Cat Flea. The other winners  were from England
and Puerto Rico for projects  on climbing  ability  of cockroaches  and the life
cycle of Sevicocer  krugii. .

GOOD-BYE
Having finished  the manuscript  and illustrations  for Volume VII (the last
of the series, dealing with Malacopsyllidae  and Rhopalopsyllidae)  of the Roth-
schild Flea Catalogue,  I am now saying a final farewell  to the Magnificent
Fleas - and to all magnificent  colleagues. --- I shall certainly  look back in
gratitude.
Special thanks are due to my good friends, Bob & Joanne Lewis, for so suc-
cessfully  continuing  to issue Flea News (I hope to remain on the mailing list
in order to be kept informed  of what is or will be going on in the Flea World).
It gives me pleasure  to announce,  with relief, that the Flea Collection  in
the British Museum (Natural  History),  London, has now been placed in the good
care of Miss Annette Thomas. Please, do henceforth  send reprints  of your publi-
cations to her as well as requests,  etc.
Frans G. A. M. Smit

Professor LIU CHI-YING feted on the occasion of his 80th birthday -
Recently a celebration  was sponsored by the authorities of the Academy of Mil-
itary Medical Sciences, Beijing, the Peoples’ Republic of China, in honor of
Professor Liu Chi-ying for his contributions  to the fields of entomological
research and teaching, on the occasion of his 80th birthday. Approximately
180 colleagues and friends attended and congratulatory  speeches were delivered
by Dr. Chu H.-f£., President of the Entomological  Society of China, and Prof.
Kwan Z.-h., President of the Entomological  Society of Beijing.
Professor Liu was born on 24 March 1905, in Mutu, near Lake Tai, west of
Soochow, Kiangsu Province. He graduated from the University of Nanking in
1929. In 1933 he entered the graduate program of the Department of Entomology
& Economic Zoology at the University of Minnesota, St. Paul, where he studied
under Dr. William A. Riley, a medical entomologist and parasitologist,  earning
an M.S. degree. Upon returning to China he taught entomology and zoology,
first at the National Chekian University and later at the National Kwansi
University. Some years after the liberation he joined the Institute of Micro-
biology and Epidemiology,  Academy of Military Medical Sciences, Beijing, where
he resumed his researches in medical entomology, particularly  in taxonomic
studies on the Siphonaptera  of China.
During his 50 some years of active service, Professor Liu has received
many honors and has published in excess of 150 technical papers. Currently,
-1L61-
under the auspices  of the Editorial  Committee  of Fauna Sinica, Academia  Sinica,
he is editing  a Monograph  of the Order Siphonaptera  (of China) which is now in
press.
The editors  of Flea News join the many friends  and colleagues  of Professor
Liu in congratulating  him for his many years of service  to his profession  and in
wishing  him health, happiness,  and many more years of productivity.
Information  used here was provided  in a brief biography  of Professor  Liu
included  in a letter from Professors  Wang Dun-qing  and Wu Hou-yong  dated 17
April 1985.

NOTES ON THE CONSTRUCTION  OF A KEY TO CERATOPHYLLINE  GENERA *
* Key published  in: R. Traub, M. Rothschild  & J. Haddow, 1984, The Rothschild
collection  of fleas. The Ceratophyllidae.  pp. 1-36, 205 figs.
Merely on the basis of the chaetotaxy  of part of the outer side of the fore
femur and of the inner side of the mid and hind coxa, Jordan (1933) divided
Ceratophyllid  genera of the Old and New World into three groups; the distinctions
are no longer tenable. Toff (1936), with limited  material,  divided  some 20
genera/subgenera  into six major groups ("Subtriben")  within the family ("Tribus")
and left three "aberrant"  genera ungrouped.
Families  of fleas are divided  into subfamilies  on the basis of only non-
genitalic  characters  (such as cranial  structure,  frontal  tubercle,  eye, genal
ctenidium,  labial palp, antenna,  pleural  rod of mesothorax,  pleural  ridge of
metathorax,  striarium  on metepimeron  or basal sternum,  chaetotaxy  of coxa, tibia
and distitarsomere,  chaetotaxy  of terga, tergal ctenidia  and spinelets,  ante-
sensilial  setae, sensilium  and anal stylet of female). These non-genitalic
structures  are on the whole fairly uniform  in Ceratophyllids  and I have been
unable to divide this large 'family'  into satisfactory  'subfamilies'.  Certain
of the genera form reasonably  neat seemingly  natural  groups but if one were to
designate  such groups as subfamilies,  quite a large residue  of ungroupable
genera  would be left, several  of which deserving  a subfamily  status of their own.
Stark (1970) remarked  that "Apparently  having undergone  recent evolutionary
radiation,  this compact  group [Ceratophyllidae]  shows few phylogenetic  gaps.
Dividing  the family and defining  subfamilies  and tribes is thus difficult,
~162-
A few years ago I demoted this presumed  family to subfamily  status and
placed Ceratophyllinae  alongside  Amphipsyllinae  and Leptopsyllinae  in Cerato-
phyllidae;  Ischnopsyllidae and. Ceratophyllidae  together  constituting..the
superfamily  Ceratophylloidea  (Smit, 1982, in: Synopsis  and classification  of
living organisms. New York.” pp. 557-563, pls. 121, 122).
In constructing  a key to genera and subgenera  I have tried to consider
all morphological  characters  - not just a selection  - of most of the species
concerned. It was found that numerous  structures  are either too stable or too
variable  for generic usage. Tangible  differences  are not seldom elusive
(occasionally  by being too obvious to attract attention).  As my tendency  is
for lumping, it was surprising  to find that no fewer than 8 new genera and 9
new subgenera  were erected during the study. Some genera are demoted to sub~
genera, no subgenera  have been promoted  to genera. Perhaps some more genera
may eventually  be treated as subgenera  or vice versa, or certain amalgamations
may take place later on. The fauna of fleas is still rather imperfectly  known
although  the northern  hemisphere,  where most of the Ceratophyllids  occur,
compares  favourably  with the southern  one.
Only about 800 hours (apart from some 300 hours used for drawing) could
be spent on this particular  task and the resulting  key to genera is definitely
not an entirely  satisfactory  one. As is usually the case, the more distinct
taxa tend to come out first in the key, the more troublesome  groups relegating |
themselves  to the rear. It will be realised that most of the eighty or so |
different  structures  mentioned  in the key will only show up in well-cleared
and well-mounted  specimens.
It is hoped that improvements  to classification  and key will gradually  be
made. A final word of advice: anyone considering  an attempt (a) to divide
the Ceratophyllinae  into satisfactory  'natural  groups', (b) to change generic
or subgeneric  definitions  or (c) to compose a better key, must realise that
this should only be done by a detailed  study of all members of the family, not
by selecting  certain  groups or geographical  regions.
F. G. A. M. Smit
RECENTLY  PUBLISHED
The Fleas of Canada, Alaska and Greenland  (Siphonaptera)  by George P. Holland,
1985. (ISSN 0071-075X) Memoirs of the Entomological  Society of Canada -
No. 130, 631 pp., 508 figs., 109 maps. (Prices in $Canadian  32.00 members,
41.00 non-members).
Workers familiar  with the 1949 publication  by this author on the Siphon-
aptera of Canada are already acquainted  with the high standard  of excellence
that Dr. Holland has maintained  throughout  his professional  career. His new
book is further evidence,  if more is needed.
As the author points out in the introduction,  " ... we have been able
to increase the total of Canadian,  Alaskan and Greenland  fleas to 183 valid
forms from the 127 species and subspecies  recorded  from Canada in 1949. Fur-
thermore,  in the 36+ years that have elapsed there have been many changes in
flea classification  and nomenclature  as well as increased  information  on dis-
tribution,  host preferences,  seasonal  abundance  and many other factors worthy
of reporting. The end result of all this is embodied  in’ the following  mono-
graph which undertakes  to summarize  all the taxonomic  information  available
on the fleas known, or suspected,  to occur within the political  boundaries  of
-163-
Canada, Alaska and Greenland,  that is, all of the New World north of the southern
border of Canada."
After the introductory  notes and acknowledgments  is a synoptic  list of the
taxa known from the area under consideration,  followed  by a tabular  distribution
by political  areas. This is followed  by a 15 page exposition  on flea anatomy
in relation  to taxonomy,  brief notes on the illustrations  and a glossary  of
abbreviaions  used in the text and the keys. The next 451 pages constitute  the
systematic  portion  of the work, to which I shall return in the next paragraph.
The book concludes  with a host/flea  index, a glossary  of collectors,  an exten-
sive reference  section,  109 distribution  maps, and an index.
In his 1949 study, Holland (p. 53) states "From the standpoint  of identi-
fication  only, an artificial  key, separating  genera by means of more readily
discernible  characters,  is far more satisfactory."  [than keys to the families
and subfamilies.]  This is the approach  followed  in the present  work, and the
systematic  section  begins with such a key to the genera and subgenera. In the
remainder  of the section,  however,  the taxa are treated  in conventional
fashion,  beginning  with a short diagnosis  of the order followed  by treatments
‘ of the infraordinal  categories  of decreasing  magnitude.  Keys to the sub-
families,  where recognized,  are provided,  as are keys to the species and sub-
species  where more than one taxon belonging  to that genus is present in the
area under consideration.  Accounts  for the genera, species,  and subspecies  all
contain  rather exhaustive  synonymy  sections  with emphasis  on the literature
dealing  with Canada, Alaska and Greenland. This is followed  by a brief dis-
cussion  of the taxon, and in the species and subspecies  accounts,  is concluded
with a "New Records"  section  which, in some cases, may be rather lengthy.
Illustrations  are interwoven  into the text in such a way as to make them readily
accessible  to the reader, a vast improvement  over the custom of including  all
illustrations  at the end of the text. Some of these were used in the 1949
volume but many have been redrawn  or are new. In all cases, the quality  of
illustration  is excellent.
The system of classification  is that followed  by most western  students  of
the order. However,  the 219 pages devoted to the Ceratophyllidae  were too far
advanced  to permit conversion  to the recent classification  of this family as
set down in Traub, Rothschild  and Haddow (1983) and the older classification
has been followed  for this family. Since new classifications  are seldom
adopted  quickly and, since all North American  workers are more familiar  with
the older classification  than they are with the new, I do not consider  this to
be a serious shortcoming.  The synoptic  list on pages 6 through 9 provides
ample room for marginal  updating  should the reader wish to do so.
In summary,  Dr. Holland  has provided  students  of the order Siphonaptera
with an invaluable  tool in continuing  studies of the fleas of North America.
Much of the book applies to the fauna of the United States as well, and since
we are currently  lacking  a comparable  volume for this area, it will doubtless
come to occupy a prominent  position  in North American  workers' libraries.
Congratulations,  George, for a job well done! =--R.E.L.

Dear Lord Rothschild. Birds, butterflies  and history by Miriam Rothschild,  1983,
(ISBN 0-86689-019-X)  Balaban Publishers  (Philadelphia/Rehovet)  i-xx, 398 pp. +
12 colored plates and 92 black & white plates.
In spite of the fact that this book has been widely reviewed  in the western
countries,  brief mention is made of it here for the benefit of colleagues  in
the east.
The central figure, as the title indicates,  is Lionel Walter Rothschild
(1868-1937),  2nd Baron Rothschild  of Tring and uncle of the author. There are,
however, other themes interwoven  with the account of this eccentric  and per-
plexing man. In short, it is a selective  history of the British branch of the
Rothschild  family, with emphasis  on Walter's contributions  in the biological
sciences  and his role in precipitating  the Balfour Declaration  which ultimately
led to the creation  of the State of Israel.
Of perhaps most interest to recipients  of Flea News is the inventory  of
natural history specimens  amassed at the Rothschild  Museum at Tring. The re-
search collection  contained  1400 mammal skins, 300,000 bird skins, 200,000
birds' eggs, 300 dried reptiles,  2} million Lepidoptera  including  thousands  of
types, and a library of approximately  30,000 books.
While fleas do not figure prominently  in this account, N. Charles Roth-
schild, the author's  father, frequently  collected  for Walter, and it was he
who collected  and ultimately  described  the Plague flea, Xenopsylla  cheopis.
Photograph  58a in the grouping  between pages 168-169 shows the camp at Shendi,
Sudan, where this species  was first discovered.
The book provides  a wealth of history about the Rothschild  family and a
fascinating  insight into the life and times of one of its more interesting
members. ---R.E.L.

GEORGE PEARSON  HOLLAND
27-VIII-1911 10-XI-1985
It is with deep regret that we announce  the accidental  death of Dr. George
P. Holland.
Dr. Holland  was born in Vancouver,  British  Columbia. He received  the
Bachelor  of Arts degree in 1933 and the Master of Arts degree in 1937, both
from the University  of British  Columbia. In 1963 the Doctor of Science  degree,
honoris  causa, was bestowed  upon him by Carleton  University.  Most of his pro-
fessional  career was spent with the Canadian  Department  of Agriculture.
His first position  was with the Livestock  Insects  Laboratory,  Kamloops,
British  Columbia,  where he first worked on problems  of ecology  and control  of
warble flies, mosquitoes  and ticks. Later he developed  an interest  in fleas
and their taxonomy,  zoogeography  and host-associations,  which culminated  in
the publication  of "The Siphonaptera  of Canada" in 1949. His tenure at Kamloops
extended  from 1936 to 1948.
In 1948 K. W. Neatby, Director  of Science  Service,  invited  Dr. Holland  to
become Chief of the Systematic  Entomology  Unit of the Entomology  Division  and
Curator  of the Canadian  National  Collection  of Insects  in Ottawa, Ontario. In
this position  he was responsible  for identifications  and taxonomic  research  for
the Department.  In 1955 he was appointed  Chief of Insect Systematics  and Bio-
logical  Control  Unit of the Entomology  Division. In 1959 he was made the
Director  of the Entomology  Research  Institute,  Research  Branch, a position  he
occupied  until poor health compelled  him to step down in 1969. However,  he
retained  a research  position  in the Institute  to continue  his work on Siphon-
aptera. During his tenure of leadership,  the entomology  unit with six
-180-
scientists  developed  into an institute  with 45, the Canadian  National  Collect-
ion grew from about one million  to seven million  specimens  and the status and
productivity  of the E.R.I. and the scope of its collections  grew to one of the
top three in the world.
Other important  offices  occupied  by Dr. Holland  include:
Chairman,  Program  Committee,  Tenth International  Congress  of Entomology,
Montreal,  1956
Chairman,  Defence  Research  Board Advisory  Committee  on Entomological  Research,
1963-1967
Chairman,  Centennial  of Entomology  in Canada, 1863 to 1963, 1963.
He was also the Canadian  member of the Permanent  Committee  of the International
Congresses  of Entomology.  Field work and attendance  at international  confer-
ences involved  him in extensive  travel in the United States, the United  Kingdom,
Hawaiian  and Figi Islands,  Australia,  Territory  of Papua and New Guinea, the
Soviet Union and Japan.
Dr. Holland  was active in a number of professional  and scientific  soci-
eties. He was a Fellow of the Royal Entomological  Society  of London  and the
Royal Society  of Canada. As a member of the Entomological  Society  of Canada
he served as president  in 1957-1958;  was made an Honorary  Member in 1973, a
Fellow in 1976 and in 1979 was presented  the E.S.C. Gold Medal for Outstanding
Achievement  in Canadian  Entomology.  He was a member of the Entomological
Society  of America  and in the 1950's and 1960's served on committees  on Ento-
mological  Nomenclature  and International  Relations  and chaired  the Taxonomy
Section  in 1952. He belonged  to the Entomological  Society  of Ontario,  was
Director  in 1949-1950  and elected  a Fellow in 1971. He was also a member of
the Entomological  Society  of British  Columbia,  Society  of Systematic  Zoology,
Canadian  Society  of Zoologists  and the Australian  Mammal Society.
In spite of heavy administrative  responsibilities,  Dr. Holland  was still
able to publish  over 50 technical  studies  including  two books on the fleas of
Canada in 1949 and 1985, and a work on the fleas of New Guinea in 1969. A
copy of his bibliography  appears  at the end of this issue.
Dr. Holland  is survived  by his wife, a son, two daughters  and four grand-
children.
Those of us who counted  George Holland  as a friend as well as a colleague
remember  him as a witty, generous  person  who always could be counted  on for
assistance.  His passage  is a great loss to the scientific  community  as well
as to his friends.

RECENTLY  PUBLISHED  - Synopsis  and Classification  of Living Organisms.
Sybil P. Parker (Editor in Chief), 1982. (ISBN 0-07-079031-0  (set)). McGraw-
Hill Book Company (New York, etc.). Vol. 1, i-xviii,  1-1166; Vol. 2, 1-1232.
US $175.00 (2 volume set).
As the title proclaims,  these monumental  volumes  present  a classification
of all known living organisms,  from viruses  to vertebrates.  The bulk of the
volumes  consists  of 8200 synoptic  articles  which give a brief overview  of the
characteristics,  biology,  ecology  and distribution  of the various  taxa. The
classification  extends  from the two superkingdoms,  the Prokaryotae  and Eukary-
otae, down to the family level. Most family treatments  include  the number of
known genera and the major genera may be named and briefly  discussed.  Distri-
butional  data are also included. Each synopsis  ends with one or more litera-
ture citations  which may be consulted  for additional  information.
It is a recognized  paradox  that there are almost as many biological
classifications  as there are classifiers.  Modern biologists  arrange  the living
world in different  ways, from the plant and animal kingdoms  in the simplest
classification  to a system  where the prokaryotes,  protists  and fungi are rele-
gated to their own separate  kingdoms. The system followed  here recognizes
only 4 kingdoms: Virus, Monera, Plantae  and Animalia. Some might argue that
the Protista  should be recognized  as a separate  kingdom  but the system followed
in this work seems quite satisfactory.  An examination  of the two groups of
organisms  with which I am most familiar,  namely, insects  and vertebrates,
revealed  a relatively  conservative  approach  to the subject. Of particular
interest  to readers  of this newsletter  is the classification  of the Siphonaptera
by F.G.A.M.  Smit which is discussed  in more detail in this issue.
This is not the type of book that most of us would purchase  for our per-
sonal libraries,  particularly  at that price, but it is comforting  for me to
know that such a compendium  is as close as the reference  room of our library.
-+-R.E.L.

A REVISED  CLASSIFICATION  OF SIPHONAPTERA  ~ In his personal  bibliography
which accompanied  Flea News 20, Frans Smit included  the following  citation:
~184~
1980£ - Siphonaptera.  In: Taxonomy  and classification  of living organ-
isms. New York (McGraw-Hill  Co.). [in press]
In the ensuing  years I have often thought  of writing  to Frans or McGraw-Hill
to find out the fate of that particular  publication.  Since there seemed to
be no urgency  to do this and since there are only a few things upon which I
can procrastinate,  nothing  was ever done. Then, recently,  while doing her
thing in the library,  J.H.L. happened  onto a 2-volume  set with a suspiciously
familiar  sounding  title: "Synopsis  and Classification  of Living Organisms".
(A brief review of these volumes  appears elsewhere  in this issue of Flea News.)
A cursory  examination  revealed  that the section  on the Siphonaptera  had indeed
been written  by F.G.A.M.  Smit and that it contained  a classification  of the
order which differed  somewhat  from that in use during the past few decades.
A diagramatic  representation  of the Smit classification  is presented  here
along with a brief discussion.
First, the order is divided  into 5 superfamilies  which collectively  con-
tain 15 families. The families  Coptopsyllidae,  Ancistropsyllidae,  Xiphiopsyl-
lidae and Malacopsyllidae  remain as originally  conceived  and have no sub-
families. The Tungidae  has been resurrected  as a full family, also without
subfamilies,  and contains  only the genus Tunga. The Stephanocircidae,  Chim-
aeropsyllidae,  Ischnopsyllidae  and Rhopalopsyllidae  are also unaltered  and
still contain  their traditional  subfamilies.  The remaining  families  have been
altered  in their subfamily  content.
The Hystrichopsyllidae  has been reduced  to 2 subfamilies.  The Hystri-
chopsyllinae  contains  the 4 hystrichopsyllid  genera the females  of which have
paired spermathecae  (Hystrichopsylla,  Atyphloceras,  Typhloceras  and Ctenoparia).
The Macropsyllidae  has been reduced  to subfamily  status and constitutes  the
other subfamily.  Females  of both Macropsylla  and Stephanopsylla  also have 2
spermathecae.  All of the remaining  subfamilies  normally  assigned  to the
Hystrichopsyllidae  are grouped  under a new family name, the Ctenophthalmidae.
The Pygiopsyllidae  contains  4 subfamilies.  The Lycopsyllinae  and Pygio-
psyllinae  were previously  recognized  and the tribes Choristopsyllini  and Uro-
psyllini  have been elevated  to subfamily  rank. The previously  recognized
Stivaliinae  has been eliminated.
As pointed  out by Smit (1983), the Ceratophyllidae  and the Leptopsyllidae
are closely  related  and there is some overlap  in certain  characters.  As a
result, in this classification  the Leptopsyllidae  is eliminated  and the sub-
families  Leptopsyllinae  and Amphipsyllinae  are placed in the Ceratophyllidae
along with the Ceratophyllinae.  (Those noting the discrepancy  between  Smit's
1982 classification  and his 1983 treatment  of the Ceratophyllidae  in Traub,
Rothschild  and Haddow should be aware that the latter was written  in the mid
1970's but not published  until 1983. In the intervening  years there was
ample time for Smit to further  firm up his ideas on subordinal  classification.)
The Vermipsyllidae  has been divided  into 2 subfamilies:  the Vermipsyllinae
for Vermipsylla  and Chaetopsylla  and the Dorcadiinae  for Doreadia.
In the Pulicidae,  removal  of Tunga to its own family allowed  the elevation
of the remaining  5 tribes to subfamily  status. Retaining  Neotunga  in the

Pulicidae  necessitated  the erection  of a subfamily  for it, resulting  in the 6
subfamilies  as shown. The relationship  of Tunga and Hectopsylla  to the remain-
ing pulicid  genera has historically  been questionable.  Removal  of Tunga
solves part of the problem,  but retaining  Neotunga  as a pulicid  genus does not
eliminate  the problem  completely.
New classifications  are seldom quickly  accepted  and it is doubtful  if this
one will be eagerly  embraced  by pulicologists.  However,  after considerable
reflection,  I find a certain  unity in the Smit classification  that has been
lacking  in earlier  systems. His long and continuous  exposure  to the world
fauna has given him an insight  into relationships  within the order which most
of us with our varied responsibilities  and distractions  could probably  never
develop. It is unfortunate  that it has been published  in such an obscure
and expensive  volume,  but even so I expect that it, or some modification  of
it, is likely to be around for some time to come. ---R.E.L.

The George P. Holland  Memorial  Fund
Most of you know the tragic  news that George  P. Holland,  14 KitimatCrescent,  Nepean,  Ontario  K2H 7G5, died on 10 November  1985 fromexposure  during a hunting  trip to his favorite  lodge near Ottawa.George  retired  in 1976 and sincehas  devoted  much of his time tofinishing  his monograph  on the fleas of Canada,  Alaska,  and Greenland(published  in early 1985).
George  was known world-wide  for his many contributions  to thetaxonomy  of fleas. He began his career in entomology  at the CanadaDepartment  of Agriculture  laboratory  at Kamloops,  British  Columbia,and then moved to Ottawa  to serve as head of the old Systematic
Entomology  Unit and then as director  of the Entomology  (now Bio-systematics)  Research  Institute.
Under George's  leadership,  the Canadian  National  Collection  (CNC)of insects  and related  arthropods  grew to be one of the best col-lections  of its kind in the world with extensive  nearctic  holdings,especially  from the arctic region, and with good collections  fromother areas of the world, such as New Guinea,  Mexico,  Jamaica,
Europe,  etc. During  his tenure as director,  the CNC grew from arelatively  small collection  of about 1,000,000  specimens  to one withabout 10,000,000  specimens.
The George  P. Holland  Memorial  Fund has been established  ly theCanaColl  Foundation  in his memory. The fund is ongoing  and can beadded to at any time. CanaColl  is an independent  organizationdevoted  to promoting  research  and development  of the CNC. ‘Theaccrued  interest  from this memorial  fund will be used to supportcuration  on the CNC.
Donations  in memory of George  may be sent to the CanaColl  Foundation(address  below);  receipts  for income tax purposes  will be sent forall donations  of $5.00 or more. The Holland  family  will be informedof the names of those who have made donations  to the fund.
Please share this notice with anyone else who might be interested.If you want more information,  please  don't hesitate  to ask.
May this and other sentiments  from friends  be a source of comfortto the Holland  family  at this time.

HARRY HOOGSTRAAL
24-11-1917 24-11-1986
We have been informed  by Dr. Robert Traub that Dr. Harry Hoogstraal  died of
lung cancer in Cairo, Egypt, on February  24, his 69th birthday. Although  he was
best known for his exhaustive  studies on ticks and arboviruses,  entomologists,
parasitologists  and medical scientists  were among the beneficiaries  of many of
his studies.
Dr. Hoogstraal  was born in Chicago, Illinois. He received  the Bachelor  of
Arts degree from the University  of Illinois,  Urbana, in 1938 and the Master of
Science degree in 1942. During this time he organized  and led four zoological
expeditions  to Mexico. In 1943, he joined the United States Army as Malariol-
ogist and Head of the Entomology  Department,  4th Area Medical  Laboratory,
Northington  General Hospital,  and 19th Medical General Hospital,  retiring  in
1946 with the rank of Captain  MSC. Later that year he headed the Philippine
Zoological  Expedition,  a joint venture between the Philippine  Government  and the
Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago, Illinois. Upon his return, he was
appointed  Medical Zoologist  with the United States Navy Bureau of Medicine  and
Surgery and participated  in the University  of California  Expedition  to Africa
and Madagascar  in 1948-49. In 1949-50 he headed the Sudan (Equatoria)  Sub-unit
of the United States Naval Medical Research  Unit No. 3 (NAMRU-3)  and was ap-
pointed Head of Medical Zoology of NAMRU-3 in 1950, a position  he held until
his death. In 1959 he received  the PhD from the London School of Hygiene and
Tropical  Medicine,  the ScD from the same institution  in 1971, and the Doctorate
(honoris  causa) from the Faculty of Medicine,  Ain Shams University,  Cairo,
Egypt, in 1978.
From the beginning  of his professional  career, Dr. Hoogstraal  was inter-
ested in the distribution  of animals and disease. At NAMRU-3 he supervised  a
-204-
program  which concentrated  on the interrelationships  between  vertebrate  hosts,their ectoparasites  and pathogens,  especially  viral and rickettsial,  causinghuman and animal diseases. Parts of this program  extended  to all parts of theworld, but most of his early studies  were performed  in Egypt and adjacent
countries  in the eastern  Mediterranean  area. Early on, it became apparentthat knowledge  of the fauna of Egypt was poor so he set out to conduct  a naturalhistory  survey of the country  that was almost unparalleled  in the history  ofthe natural  sciences. As a result, Egyptian  birds and mammals  are now as wellknown as those of western  Europe or the United States. Tick speciation,biology,  ecology,  and their relationship  to disease  were subjects  of particularinterest  to him. In the early 1950's tick species  were unidentifiable  in thelarval and nymphal  stages and there was much nomenclatural  confusion  among thenamed adults. Working  from the principal  that each species  has unique biologi-cal properties  which determine  the significance  and nature of the role of thespecies  in disease  transmission,  he initiated  a program  of defining  the tickspecies  in Egypt and the Sudan. To do so properly,  the investigation  extendedinto the neighboring  countries  and eventually  to all of Africa, Europe, Asia,Australia,  numerous  oceanic islands,  and frequently  North and South America.More than 350 of the approximately  800 known species  were studied,  named anddescribed,  if new to science,  or redescribed,  if poorly known. Concomitant  tothese studies,  the largest  and most varied collection  of ticks in the world wasamassed  and a rearing  program  was begun in order to obtain the immature  stagesthat could be associated  with known adults.
Although  the bulk of the studies  directed  by Dr. Hoogstraal  concernedthemselves  with ticks and their relationships  to disease  transmission,  theyproduced  enormous  amounts  of peripheral  data and specimens  which were gladlyshared with specialists  throughout  the world. Literally  hundreds  of scientistswere the beneficiaries  of field studies  conducted  or supported  by him throughNAMRU-3. In addition,  because  of his extensive  travels,  he developed  a keenappreciation  of the zoogeographic  relationships  of not just ticks and theirhosts but of animals  in general  which would strongly  influence  his laterstudies.
As a natural  corollary  of his studies,  the Hoogstraal  Library  on Ticksand Tickborne  Diseases  was established.  It is the largest  library  of itskind in the world and contains  over 95,000 reprints  and reports,  as well asseveral  thousand  biomedical  periodicals,  textbooks  and specialized  scientific,zoological  and geographical  books. Since much work on ticks has been carriedout in the U.S.S.R.  and the eastern  European  countries,  a translation  sectionwas organized  and hundreds  of translations  have been produced,  copies ofwhich have been provided  to the scientific  community.  Beginning  in 1970, andextending  through  1982, the library  was catalogued  in a 7-volume  Bibliographyof Ticks and Tickborne  Diseases  from Homer (about 800 B.C.) to 31 December1981, which comes to 3576 pages. It includes  all known publications  ontickborne  diseases,  including  diagnosis,  treatment,  epidemiology,  etc., aswell as tick taxonomy,  systematics,  morphology,  biology,  ecology,  host relation-ships, behavior,  distribution,  physiology  and biochemistry.  Three thousandcopies of each volume  were distributed  to libraries  and scientists  throughoutthe world.
Dr. Hoogstraal  was a member, a life member, or a charter  member of 32professional  societies.  Over the years he served on a myriad of national  and
=-205=
international  committees,  panels, councils  and delegations.  He also served
in a number of editorial  posts and was an external examiner  and visiting
lecturer at universities  in Egypt, India, Australia,  South Africa, England and
the United States. He was the recipient  of a multitude  of professional  honors
and delivered  lectures on various topics relating to medical zoology and epi-
demiology  to gatherings  of scientists  all over the world. Finally, in addition
to the involvements  listed above, he also authored or coauthored  more than 500
scientific  papers in various technical  journals.
During his years in Egypt, Dr. Hoogstraal  became a respected  egyptologist,
and his villa in Maadi, south of Cairo, abounded  with artifacts  acquired dur-
ing his world travels. He was also a talented sculptor, and usually had a bust
in progress  when he could steal time from his travels and professional  obliga-
tions.
Even with such awesome involvement  in his profession,  perhaps none of his
contributions  compares to the constant support and encouragement  meted out to
the hundreds of colleagues,  young and old, with whom he corresponded.  There
is hardly an aspect of entomology,  parasitology,  or medical zoology today that
remains untouched  by his influence,  directly  or indirectly. That he was a
respected  professional  is attested to by the fact that over 40 species of plants,
reptiles,  birds, mammals, insects, mites, ticks and protozoans  bear the
specific  name hoogstraali  in his honor.
In addition  to being a scientist  of the first order, Harry Hoogstraal  was
a naturalist  who believed that his profession  was an art as well as a science.
This seems to be a view unshared  by younger professionals,  and perhaps his
passing is symbolic of what is happening  today in the natural sciences. His
gentle voice and quiet dignity will be sorely missed by friends and colleagues
alike. ---R.E.L.

RECENTLY  PUBLISHED
Coevolution  of Parasitic  Arthropods  and Mammals. K. C. Kim, ed. 1985. (ISBN
0-471-08546-4)  John Wiley & Sons, Inc., New York. 800 pp. $56 (ESA members),
$69.95 (nonmembers).
Interactions  between plants and animals have long been recognized  by both
botanists  and zoologists,  and the presence  of terpenoids,  alkaloids  and various
other compounds  in some plants is thought to be an evolutionary  response to
phytophagous  insects. Observations  of these interactions  over the years has
gradually  given rise to the theory of coevolution  between plants and their
herbivores  involving  such diverse entities as host specificity,  pollination
strategies  and seed dispersal. Similar interactions  between various groups of
animals, also resulting  in coevolutionary  phenomena,  are not easily demonstrated
and appear in the earlier literature  under the guise of host specificity.
During the last 30 years there have been two symposia  devoted to the host speci-
ficity of vertebrate  parasites:  the first at Neuchatel,  Switzerland,  in 1957;
the second in Paris, France, in 1981. In both instances  the emphasis  was
directed  toward the non-arthropod  parasites  of vertebrates.
~206-
The appearance  of Adrian  Marshall's  The Ecology  of Ectoparasitic  Insects
(1981) marked the first concerted  effort to summarize  the extensive  literature
on the subject  of ectoparasites  and their interrelationships  with each other
and with their hosts. While coevolution  is not discussed  as such, it is amply
alluded  to in various  chapters  under other headings,  thus laying the groundwork
for such a study as this. This book consists  of 13 chapters,  divided  into 4
parts and concluded  by 2 appendices  and an index.
Part one contains  3 chapters  that attempt  to introduce  the subject  from
different  points of view. In chapter  one Kim discusses  the various  aspects  of
the evolutionary  relationships  of parasitic  arthropods  and mammals,  including
host-parasite  associations,  parasitism  as opposed  to commensalism,  and ecto-
parasites  as opposed  to endoparasites.  The chapter  continues  with a considera-
tion of the host as a habitat,  the biology  of parasitic  arthropods  and their
population  patterns  and dynamics. Interactions  between  parasitic  arthropods
are discussed,  as are interactions  between  them and their hosts. In conclusion,
the evolutionary  aspects  of these associations  are reviewed  and some conclusions
drawn concerning  possible  evolutionary  pathways  to the ectoparasitic  condition.
Of the remaining  2 chapters,  the first is a short consideration  of coevolu-
tion as a process. It includes  a table of general  differences  between  plant
and mammalian  ectoparasites  and discusses,  in general  terms, many of the con-
siderations  involved  in the ectoparasite  mode of existence.  Chapter  three
reviews  mammals  as the evolutionary  partners  in coevolution,  first by consider-
ing them as a habitat  for ectoparasitic  arthropods,  and then by reviewing  the
origins  and geological  history  of the class Mammalia. Approximately  half of
this chapter  is devoted  to a review of the diversity  and geographical  distri-
bution of recent mammals.
Part two contains  chapters  4 through  8, which deal with insect ectopara-
sites of mammals. In chapter  four, which deals with patterns  of insect para-
sitism in mammals,  the authors  point out that ectoparasitic  insects  of mammals
constitute  less than 0.5% of all insects  and belong to only 7 orders. Of
these the Anoplura,  Mallophaga  and Siphonaptera  are exclusively  ectoparasitic
and are discussed  in subsequent  chapters. A small number of minor taxa belong-
ing to the orders Dermaptera,  Hemiptera,  Coleoptera  and Diptera  are the sub-
jects of this chapter. Adaptations  and evolutionary  strategies  of these
species  are discussed,  along with their host associations  and geographical
distributions.  The chapter  concludes  with a consideration  of parasitic  adapt-
ations, including  convergence  of body form and structure  and a discussion  of
host associations  and specificity. 
|
Chapter  five deals with the evolution  and host associations  in the order
Anoplura. It begins with a review of adaptations  and evolutionary  trends im-
posed by the habitat  provided  by the host. This is followed  by an analysis  of
the host-parasite  associations,  arranged  by order of the host, and a discussion
of host specificity.  The chapter  concludes  with an analysis  of the origin and
evolution  of the class Mammalia,  the origin of host associations  and their
evolution,  and a brief consideration  of phylogenetic  relationships  and
historical  biogeography.
Chapter  six is concerned  with the evolution  of the Mallophaga  on mammals.
Since most of the members  of this order are associated  with birds, the chapter
-207-
is shorter than most. Representatives  of all three mallophagan  suborders  occur
on mammals and the authors conclude  that mammal-infesting  mallophagans  could be
useful in tracing the evolutionary  affinities  of their hosts, as has been done
with some groups of birds. They also postulate  that less than half of the exist-
ing species of mammal-infesting  mallophagans  are currently  known to science
(thanks to the inherent  resistance  on the part of most mammalogists  to collect
ectoparasites).
Chapter seven is entitled  Evolutionary  Aspects  of the Disjunct  Distribution
of Lice on Carnivora. After noting that endemic anoplurans  are absent from ter-
restrial  carnivores  and endemic mallophagans  are absent from marine carnivores,
the author poses four questions,  the answers to which may be reached by two
alternative  hypotheses.  A detailed  discussion  of adaptive  strategies  and host
associations  of both groups on mammals in general is followed  by a review of
the classification  and evolution  of the order Carnivora,  and a synthesis  of
louse associations  and distribution  within the order. In a section on coloniza-
tion and extinction  the author advances  some interesting  hypotheses  to explain
the current distribution  of lice on carnivores,  based on competition  for avail-
able space on the host and the ability to adapt to the change to an aquatic
habitat on the part of their arctoid (bear-like)  hosts.
Chapter eight deals with the coevolution  of fleas and mammals. After a
brief commentary  on the interactions  between fleas and their mammalian  hosts,
the author addresses  the matter of host specificity  and distribution.  This is
done by dividing  the species of fleas into a few categories  that are determined
by degrees of specificity.  Thus, for example, ultraspecific  fleas are those
that are restricted  to a single host species; generispecific  fleas those that
infest a genus, or group of closely related hosts, etc. There follows a short
consideration  of zoogeography  and evolution  within the order Siphonaptera  and a
presentation  of evidence  of convergence,  divergence  and various adaptations  to
hosts and habitats. In the discussion  the author synthesizes  information  about
the host relationships,  zoogeography,  evolution  and coevolution,  and morpholog-
ical adaptations  in fleas, and posits a series of conclusions  which suggest that
there is more host specificity  in the Siphonaptera  than has generally  been
supposed,  and that much of what we know about the order indicates  an intensely
close association  between  fleas, their mammal hosts and coevolution.
Part three contains  chapters  9 through 12 and deals with coevolution  in the
Acari. Chapter nine treats the evolution  of mesostigmatid  mites and begins with
a description  of the group and a short section  on its preadaptation  for parasit-
ism. Since not all mesostigmatid  mites are parasites,  the author next discusses
the diversity,  distribution  and phylogeny  of the group and then progresses
through its evolutionary  strategies  and adaptations  for parasitism  by dealing
with the individual  families  and subfamilies.  In conclusion,  it is emphasized
that mesostigmatid  mites show an unusual ecological  diversity  while retaining  a
remarkably  uniform  habitus. The dermanissoid  families  in particular  demonstrate
a variety of ecological  and vertebrate  relationships  which combine to make them
the most successful  mammal parasites  among the Mesostigmata.
Chapter ten deals with tick and mammal coevolution  with emphasis  on the
ixodid genus Haemaphysalis.  The authors begin with the premise that ixodid
ticks evolved as obligate  parasites  of reptiles  in the late Paleozoic  or early
~208-
Mesozoic  eras and that their subsequent  coevolution  with birds and mammals  has
been conservative.  The least conservative  have been the species  associated
with livestock,  man and dogs. The premammalian  evolution  of ticks is dis-
cussed, followed  by sections  on the evolution  of mammalian  ticks and host
specificity.  The bulk of this chapter  deals with the coevolution  of ticks and
mammals  using the genus Haemaphysalis  as a model. After a brief discussion  of
generic  characters,  the species  are segregated  into categories,  depending  upon
whether  they are considered  to be structurally  primitive,  intermediate  or ad-
vanced, and the subgenera  of each of these subdivisions  are discussed.  The
summary  includes  a brief resumé of the distribution  and host relationships  for
the Argasidae  and the subfamilies  of the Ixodidae.
Chapter  eleven, entitled  Prostigmata-Mammalia  Validation  of Coevolutionary
Phylogenesis,  begins with a section  on coevolution  and symbiosis  in which it
was deemed necessary  to include  a table of the definitions  of such arcane terms
as polyhospitality,  polybioty,  asymbiospecificity,  symbiophylogeny,  (A) symbio-
specific  and other semantic  nonsense. These are then employed  in subsequent
sections  to make a case for coevolution  in 3 families  of the Prostigmata.  I |
leave it to other readers  to determine  the success  of this author.
Chapter  twelve is concerned  with the evolution  of astigmatid  mites on
mammals  and begins with a brief consideration  of the requirements  of a parasitic
way of life. It is pointed  out that both constructive  and regressive  anatomical
adaptations  are required,  in addition  to various  biological  modifications,  to be
a successful  parasite. The authors  then proceed  to review the more important
families  that are parasitic  on mammals. They conclude  that there is strong evi-
dence for coevolution  in this group, especially  in parasites  that spend their
entire lives on the host.
Part four, entitled  Overview,  contains  chapter  thirteen,  Parasitism  and
Coevolution:  Epilogue,  and 2 appendices.  In chapter  thirteen  the author sum-
marizes  the contents  of the preceding  chapters  and makes the case that coevolu-
tion, to varying  degrees,  does exist between  parasitic  arthropods  and mammals.
He also stresses  that the process  involves  both interspecific  interactions  and
strategies  to promote  coexistence  with other associating  species. The chapter
concludes  with a discussion  of the origin and phylogeny  of parasite-host
associations  and examples  of resource  and phylogenetic  tracking  models.
Appendix  A is a list of parasitic  arthropods  associated  with mammals  and
Appendix  B is a list of mammals  and their parasitic  arthropods.
In spite of the somewhat  restrictive  title, this book contains  a wealth
of information  of interest  to entomologists  and acarologists  in general,  and is
a must in the library  of medical  and veterinary  entomologists.  It is well
organized,  printed  in a pleasing  typeface  and is remarkably  free of mechanical
errors.
Although  Professor  Kim is listed as the editor, in fact he is the sole
author of four of the chapters  and a co-author  of three more, in addition  to
his contributions  as an editor. Both he and the other authors  are to be
congratulated  on their treatment  of this fascinating  subject. aeoR Eda

A Colour Atlas of Insect Tissues Via the Flea by Miriam Rothschild,  Yosef Schlein
and Susumo Lto, 1986. (ISBN 0 7234 0891 2) Wolfe Publishing  Ltd., Wolfe House,
3 Conway Street, London WIP GHE, 184 pp. + 261 figs. (188 in colour). $79.95
The title of this book quite accurately  describes  its content. After a
brief preface and introduction,  there are three pages entitled  Techniques. In-
cluded here are explanations  of the various techniques  and equipment  employed in
obtaining  the light microscope,  stereoscan  and transmission  electron  photomicro-
graphs. There is also a glossary for electron  micrographs,  a description  of
fixing and staining  methods, solutions  and a short list of abbreviations.  Fol-
lowing this are 14 detailed  drawings,  most originals  by Y. Schlein, showing the
principal  internal organs of the flea, based upon both sexes of Xenopsylla
cheopis. The remainder  of the book is divided into 25 sections,  each dealing
with an organ system or other anatomical  manifestation  such as resilin, blood
cells, the sensilium,  endocrine  glands, etc. Each section is prefaced  by a
brief introduction,  followed  by a series of illustrations.  Where both black and
white and coloured  plates are used, the coloured  plates come first. Structures
in the coloured  plates are numbered corresponding  to a labeling  key for each
set of plates. Black and white plates are labeled with letters which are ex-
plained in the captions. Appendix  I includes illustrations  of structures  not
found in fleas such as flight muscles, compound eyes and wing scales. Appendix
II illustrates  various parasites  and symbionts  in the internal organs of fleas.
These include helminths,  protozoans  and bacteria. Ten references  to other works
are listed and there is a comprehensive  index.
Many of the illustrations  are of sections of the European  rabbit flea,
Spilopsyllus  cuniculi. However, in total, 20 species representing  7 families
are shown in the plates.
The book is logically  organized  and the printer has done an excellent  job
with the colour plates. The authors are to be congratulated  for the production
of this remarkable  volume and the contribution  it makes to our understanding  of
flea anatomy. ---R.E.L.
Insects of Southern  Africa. C. H. Scholtz and Erik Holm, eds. 1985. (ISBN
0409 10486 8 Limited edition, 0409 10487 6 Hard cover) Butterworths,  Durban,
502 pp., price not available.
Although  not of direct interest to the readers of Flea News, attention  is
called to the availability  of this volume on the Southern  Africa fauna.
There has long been a need for such a work and, although it has been estimated
that no more than 5% of the Southern  African insect fauna is known to science,
this work is a creditable  treatment  of the known fauna. In passing, it should
be noted that the siphonapteran  fauna of the region is quite well known thanks
to the works of DeMeillon,  Haeselbarth,  Segerman,  Davis, Hardy and Zumpt.
Fleas figure in this volume in two ways. First, the 5-page account of
the order was written by Ms. Joyce Segerman  of the South African Institute  for
Medical Research. Second, throughout  the myriad of black and white figures a
stylized  silhouette  of a cat flea is used to indicate  scale. This system
has been used previously  in field guides to vertebrates,  but to my knowledge
this is a first in a book on insects. ---R.E.L.

The Oxford Dictionary  of Natural  History. Michael  Allaby, ed. 1985. (ISBN
0-19-217720-6)  Oxford University  Press, Oxford, New York, 688 pp. $38.00
Again, this book may be of only passing  interest  to many recipients  of
Flea News. However,  as horizons  in Biology  and related  disciplines  expand,
so, too, does the plethora  of new terms and old terms with new definitions,
creating  the need for a new, updated  lexicon  on the average  of every 5 to 10
years. The term "natural  history"  is not defined  in this work, but Lincoln,
Boxshall  and Clark, 1982, A Dictionary  of Ecology,  Evolution  and Systematics,
define it as "The study of  nature, natural  objects  and natural  phenomena".
It would seem that the editor had this definition  in mind, since he allotted
space for earth and atmospheric  sciences,  genetics,  cell structure  and
function,  biochemistry,  parasitology  and a few other disciplines.  Fifty-six
contributors  and consultants  participated  in this compilation  of over 12,000
entries.
It is axiomatic  that no totally  complete  lexicon  has ever been written,
and likely never will be. The appearance  of this volume does not alter the
axiom, although  the approach  followed  by the editor and contributors  is some-
what different  from most similar  treatments.  For example,  the names of taxa
in the higher classification  of both plants and animals  are included  (but not
the viruses,  etc.). In some cases, even genera are discussed.  However,  the
treatment  is very uneven and neither  the order nor any of the families  of the
Siphonaptera  are mentioned,  for example. Even the word "flea" only appears
in association  with "flea beetle"  and "water flea", an insect and a crustacean,
respectively.  Still, the terminology  is current,  the coverage  broad and the
price reasonable,  and it now resides  with the eight other dictionaries  and
glossaries  on my desk, and the 20 or 30 additional  word books in my library.

GLEN M. KOHLS
23-X-1905 3-VIII-1986
We have recently  been informed  by Dr. William  L. Jellison  that Dr. Glen
M. Kohls died of natural  causes at his home in Hamilton,  Montana,  on Sunday,
August 3rd.
Dr. Kohls was born in Vesta, Minnesota.  He received  the B.S. degree in
entomology  from Montana  State University  in 1929 and the M.S. degree from the
University  of Minnesota  in 1937. He began his career at the Rocky Mountain
Laboratory,  Hamilton,  Montana,  in 1927 under Dr. R. A. Cooley. His primary
assignment  was to work with ticks and the diseases  they transmit,  including
Rocky Mountain  Spotted  Fever. During World War II he was commissioned  a
captain  in the Medical  Service  Corps to serve on the Scrub Typhus Commission.
He also taught at the Army Medical  School, Walter Reed, in Washington,  D.C.
-227-
and served in the Burma Theatre of operations. He was discharged  a lieutenant
colonel and returned to his work at Rocky Mountain  Laboratory  at the end of
his military  service.
Dr. Kohls received an honorary doctorate  degree from Montana State Univer-
sity in 1966 and was awarded the Meritorious  Service Medal by the United States
Public Health Service in 1968. During his career he was author or coauthor of
183 scientific  papers and 12 animal taxa bear his name, including  a subgenus
and 3 species of ticks, 3 species of mites, 1 each of a spider, cockroach  and
streblid, and the flea genus Kohlsia Traub, 1950, and the flea species Cory-
psylla kohlsi Hubbard, 1940.

NEWLY PUBLISHED  - The following  information  concerning  the publication  of a
volume dealing with the fleas of the People's Republic of China was provided by
Professor  LIU Chi-ying  for inclusion  in this issue of Flea News.* * *
SIPHONAPTERA,  Series Insecta, Fauna Sinica. C.-y. Liu, K.-c. Li et al., 1986
(December). Science Press, 137 Chaoyangmennei  Street, Beijing, The People's
Republic of China. 16 mo., 1340 pp., 1948 figs. US $45.00 including  surface
postage.
~228-
This monograph  was undertaken  under the auspices  of the Fauna Editorial
Committee,  Academia  Sinica, during the years 1973-1982. It is divided into
several  parts, of which Part One is a general account of the Siphonaptera.
It concerns  itself with the distribution  of Chinese fleas and their hosts,
dividing  the area into 2 regions, 3 subregions,  7 districts  and 19 subdistricts.
Part Two contains  a systematic  account of the 8 families,  71 genera and
452 species and subspecies  occurring  in the area under consideration.  This
makes up the largest part of the book and includes  keys to the various  taxa
and illustrations  for each.
Part Three is the English text and contains  a brief resumé of the book,
including  summaries  of the descriptions  of 17 new species  and subspecies.
Corresponding  Chinese descriptions  are found in Part Two. All illustrations
are numbered  and bear Latin captions. The book concludes  with a table of
the geographical  distribution  of the Chinese flea species, a Host/Parasite
index, and Literature  Cited.
NOMEN NUDUM - Through  the kind offices  of Professor  J. C. BEAUCOURNU,  a
nomen nudum has been called to our attention. In appendix  I, page 80, of
Rood, J. P., 1972, “Ecological  and behavioural  comparisons  of three genera of
Argentine  cavies" (Anim. Behav. Monogr. 5(1): 1-83), the author cites a list
of ectoparasites  collected  on members  of the Caviinae. Tiamastus  cavicola
and Panallius  atropus  are reported  from Cavia aperea. To my knowledge  the
specific-epithet  atropus has never been associated  with the genus Panallius
or with any other flea genus for that matter. In his acknowledgements  Rood
indicates  that the ectoparasites  were identified  by the late Dr. E. Del Ponte.
Whether  the species  was new and Del Ponte intended  to describe  it is a moot
question  since a description  was never published. Therefore  the name atropus
should be added to the list of nomina nuda. —--R.E.Ls

CONGRATULATIONS  - Douglas P. Schelhaas  received  his Doctor of Philosophy
degree from the University  of North Dakota on 1 August 1986. The title of
his dissertation  is "Antifreeze  production  and cold-tolerance  in overwintering
purple martin fleas, Ceratophyllus  idius Jordan and Rothschild."  Dr. Schel-
haas is now teaching  in the Biology  Department,  U.S. Air Force Academy,
Colorado  Springs,  Colorado.
PERSONALIA  - Dr. John Lane has written  to inform us of the retirement
of Dr. Brian R. LAURENCE  from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical  Medi-
cine. Dr. Laurence  is a long-time  recipient  of Flea News and we send him
our best wishes for a happy retirement.  Dr. Lane will continue  to receive
Flea News for the Department  of Entomology.

HOOGSTRAAL  CENTER - Harry Hoogstraal  willed his library and his unparal-

an international  center for tick research. The Smithsonian  has established
the Harry Hoogstraal  Center for Tick Research  and the Harry Hoogstraal  Fund,
and would welcome contributions  in his name. For further information,  con-
tact the Office of Membership  and Development,  Smithsonian  Institution,
Washington,  D.C. 20560 or call (202) 357-3355.

in Siskiyou  County, California.

MILAN JURIK
14-VI-1930 19-X-1986
, Dr. Alexander  Dudich has written to inform us of the death of Ing. Milan
Jurik, in Brno, after a long illness. Subsequently  Drs. D. Cyprich  and J. Ryba
provided  the following  obituary.
Ing. Milan Jurik was born in Vinosady,  near Bratislava,  Czechoslovakia,
where his father was an educator. Upon completing  his secondary  education  he
entered the Agricultural  University  at Brno where, from 1949 to 1953, he studied
in the Faculty of Forestry. In 1952 he was appointed  to a teaching  assistant-
ship in the Department  of Zoology. Later he was appointed  lecturer  in the
Department  of Veterinary  Sciences. In 1971 he returned  to the Department  of
Zoology, and in 1977 he was promoted  to the rank of associate  professor.
During his early years at the university  Jurik specialized  in mammalogy.
As his career progressed  he devoted  more and more of his time to ectoparasites,
with particular  emphasis  on the species composition  and ecology of bird fleas.
He also studied the problem  of fleas and their control in the breeding  farms of
fur-bearing  animals, and in later years concentrated  on studies of the fleas
associated  with moles in Czechoslovakia.  The results of these later studies
remain unpublished.
Milan Jurfk was both a scientist  and a teacher and was active both at the
University  and in public life. His unselfishness  in assistance  to his students
and colleagues,  his meticulousness  in his work and his kind words will be missed
by all who knew him.
For further biographical  information  the reader is referred  to: Rosicky,
B., 1980. Fiftieth  birthday  of Ing. M. Jurfk CSc. Folia Parasitol.,  Praha
27: 287-288.

A REQUEST FOR COLLECTORS  AND SYSTEMATISTS  - Current studies of the male
genitalia  in pulicid fleas have revealed  the great utility of scanning electron
microscopy  in the interpretation  of structure  and in comparative  anatomy. In
some cases it has proven possible to prepare slide mounted specimens  for such
examination,  but in general the lack of uncleared,  unmounted  material  has been
frustrating.
Since scanning  electron  microscopes  have become very common, and relatively
easy to use, we make the following  suggestion: Collectors  and curators should,
routinely  and whenever  possible, in preparing  fleas for study, retain at least
some specimens  uncleared  and stored in 70% alcohol. If identification  is un-
certain and examination  of slide mounted material  is necessary,  the specimens
may be cleared in xylene and temporary  mounts made in alpha terpineol. This
usually provides  enough clearing  for the examination  of most chitinous  struct—
ures. The specimens  may then be dehydrated  in ethanol and stored, or prepared
for scanning  without undue damage. Metal coated specimens,  mounted on small
copper disks in any of the standard  ways, may be stored indefinitely  and do
not take up much more room than slide mounted material. The general avail-
ability of material  prepared in this way could be a great boon to students of
the order. ---T. B. Cheetham
