Editorial
 “Flea larvae"
"The discussion is based largely upon the immature stages. This choice is not made because it is
thought that they reveal phylogenetic relationships more clearly than do the adults, but 
because much less is known about the larvae. Their structure makes clear certain 
relationships previously unsuspected and precludes some derivations once thought 
possible on the basis of the better known adult structures." - H.E. Hinton (1958)
"The systematics of flea larvae are the least known among larvae of medically important 
holometabolous insects." - J.R. Kucera (1990)
Dear Flea News Reader,
  Most fleas are immature. I found over 90% of fleas in a bat roost were immature stages 
(Bossard 2017). Identification of immature fleas would aid studies of life history, populations, and 
communities (Haas & Kucera 2004). 
In addition, immatures inform phylogenies. Adult and immature phylogeny should in theory be 
congruent, but in practice they are often in conflict, oft illustrated by other holometabolic insects (e.g. 
Diptera, Elbel 1988). We might expect "ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny" in flea characters, however, 
characters may show "caenogenesis", that is, new characters not found in presumed ancestors 
("apomorphic" characters).
Holometabolic larvae often have fewer, less complex characters than adults but there are 
exceptions. Flea larvae sensilla are a possible example: "In holometabolous insects larval sensilla 
appear to be structurally quite advanced, and more complex than in the adult." (Hallberg & Hansson 
1999). Taste is little studied in fleas (King & Gunathunga 2023) although there are studies on food 
selection.
Some flea larvae reportedly show grouping more distinctively than adults, such as 
Ctenophthalamus that Elbel (1991) placed between Pulicidae and Ceratophyllidae, Anomiopsyllus, and 
with Rhadinopsylla possibly a distinct family, similar to the allied group Stenoponiidae.
Elbel also found flea groups he described as having distinct adults but without distinct larvae: 
the Pulicidae tribes of Archaeopsyllini,  Spilopsyllini, and Xenopsyllini group together but are different
from Pulicini (contains Pulex). Another example is Stenoponiidae whose larvae are not distinct from 
Hystrichopsyllidae.
Finally, there are flea groups in conflict between larva and adult: Echidnophaga larvae resemble
Tungidae or Ctenophthalminae not Pulicidae, the bat flea Sternopsylla larvae resemble 
Hystrichopsyllidae not other Ischnopsyllidae, and Mioctenopsylla larvae resemble Hystrichopsyllidae 
not Ceratophyllidae (Elbel 1988, 1996).
Flea larvae description methods are described by Elbel, Smith and Clay 1988, Kucera 1990, 
Pilgrim 1992, Elbel and Bossard 2007, using light microscope to 800x and Scanning Electron 
Microscopy (SEM). Larval characters include setae (length, position, pattern, number, morphology), 
sensilla, antennae papillae and other likely sensory structures, mandibles, and surface denticles. Elbel 3
thought SEM not worth the trouble, instead opting for DNA as the larvae and their shed exoskeletons 
(molted exuvia) enables molecular and morphological description (Gurney et al. 2000a, b).
Yours in fleas,
R.L. Bossard

Morphological studies showed that the epithelial cells of the mid-gut of third-instar larvae of 
Ceratophyllus sciurorum (Schr.) are of the cylindrical type. The apical surface of the cells is modified 
into microvilli. Very thin filaments of glycocalyx are connected with the outer layer of the membrane 
of the microvilli. A basal plate, composed of alternating thick and thin fibrilli, underlies the base of the 
cells. Secretion of enzymes is of merocrine type. Crystals were seen in the cell nuclei; hitherto such 
crystals had been observed only in adult fleas. A peritrophic membrane was seen in the cavity of the 
mid-gut of engorged larvae.

Parasite Conservation
"New IUCN Species Survival Commission Parasite Specialist Group Launched in 2023"
"In January 2023, a Parasite Specialist Group was created within the IUCN (International Union
for Conservation of Nature) Species Survival Commission. This international group of researchers and 
practitioners will work to assess the conservation status of parasite biodiversity globally, develop 
recovery plans and best-practice protocols for parasite conservation, build networks and partnerships 
for parasite conservation, and communicate the intrinsic and functional importance of parasite species 
in ecosystems.
The Parasite Specialist Group faces a great challenge. Although approximately half of all 
animal species are parasitic during at least one life stage, few parasitic species have been assessed for 
the IUCN Red List or targeted for conservation efforts. Rather than considering all 15 hyperdiverse 
phyla of understudied and underprotected animal parasites, the Parasite Specialist Group will focus on 
a subset of parasite biodiversity: metazoan parasites that use vertebrate hosts. This group includes 
parasitic worms (Cestoda, Trematoda, Acanthocephala, Nematoda), insects (e.g. Phthiraptera, 
Siphonaptera, Hippoboscoidea, Oestridae, Polyctenidae, Cimicidae) and arachnids (e.g. Ixodida, 
Spinturnicidae, Trombiculidae). By 2025, the Parasite Specialist Group aims to have assessed the 
conservation status of at least one representative species of each taxonomic group.
Just as habitat conservation is critical for the conservation of free-living species, host 
conservation is critical for parasite conservation. Therefore, the Parasite Specialist Groups is seeking 
new partnerships with vertebrate conservation groups interested in finding ways to conserve parasites 
along with host species. For example, ex situ vertebrate conservation programmes have resulted in the 
extinction of some rare parasite species (e.g. the condor louse Colpocephalum californici), but they 
have also sustained some rare and endemic parasite species along with their threatened hosts (e.g. the 
chewing louse Ardeicola nippon on the crested ibis Nipponia nippon). An immediate priority for the 
new Parasite Specialist Group is to develop best practice guidelines for ex situ parasite conservation 
and work to with interested partners to begin new parasite co-conservation programmes.
The Parasite Specialist Group invites researchers and practitioners in the fields of 
parasitology, ecology, veterinary medicine and conservation to reach out with questions, requests 
for support or ideas for new collaborations."
–Hopkins, S., & Kwak, M. (2023).  Oryx, 57(3), 283-283.

Lack of data to properly model key biological characteristics like abundance or distribution, 
seriously hinder comprehension of biodiversity patterns and their drivers — even for historically well-
studied and charismatic organisms. Knowledge shortfalls are more extreme in the case of parasites, 
which are mostly part of the “hidden biodiversity” and generally have a bad reputation. However, being
an extremely large portion of biodiversity and a fundamental part of ecosystems, failure to consider 
parasites is itself an information shortfall for conservation, and can result in important consequences 
not only for planning strategies to conserve biological diversity, but also to understand fully the 
patterns and processes that shape ecosystems. Parasites exhibit a marked duality: while some species 
are pathogenic and do compromise their host's survival (and human interests), the majority exert 
apparently negligible negative effects on their hosts and could be considered non-pathogenic; indeed, 
parasites are beneficial as they provide important ecosystemic functions and services. Using a 15
comprehensive dataset of fish host-helminth parasites in Mexico as a case study, we review knowledge 
shortfalls relating to parasites, exemplifying their impacts — both positive and negative. A holistic 
appreciation of parasites should consider both their (many) beneficial and (a few, proven) detrimental 
impacts, something which could be operationally incorporated into conservation assessments and 
strategies (e.g., IUCN Green and Red Lists, respectively). Outreach and education are key to modify 
negative perceptions towards parasites, and to induce recognition of their importance for ecosystemic 
function and structure.

Adult fleas are blood-feeding insects that exclusively infest mammals, acting as parasites and 
disease vectors. Although certain species exclusively inhabit nests, others are commonly found on the 
bodies of mammals. Immature stages develop in the soil, inside or near the nests of their respective 
hosts, making them susceptible to environmental alterations. On hosts, flea infestations are usually 
defined by abundance, prevalence, and diversity, varying according to host age, sex, size, behavior, 
habitat, and climate. However, in spite of their vast parasitological importance, fleas have only 
occasionally been used in applied research. This review focuses especially on the use of mammal fleas 
as tools or indicators in solving biological, epidemiological, ecological, and phylogenetic questions, 
and raises new perspectives for future studies.

The Holy Grail of an Insect Tree of Life can only be ‘discovered’ through extensive 
collaboration among taxon specialists, phylogeneticists and centralized frameworks such as Open Tree 
of Life, but insufficient effort from stakeholders has so far hampered this promising approach. The 
resultant unavailability of synthesis phylogenies is an unfortunate situation given the numerous 
practical usages of phylogenies in the near term and against the backdrop of the ongoing biodiversity 
crisis. To resolve this issue, we establish a new online hub that centralizes the collation of relevant 
phylogenetic data and provides the resultant synthesis molecular phylogenies. This is achieved through 
key developments in a proposed pipeline for the construction of a species-level insect phylogeny. The 
functionality of the framework is demonstrated through the construction of a highly supported, species-
comprehensive phylogeny of Diptera, built from integrated omics data, COI DNA barcodes, and a 
compiled database of over 100 standardized, published Diptera phylogenies. Machine-readable forms 
of the phylogeny (and subsets thereof) are publicly available at insectphylo.org, a new public repository
for species-comprehensive phylogenies for biological research.

The Darwin Tree of Life (DToL) project aims to sequence and assemble high-quality genomes 
from all eukaryote species in Britain and Ireland, with the first phase of the project concentrating on 17
family-level coverage plus species of particular ecological, biomedical or evolutionary interest. We 
summarise the processes involved in (1) assessing the UK arthropod fauna and the status of individual 
species on UK lists; (2) prioritising and collecting species for initial genome sequencing; (3) handling 
methods to ensure that high-quality genomic DNA is preserved; and (4) compiling standard operating 
procedures for processing specimens for genome sequencing, identification verification and voucher 
specimen curation. We briefly explore some lessons learned from the pilot phase of DToL and the 
impact of the Covid-19 pandemic.

providing a representative picture of the global distribution of insects. Systematic Entomology, 48(4), 
489-497.
The Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) is the largest databank on primary 
biodiversity data. We examined the completeness and geographical biases for all insect data on GBIF to
determine its representativeness. Our results demonstrate that GBIF is far from providing a reliable 
representation about the global distribution of insects. Despite the growing number of records during 
the last years, few spatial units are well-surveyed. At coarse resolutions, 34% of the world terrestrial 
cells lack data and barely 0.5% have completeness values above 90%. Insects are crucial in many 
ecological functions, and their alarming decline makes it more pressing to have a representative sample
to improve our predictive capacity. However, the dynamic nature of species distributions and the 
strength of anthropogenic forces call for immediate conservation decisions that cannot wait for the 
empirical data on the identity and distribution of insects.

Classification of the biological diversity on Earth is foundational to all areas of research within 
the natural sciences. Reliable biological nomenclatural and taxonomic systems facilitate efficient 
access to information about organisms and their names over time. However, broadly sharing, accessing,
delivering, and updating these resources remains a persistent problem. This barrier has been 
acknowledged by the biodiversity data sharing community, yet concrete efforts to standardize and 18
continually update taxonomic names in a sustainable way remain limited. High diversity groups such as
arthropods are especially challenging as available specimen data per number of species is substantially 
lower than vertebrate or plant groups. The Terrestrial Parasite Tracker Thematic Collections Network 
project developed a workflow for gathering expert-verified taxonomic names across all available 
sources, aligning those sources, and publishing a single resource that provides a model for future 
endeavors to standardize digital specimen identification data. The process involved gathering expert-
verified nomenclature lists representing the full taxonomic scope of terrestrial arthropod parasites, 
documenting issues experienced, and finding potential solutions for reconciliation of taxonomic 
resources against large data publishers. Although discordance between our expert resources and the 
Global Biodiversity Information Facility are relatively low, the impact across all taxa affects thousands 
of names that correspond to hundreds of thousands of specimen records. Here, we demonstrate a 
mechanism for the delivery and continued maintenance of these taxonomic resources, while 
highlighting the current state of taxon name curation for biodiversity data sharing.

Ticks (Ixodida) and Fleas (Siphonaptera) are considered amongst the most important arthropod 
of public health concern due to their ability to transmit vector borne pathogens to humans. By sharing a ‐
common environment, vector borne diseases constituted major setbacks to the development of a pet ‐
population in Bangladesh. This study aimed to determine companion animal associated ticks and fleas ‐
based on morpho-molecular approaches. Between December 2021 and May 2022, 74 animals (62 cats 
and 12 dogs) were examined, of which 17 (27.4%) cats and 9 (75.0%) dogs had ectoparasitic 
infestations, with 35.1% overall prevalence. Morphometrical examination showed the ectoparasites in 
these animals were Ctenocephalides spp. (flea) and Riphicephalus spp. (tick). Genetic analysis using 
the mitochondrial markers i.e. Cytochrome c oxidase subunit 1 (cox1) revealed the presence of two flea
genera i.e., Ctenocephalides canis, Ctenocephalides felis, and one tick genera Rhipicephalus 
sanguineus. Interviews of animal owners indicate that 35.14% of them had no concern about 
ectoparasitic infestation or ectoparasites-borne diseases. Our results indicated that fleas and ticks were 
the most common ectoparasites in companion animals of this area. The zoonotic nature of some 
ectoparasites can be regarded as a public health alert.

The geographical ranges of many mammals and their associated parasites are dynamic. 
Comprehensive documentation of these communities over time provides a foundation for interpreting 
how changing environmental conditions, driven by accelerating climate change, other anthropogenic 
disturbances, and natural events, may influence host-parasite interactions. Fleas (Order Siphonaptera) 
are obligate, hematophagous parasites of birds and mammals with medical interest because of their role
in transmitting pathogens. From 2016 to 2019, we sampled the small mammal and associated flea 
communities in El Malpais National Conservation Area (El Malpais) in Cibola County, New Mexico. 
Among 898 mammalian specimens, 925 fleas representing 29 species were collected from 18 host 
species. Pleochaetis exilis was the most abundant flea species, composing 27% of the total fleas 
collected, whereas Aetheca wagneri was the most prevalent flea species, parasitizing 8% of the 
community sampled. Across a total of 284 hosts recorded with fleas, A. wagneri, Malaraeus eremicus, 
and Peromyscopsylla hesperomys adelpha parasitized the most host species (n = 6 each). Onychomys 
leucogaster (Wied-Neuwied, 1841), the northern grasshopper mouse, a rodent highly implicated in 
plague dynamics, was host for the highest number of flea species (n = 15), followed by Peromyscus 
truei (Shufeldt, 1885) (n = 10). Our aims are to (a) describe the flea-mammal assemblage of a central 
New Mexico site, creating a baseline for diversity against which changing patterns of association can 
be assessed over time; (b) identify previously unrecognized host associations; and (c) examine 
infestation parameters, including the relationships of flea prevalence and mean abundance to host sex, 
host abundance, and seasonality. As such, our study exemplifies the Documentation and Assessment 
phases of the DAMA protocol (Document, Assess, Monitor, Act), a central component of exploring 
distribution and diversity of complex pathogen-host communities across space and time that are 25
essential to a proactive understanding of emerging disease.

mammals in the northern taiga of Western Siberia; and to summarize information on fleas in the studied

The fleas of the Stephanocircidae family are known as "helmet fleas" due to a distinctive 
morphological modification in their head that resembles a helmet. This adaptation allows them to 
navigate through the fur of their hosts more easily and includes an additional ctenidium that provides 
them with enhanced anchorage. Stephanocircidae is divided into two subfamilies: Stephanocircinae, 
distributed in Australia, and Craneopsyllinae, distributed in South America. Craneopsyllinae is 
composed of seven genera, three of which, Cleopsylla, Plocopsylla, and Sphinctopsylla, have isolated 
records in Colombia. Studies on these fleas in the country and South America are scarce and 
fragmented. Therefore, to consolidate knowledge and understand the ecology of helmet fleas in 
Colombia, a systematic review of the records of Cleopsylla, Plocopsylla, and Sphinctopsylla, as well as
the documented associations with their hosts in South America between 1911 and 2023, was conducted.
Additionally, noteworthy new records and associations with bats in Colombia are presented. Based on 
this information, the distribution was evaluated, and a parasite-host interaction network for South 
America was constructed. In this study, the first records of Cleopsylla townsendi and Plocopsylla 
scotinomi in Colombia are presented. Furthermore, the distribution of seven species is expanded to the 
departments of Arauca, Boyacá, and Caldas, and a new association between Cleopsylla townsendi and 
Plocopsylla thor with the bat Myotis handleyi is recorded in the country. Distribution patterns and 
interactions revealed a close association between Plocopsylla with Cleopsylla and Sphinctopsylla, and 
apparent competition is observed between the species of the latter two genera. Finally, the flea-host 
interaction network reflects that these fleas exhibit a low degree of specialization, meaning their 
behavior is primarily generalist. However, their preferred hosts include rodents and other Andean-
distributed mammals, which explains their distribution.

To investigate the species composition of rodents and ectoparasitic fleas on rodents as well as 
the spatiotemporal distribution and changes of the flea index of dominant rodents in Xilin Gol League, 
Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, China, and to provide a basis for plague risk assessment and its 
prevention and control decisions-making. Methods: With the monitoring data of 12 plague surveillance 
points in Xilin Gol League from 2012 to 2021, we used descriptive epidemiological methods to analyze
the temporal and spatial distribution characteristics of main rodents and their flea indexes. Results: 
From 2012 to 2021, a total of 50 551 rodents were captured in Xilin Gol League, involving 18 species, 
13 genera, and 4 families. Among them, 19 958 rodents carried fleas, with an average flea infestation 
rate of 39.48%. A total of 83 147 fleas were collected, belonging to 35 species/subspecies, 14 genera, 
and 5 families, with an overall flea index of 1.64. Meriones unguiculatus, Spermophilus dauricus, and 
Lasiopodomys brandtii were the dominant rodent species. Citellophilus tesquorum mongolicus, 
Xenopsylla conformis conformis, Frontopsylla luculenta, and Nosopsyllus laeviceps kuzenkovi were 
the main parasitic fleas. M. unguiculatus carried more diverse flea species on the body surface than L. 
brandtii and S. dauricus. The mixed flea index (S=-25.000, P=0.032) and S. dauricus flea index (S=-
23.000, P=0.049)showed a downward trend in Xilin Gol League during the ten years. The M. 
unguiculatus flea index and L. brandtii flea index had no significant changes. The S. dauricus flea 
index was significantly higher than the L. brandtii flea index (H=15.000, P < 0.001)and the M. 
unguiculatus flea index (H=-15.000, P < 0.001). There was no significant difference between the L. 
brandtii and M. unguiculatus flea indexes (H < 0.001, P=1.000). The mixed flea index peaked in July at27
4.47. The M. unguiculatus flea index was significantly different between banners/counties of Xilin Gol 
League (H=52.579, P < 0.001), which was highest in Sonid Left and Xianghuang banners. The S. 
dauricus flea index was significantly different between banners/counties of Xilin Gol League 
(H=73.253, P < 0.001), which was highest in West Ujimqin and Zhengxiangbai banners. The L. 
brandtii flea index showed no significant difference between banners/counties of Xilin Gol League 
(H=5.864, P=0.118). Conclusion: The three types of plague foci in Xilin Gol League overlap. Meriones
unguiculatus carries a diversity of fleas, with a high risk of transmitting plague bacteria. Surveillance 
points should comprehensively monitor plague epizootics to prevent plague from resurging among 
animals and expanding to human beings.

The act of blood-feeding can be nutritionally rewarding for blood-feeding arthropods. However,
blood digestion can release pro-oxidant molecules such as heme and iron at potentially harmful levels. 
If left uncontrolled, this heme/iron can cause oxidative damage and eventually cell death. This has led 
to the evolution of various adaptations that protect blood-feeding arthropods against iron- and heme-
associated damage. Here I postulate that the signature of this adaptation can be observed in patterns of 
gene family size. To test this hypothesis, I explore convergent evolutionary expansions and contractions
of gene families in distinct lineages of hematophagous insects. Specifically, I compare the gene content
present in available genomes from blood- feeding and non-blood feeding arthropods (including 
outgroup taxa in the Lepidoptera [moths & butterflies]), to identify possible changes in gene family 
size in the blood-feeding taxa. Of the 206 heme/iron-associated genes identified from the model insect, 
Drosophila melanogaster, five were overrepresented (potentially duplicated) in the blood-feeding taxa: 
spook (cyp307A1), spookier (cyp307A2), cytochrome P450 12e1 (cyp12e1), hormone receptor and 51 
(Hr51), NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) B16.6 subunit (ND-B16.6), and seven were 
underrepresented (potentially lost). However, when only Dipteran (fly) and Siphonaptera (flea) 
genomes were included in the analysis, just one iron gene and one heme gene (NADH dehydrogenase 
(ubiquinone) PDSW subunit (ND-PDSW) were overrepresented in the blood- feeding taxa. 
Interestingly, the expanded cytochrome genes are known detoxifiers of many compounds, including 
heme and iron. More broadly, the analytical approach I employee here could be used to evaluate 
functional convergence for other phenotypic traits, conditional on the availability of annotated genomic
data.

Antibiotic resistance is a significant and growing threat to global public health. However, 
antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have shown promise as they exhibit a broad spectrum of antibacterial 
activities with low potential for resistance development. Insects, which inhabit a wide range of 
environments and are incredibly diverse, remain largely unexplored as a source of novel AMPs. To 
address this, we conducted a screening of the representative transcriptomes from the 1000 Insect 
Transcriptome Evolution (1KITE) dataset, focusing on the homologous reference genes of Cecropins, 
the first identified AMPs in insects known for its high efficiency. Our analysis identified 108 Cecropin 
genes from 105 insect transcriptomes, covering all major hexapod lineages. We validated the gene 
sequences and synthesized mature peptides for three identified Cecropin genes. Through minimal 
inhibition concentration and agar diffusion assays, we confirmed that these peptides exhibited 
antimicrobial activities against Gram-negative bacteria. Similar to the known Cecropin, the three 
Cecropins adopted an alpha-helical conformation in membrane-like environments, efficiently 
disrupting bacterial membranes through permeabilization. Importantly, none of the three Cecropins 
demonstrated cytotoxicity in erythrocyte hemolysis tests, suggesting their safety in real-world 
applications. Overall, this newly developed methodology provides a high-throughput bioinformatic 
pipeline for the discovery of AMP, taking advantage of the expanding genomic resources available for 
diverse organisms.

This review summarizes which body parts have taste function in which insect taxa. Evidence of 
taste by mouthparts, antennae, and tarsi is widespread. Mouthparts that commonly have taste function 
are the labium, including the labella and labial palps, the maxillae, including the galeae and maxillary 
palps, the inner surface of the labrum or clypeolabrum of chewers, and inside the precibarium/cibarium
of hemipterans, which have piercing-sucking mouthparts. Tasting with mandibles has not been found, 
and tasting with the hypopharynx is seldom reported. Use of the antennae appears uncommon among 
fly species, but common among species of lepidopterans, hymenopterans, beetles, and bugs. Although 29
tasting with legs, especially tarsi, is reported mostly for fly and lepidopteran species, there is also 
evidence of it for multiple species of beetles, grasshoppers, and hemipterans, and one species of a 
roach, an ant, and a bee. Ovipositor taste function has been supported for some species of flies, 
lepidopterans, hymenopterans, orthopterans, and odonates. Taste by wings has been much less studied, 
but has been documented in a few fly species. Taste remains unstudied for any species or any body 
parts of Archaeognatha, Dermaptera, Mantodea, Mecoptera, Phasmatodea, Megaloptera, Neuroptera, 
Phthiraptera, Psocoptera, Siphonaptera, as well as Raphidioptera, Strepsiptera, Embioptera, Notoptera, 
and Zoraptera. Across holometabolous insects, larvae have not often been examined, the exception 
being some species of lepidopterans, flies, and beetles. Taste studies of antenna and legs are uncommon
for even lepidopteran and beetle larvae.

We studied latitudinal patterns in the species richness (SR), the phylogenetic diversity (PD), and
the functional diversity (FD) of fleas and their mammalian hosts. We asked whether these patterns in 
either fleas, hosts, or both 1) conform to a classical latitudinal gradient; 2) vary geographically; and 3) 
differ between fleas and hosts. We also asked whether the patterns of PD and FD follow those of SR. 
We collected data on the latitudinal distribution of 1022 flea and 900 mammal species from literature 
sources and calculated the SR, PD, and FD of both groups in 1° latitude bands. Then, we used broken-
stick regression models to analyse separately the latitudinal variation of 1) each diversity facet and 2) 
fleas and hosts in each geographic quadrant. The classical latitudinal gradient pattern was not found in 
either fleas or hosts across any facet of diversity or geographic quadrant, except for the PD of fleas in 
the southeastern quadrant and the FD of hosts in the southwestern quadrant. Latitudinal patterns of the 
SR, PD and FD of fleas and hosts differed substantially between geographic quadrants. Furthermore, 
the latitudinal distributions of flea and host SR were similar in three of four quadrants (except the 
northeastern quadrant), whereas the latitudinal distributions of flea and host PD were similar in the 
southwestern quadrant only. No similarity in flea versus host FD was revealed. The latitudinal patterns 
of flea and host PD and FD mostly did not follow those of their SR. We conclude that latitudinal 
gradients of species richness and phylogenetic and functional diversity appeared not to be universal 
phenomena. Instead, the latitudinal distributions of these diversity facets represent an interplay of 
ecological (current and past) and historical processes. For parasites, the processes acting on hosts add 
another layer of complexity underlying their latitudinal diversity patterns.

the immune response of adult cat fleas (Ctenocephalides felis). Honors College Theses. 
908.https://digitalcommons.georgiasouthern.edu/honors-theses/908
In holometabolous insects, conditions during the larval stage can affect the adult stage. For 
instance, in mosquitoes, reduced larval food and high density can make adults more susceptible to 
infection. Fleas (Siphonaptera), like mosquitoes, go through complete metamorphosis and have adult 
stages that exclusively feed on the blood of vertebrates, including humans. However, flea larvae have 
chewing mandibles and rely on nutrients from dried fecal matter containing vertebrate blood proteins. 33
Their limited mobility and unique nutritional needs confine their development to specific areas, likely 
leading to frequent larval competition in natural conditions. Yet, the influence of larval density on the 
subsequent adult stage has not been explored. In our study using cat fleas (Ctenocephalides felis), we 
investigated the impact of larval competition on development to adulthood, adult body size, and adult 
immunity. We collected eggs to form three groups with different larval population densities (n = 50, 
100, and 150), and maintained consistent nutritional conditions between all groups. We tracked 
development from eggs to pupae and adulthood, measured head and total body length of adults, and 
exposed eclosed adults to a blood meal with live bacteria (Serratia marcescens) for 24 hours to 
determine infection loads. Our findings indicate that low larval density negatively impacts the 
transition from pupa to adults, decreases adult size, and increased adult female susceptibility to 
infection. Overall, our study provides valuable insights into how larval density shapes the biology of 
resulting adult fleas.

Climate change is causing many vectors of infectious diseases to expand their geographic 
distribution as well as the pathogens they transmit are also conditioned by temperature for their 
multiplication. Within this context, it is worth highlighting the significant role that fleas can play as 
vectors of important pathogenic bacteria. For this purpose, our efforts focused on detecting and 
identifying a total of 9 bacterial genera (Rickettsia sp.; Bartonella sp.; Yersinia sp.; Wolbachia sp., 
Mycobacterium sp., Leishmania sp., Borrelia sp., Francisella sp. and Coxiella sp.) within fleas isolated 
from domestic and peridomestic animals in the southwestern region of Spain (Andalusia). Over a 19-
months period, we obtained flea samples from dogs, cats and hedgehogs. A total of 812 fleas was
collected for this study. Five different species were morphologically identified, including C. felis, C. 
Canis, S. cuniculi, P. irritans, and A. erinacei. Wolbachia sp. was detected in all five species identified 
in our study which a total prevalence of 86%. Within Rickettsia genus, two different species, R. felis 
and R. asembonensis were mainly identified in C. felis and A. erinacei, respectively. On the other hand,
our results revealed a total of 131 fleas testing positive for the presence of Bartonella sp., representing a
prevalence rate of 16% for this genus identifying two species B. henselae and B. clarridgeiae. Lastly, 
both Y. pestis and L. infantum were detected in DNA of P. Irritans and C. felis, respectively isolated 
from dogs. With these data we update the list of bacterial zoonotic agents found in fleas in Spain, 
emphasizing the need to continue conducting future experimental studies to assess and confirm
the potential vectorial role of certain synanthropic fleas.

This epidemiological survey aims to provide an update on the main flea species that parasitize 
domestic animals in the Western Andalusia assessing several ecological features that could be 
considered as possible risk factors for flea infestation. Over a 19-month period (June 2021 to January 
2023), we obtained a total of 802 flea samples from 182 dogs (Canis lupus familiaris, Carnivora: 
Canidae, Linnaeus, 1758) and 78 cats (Felis silvestris catus, Carnivora: Felidae, Schreber, 1775). For 
each parasitized host, an epidemiological survey was completed, including the following information: 
geographical origin, age, sex, rural or urban habitat, type of animal's lifestyle (domestic or non-34
domestic), health status, cohabiting or not with other animals and the total number of collected fleas. 
The most common species was Ctenocephalides felis (Siphonaptera: Pulicidae) (Bouché, 1835) with a 
total of 713 specimens, which accounted for 89% of the total fleas. The second most abundant species 
was Pulex irritans (Siphonaptera: Pulicidae) (Linnaeus, 1758) with a total of 46 collected fleas (6% of 
the total). The remaining species identified were Archaeopsylla erinacei (Siphonaptera: Pulicidae) 
(Bouché, 1835) (25 specimens), Spilopsyllus cuniculi (Siphonaptera: Pulicidae) (Dale, 1878) (12 
specimens) and Ctenocephalides canis (Siphonaptera: Pulicidae) (Curtis, 1826) (6 specimens), which 
accounted for 3%, 1% and 1%, respectively, of the total fleas collected. The months with the highest 
number of collected fleas were, in ascending order, May 2022, September 2021 and July 2021. Dogs 
had a greater diversity of flea species, and flea sex ratios were female biased in all identified species 
and among all studied hosts. Finally, we identified some potential host risk factors that promoted higher
flea intensities, such as living in rural areas, or presenting other pathologies.

Book Review
House of Trelawney
(2020)
by Hannah Rothschild, Bloomsbury Publ., London.
It's a fictional novel, but one of the characters is a "flea-trapper" and great aunt. She resembles 
Dame Miriam Rothschild, one of the great entomologists of the 20th century. The Trelawney family 
live on an ancient estate that sprawls along 40 miles of wooded riverside in the English countryside.
 
The great aunt lives away from the main house among the woods in a derelict cottage with 
microscopes, computers, journals, and tens of thousands of preserved flea specimens, at least until she's
run out of hearth and home by her pet mice that served before escaping as hosts for her fleas. She 
frequently searches for and examines carefully carcasses in the woods and on roads to collect more 
fleas. 
The great aunt wins world awards and makes important contributions to agriculture, 
conservation, and science. The reader learns that the British protect their bats better than the U.S. For 
the "flea-trapper", bats, rodents, and fleas are neither trivial nor hobby. 
A whimsical and humorous portrait of a family, the novel perspective on the great aunt rounds 
out our understanding of eccentrics and geniuses. It could make an interesting movie.
–R.L. Bossard, Editor

"Although the argument for studying parasites is clear, the proposed protocols are too limited to 
advance the understanding of ecological (much less evolutionary) responses to species invasions, 
changes in climate, and land use (Kao et al. 2012) or even the long-term dynamics of rodent– parasite 
systems. We offer a critique and an expanded vision for NEON's mammal–parasite protocols beyond 
select tick-, mosquito-, and rodent-borne pathogens. We encourage expanded sampling of (a) the 
parasite assemblage and (b) the host assemblage, along with (c) a two-pronged sampling design based 
on both rigorous sample archival and “mark-release” approaches. To fail to do either (a) or (b) excludes
the possibility of both community- and ecosystem-level perspectives, and failure to do (c) effectively 
excludes sample-based studies and future work using yet-to-be- developed technologies. Reflecting on 
the long and highly productive history of specimen-based research (e.g., Suarez and Tsutsui 2004), we 
encourage NEON to take a more holistic, synergistic, and sample-intensive approach as a basis for 
long-term environmental observatories. "

The Beringian Coevolution Project: Holistic collections of mammals and associated parasites reveal 
novel perspectives on evolutionary and environmental change in the North.  Arctic Science: 3(3), 585-
617.
[The Beringian Coevolution Project (BCP), a field program underway in the high northern 
latitudes since 1999, has focused on building key scientific infrastructure for integrated specimen-based
studies on mammals and their associated parasites. BCP has contributed new insights across temporal 
and spatial scales into how ancient climate and environmental change have shaped faunas, emphasizing
processes of assembly, persistence, and diversification across the vast Beringian region. BCP 
collections also represent baseline records of biotic diversity from across the northern high latitudes at 
a time of accelerated environmental change. These specimens and associated data form an unmatched 
resource for identifying hidden diversity, interpreting past responses to climate oscillations, 
documenting contemporary conditions, and anticipating outcomes for complex biological systems in a 
regime of ecological perturbation. Because of its dual focus on hosts and parasites, the BCP record also
provides a foundation for comparative analyses that can document the effects of dynamic change on the
geographic distribution, transmission dynamics, and emergence of pathogens. By using specific 
examples from carnivores, eulipotyphlans, lagomorphs, rodents, ungulates, and their associated 
parasites, we demonstrate how broad, integrated field collections provide permanent infrastructure that 
informs policy decisions regarding human impact and the effect of climate change on natural 
populations.]54

 Editorial
 “Flea pupae"
"The pseudosetae have not yet been studied in the pupal stages but Jordan...  drew attention to 
the fact that if the mesonotum is injured in larval life the pseudosetae may develop into spines similar 
to those in the pronotal comb". 
- Rothschild (1975)
"I believed that this [spandrel] concept—a predictable form that arises as a side consequence 
rather than a direct adaptation—had important application to biology but lacked a name. (Darwin’s 
“correlation of growth” came to mind, but his term is ambiguous and never caught on in any case.) I 
thought, and continue to feel, that spandrel is the most obvious, the most useful, and the most 
historically sanctioned term available for such a central concept. Moreover, the term spandrel is 
particularly applicable to biological problems of adaptation because the architectural concept stresses 
the same point of distinction between historical origin and later utility that has proven so troublesome 
in evolutionary theory."
- Gould (1997)
Dear Flea News Reader,
In the last of the series on immature fleas, I discuss the least known, but quite interesting stage, 
the flea pupa.
 The pupa may show traits that are not necessarily subject to direct selection because the pupa is
inactive in a cocoon. However, these traits are necessary byproducts developmentally that may form 
important adaptive traits in subsequent stages. Such traits have been termed "spandrels" (Gould and 
Lewontin 1979). These characteristics make immature fleas particularly valuable to understand "evo-
devo" (evolution and developmental biology).
 Does the flea show spandrels? 
 Studying the pupa is facilitated with the "naked pupae" technique (Dryden & Smith 1994, 
Lawrence & Foil 2002): Wandering larvae, about to spin cocoons, are placed in round-bottom 
microtiter wells. Such containers seem to prevent the larvae from gaining purchase to spin a cocoon, so
the larvae pupate without a cocoon. Naked pupae allow easy viewing of exterior anatomy.
 Effects of temperature, humidity, infection (cestodes), and insecticides on pupae of limited flea 
taxa, mainly Pulicidae, have been examined (Mellanby 1933, Snodgrass 1946, Sharif 1949, Marshall 
1967, Margalit & Shulov 1972, Cerqueira and Linardi 1979, Silverman et al. 1981, Linardi & 
Guimarāes 1993, Metzger & Rust 1997, Miller et al. 1999, Krasnov et al. 2001, Kreppel et al. 2016). 
Observations on flea pupae revealed puzzling structures when Sharif (1937) saw what he 
hypothesized were vestigial wing-buds. However, Poenicke (1969) and Rothschild (1975) disputed 
this, noting that the structures were in Ceratophyllidae, but not Pulicidae. Other puzzling flea structures
that could be spandrels with developmental significance include the frontal and deciduous tubercles 
found in some fleas (Snodgrass 1946, Medvedev 2015), combs (Medvedev 2017), spiracle and trachea 
elaborations (Beaucournu and Laudisoit 2009), and unciform sclerotizations ("consistent in a given 
species, unciform sclerotizations are random with respect to genus or other taxa", Beaucournu et al. 3
2013). 
Pupal homologs and synapomorphies (shared, possibly derived characters that may indicate 
common ancestors between Mecoptera and Siphonaptera) were proposed by Kluge 2002, who 
concluded that "The pupal leg buds may replicate the initial position of larval legs in the flea ancestors 
(whereas in the present-day fleas, the larval legs are completely lost).".
I propose that the flea pupae "wing-buds" are actually spandrels -  necessary structures to 
develop the specialized spiracles, trachea, and musculature of the Ceratophyllidae adult flea. An 
advanced form of respiratory system may adapt fleas to dry or cold environments, and could have 
facilitated the diffusion of newer fleas like Ceratophyllidae around the globe.
Flea pupae and the other immature stages are intriguing and under-studied, especially in regard 
to diapause, developmental temperature, water relations (Fielden et al. 2004), and embryology. Their 
characteristics are probably as or more important for understanding some aspects of flea life, their 
ecology and evolution, as is the well-studied adult (Cerqueira and Linardi 1979, Linardi & Guimarāes 
1993, Szpila et al. 2024).
Yours in fleas,
R.L. Bossard

The Ectoparasite Collection, especially that of Siphonaptera, housed at the Department of 
Parasitology, Federal University of Minas Gerais (UFMG), Brazil, is now deposited at the René 
Rachou Institute, Oswaldo Cruz Institute Foundation (FIOCRUZ), Avenida Augusto de Lima, 1715, 
30.190-002, Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais State, Brazil.

University of Minas Gerais, who organized and expanded it for over 55 years of research and scientific 
activities. The current curator is Dr. Daniel Moreira de Avelar, e-mail: aveldan#gmai.com

Seminars of Interest to Parasitologists
 Free Online 
1. Ecological Radiations of Mammals: Before & After the K/Pg Mass Extinction
Gregory Wilson Mantilla, University of Washington, Burke Museum of Natural History
https://doi.org/10.52843/cassyni.xg75qh
2. Extinctions along the last legs of the first human migrations to Australia
Prof. Julien Louys, Griffith University
https://doi.org/10.52843/cassyni.k9y1yq
3. Conservation Biogeography of Australasian Marsupials
Assoc. Prof Diana Fisher, University of Queensland
 https://doi.org/10.52843/cassyni.4j8sdx
Abstract: "The diverse and distinctive Australasian marsupial fauna has experienced 
considerable loss over the last 200 years. Seventeen of the 176 Australian marsupial species have 
become extinct in this period (~10%), far higher than the global average (1.4%). Many extinct 
Australian marsupials were formerly abundant and widespread. About 40% of Australian marsupials 
are now threatened. The pattern of decline in Australian marsupials is broadly similar to that of 
Australia’s native rodents- invasive mammalian predators and land use that facilitates them are the 
major problems. Knowledge of the marsupial faunas of Papua New Guinea and Indonesia is relatively 
poor. Both regions have high endemism. There are 96 species of marsupials on the main island of New 
Guinea and surrounding small islands, and 15 species in Wallacea (the islands of Indonesia and East 
Timor east of Wallace’s line) including five shared with New Guinea. Although none are listed as 
Extinct, two Critically Endangered marsupials are flagged “possibly extinct.” Most threatened New 
Guinean and Wallacean species follow the globally typical pattern of high vulnerability in island 
endemics and small-range mammals with specialist habitats. The major threats to marsupials of New 
Guinea and Indonesia are habitat loss, hunting, and low levels of awareness and investment in 10
conservation and research. Many Australasian marsupial species – particularly mountain-top endemics 
are increasingly threatened by climate change."
These seminars introduce three of the contemporary researchers on mammal evolution. 
Radiations of mammals, the subject of the first seminar speaker Professor Mantilla, has been a 
mystery. The origin of the placenta is unclear. Insectivores are now a polyphyletic group. Marsupials 
never seemed common in Africa, so what was there? New fossils and understanding of the timing, 
origins, dispersal, and extinctions of mammalian lineages are critical to understanding the diversity of 
fleas and other parasites.
The second seminar looks at fossil discoveries by Professor Louys of Holocene (since 
approximately 11,700 years ago) animal extinctions in the Indo-Malay biogeographical realm. 
This realm is poorly known biotically and variable in extent, depending on the biota examined, 
usually including India, SE Asia including Indochina and southern China, Malaysia, and western 
Indonesia. It is demarcated by various hypothetical biotic boundaries such as the Kangar-Pattani 
Floristic Line, Lydekker Line, Wallace Line, and Weber Line. Eastern Indonesia (mainly Papua New 
Guinea) is generally considered in the Australian realm.
The Indo-Malay area looked much different in the Pleistocene (2.58 million to 11,700 years 
ago) because of glaciation with the sea level lower and many of the islands we see today in the 17,000 
islands of Indonesia connected by an terrestrial plain called Sunda Land (Sunda Shelf) that is now 
underwater, much like the Beringia and Doggerland, southern North Sea of today, were once dry land.
The seminar speaker Louys expounds further how migration of Homo sapiens into Indo-Malay 
had several coincidental events. Hominids disappeared such as Homo erectus and Homo floresiensis 
(the "Hobbits"). Pongids (orangutans) were formerly widely distributed in open savannah, but are 
largely extirpated except for small areas of deep forest.
This seminar notes that the megafauna, such as species related to elephants and giant lizards, 
seem to disappear with the appearance of humans approximately 10,000 to 50,000 years ago, consistent
with data from throughout the globe. Not until much later (a mere 1,500 years before the present day) 
did smaller species in Indo-Malay such as giant rats ( Comphymys, and Ratini) that are several times 
larger than the extant black rats, experience extinctions coincident with the appearance of metal tools 
and widespread deforestation by humans of trees such as sandalwood. This suggests to Louys that 
human technology can either diminish or preserve biodiversity, depending on how it is used.
Undoubtedly, these giant rats hosted fleas, so like the Neotropical realm with loss of marsupials,
the Indo-Malay realm placental mammals probably experienced extinctions of their parasites.
The last seminar introduces some of the astonishing and beautiful diversity of marsupials and 
monotremes in Australian realm. These animals can be grouped according to the presenter Professor 
Fisher into two groups: arid land animals inhabiting the western 2/3 of Australia, and animals of the 
wet forest inhabiting the eastern third, plus islands to the north such as New Guinea.11
Surprisingly, it is the arid land marsupials that are most endangered because of land use and 
invasive eutherian (placental) mammals such as fox, rabbit, cattle, sheep. This is not to say all the 
marsupials in the wet forest are doing okay; they are not. Many are extinct or critically endangered.
What does this have to do with fleas? Marsupials are host to interesting parasites. Many fleas 
that are considered primitive or basal to other fleas are on these mammals, including 
Pygiopsyllomorpha, Macropsylla, Stephanocircidae (helmet fleas), and Doratopsyllinae (marsupial and
shrew fleas). This last group is represented in Australia by two genera: Acedestia and Idilla.
I wondered why these two genera? After viewing this seminar, I surmised that Acedestia seems 
to be associated with the arid land ecosystems of the south and west Australia. and Idilla seems to be in
wet forests of east Australia. These fleas are likely adapted to contrasting thermal moisture regimes, as 
we may see with the deer mice fleas in North America, Aetheca wagneri in the west and Orchopeas 
leucopus in the east.
These seminars are worth watching if you are interested in mammal evolution.
R.L. Bossard

"Life History Strategies Among the Siphonaptera"
by A.H. Benton
Transcribed and annotated by R.L. Bossard
[The following are notes of A.H. Benton, unpublished to my knowledge, that was as I recall the 
basis for a speech by him at the University of Utah circa 1984. C.E. Hopla commented 
on the term "strategies", do fleas really "strategize"? Many of the questions remain 
unanswered. R.L. Bossard]
Many years ago, I used to teach a course called field biology, and one of the requirements of the
course was the performance of a small research project. Since it was a two hour one semester course, 
the project was of necessity pretty minor, and a good percentage of the students failed to secure any 
significant results. In those cases their paper at the end of the semester usually closed with some 
variation on this sentence: "I never realized how hard it is to establish a simple fact".
This confession is the beginning of scientific wisdom. I always felt that those who wrote such 
sentences had achieved a large part of what I had hoped they would achieve in doing the project. What 
I am going to tell you today is what I believe to be some facts about flea life histories. You will notice 
many gaps, many "maybes" and "probablys" and "I thinks". After all I've been working on fleas only 
about 35 years, so there’s a lot I don’t know yet.
I would like to begin by reviewing the flea life cycle, in case you have forgotten. Fleas are, of 
course, holometabolous insects, which means that the adults lay eggs, small oval whitish structures 
which hatch out into maggot-like larvae. These larvae feed voraciously on bits of skin and feces and 
blood and on each other, and no doubt on other things we don't know about [1]. They undergo three 
instars [2], and then pupate. The pupa is usually contained within a silken cocoon, to which may or 
may not be appended bits of sand or other detritus [3]. This pupa undergoes the necessary 
transformations, and emerges in due time as the adult flea. Adult fleas may live for a year or more, but 
probably is only a month or so during which time they feed, mate and produce the next generation. 
Most fleas move on and off their host quite freely, and mating and oviposition take place mostly in the 
nest or burrow or other habitat of the host rather than on the host itself [4]. If oviposition occurs on the 
host, most species produce eggs which will simply fall of and undergo development wherever they fall 
[5]. Larvae are very rarely found on the host, but it may be normal for larvae in severe arctic regions to 
stay on the host, at least in some species [6].
Now on to life history strategies. Obviously, this term covers a multitude of sins. It can refer to 
host selection, to reproductive strategy, to larval habits, to emergence, to host finding, and so on. Let's 
begin with some variation on the typical life cycle and habits of fleas.
Within one family, the Tungidae, the adult flea attaches itself to the host in a rather permanent 
manner, the female burrowing into the skin of the host and then swelling to a relatively enormous size. 
The process is peculiar in that growth and change occur in the imago stage, and this is called neosomy. 
The head and thorax usually remain relatively unchanged, but the abdomen swells from 100 to 1000 
times and the female quickly produces eggs. In one species, the males do not feed as larvae, but pupate 13
on the  host, emerging after the female has engorged. They mate and the male dies, without ever having
fed, having lived its entire lifespan with only the energy contained in the egg [7].
The American sticktight flea ( Echidnaphaga gallinacea) attached firmly and is partially 
imbedded [sic, embedded], but does not undergo neosomy. This is our smallest pulicid, and one of our 
most eclectic feeders: common on poultry, dogs and many wild mammals. It is one of the very few 
fleas to feed regularly on both birds and mammals.
Within the Vermipsyllidae, mostly parasites of carnivores and ungulates, neosomy also occurs 
[8].  One Asiatic species, Vermipsylla alakurt, which feeds on sheep, is said to reach more than 1.5 
centimeters in length when fully expanded. Since the average flea runs about two to four millimeters in 
length, you can readily realize that this is quite a remarkable size for a flea. In the East [U.S.A.], we 
have only one species, Chaetopsylla lotoris, which is commonly found on wild carnivores, particularly 
the raccoon and the gray fox. While not approaching the size of V . alakurt, it is quite a large flea.
Bat fleas form a distinct family, the Ischnopsyllidae. In the Northeast [U.S.A.], we have only 
three bat fleas. The life history of Myodopsylla borealis, which was described only a few years ago, 
largely unknown, but the others represent an interesting contrast in strategy.
Our Eastern [North American] bats, with few exceptions, winter in caves or attics or other 
protected sites, and breed in summer colonies which, nowadays, are usually in buildings - attics of 
large buildings - lofts of old barns, and such places. Myodopsylla insignis is a parasite of the little 
brown bat, Myotis lucifugus, and less commonly other Myotis. In this species, [flea] reproduction 
occurs in the [bat's] breeding colony. Two recent studies, one by Mary Ellen Tracy at Boston University
and the other by Stephen Smith at Ohio State University, have given us a fairly good knowledge of this 
species, though their accounts differ in one way which will become evident in a moment. Eggs laid at 
the time of breeding fall from the host into the guano under the bats hanging from the rafters. Here the 
flea develops through the larval stage, requiring both blood and bat guano to mature. The blood 
presumably comes from adult flea above, squirting out feces which consist of partially digested blood. 
After pupation, the adult flea emerges, and is then presented with a major problem. How does it get to 
the bats, several feet away vertically? One way would be for them to crawl away from the bats to the 
eaves, then up a slanting rafter till they reach a bat. Some authorities believe this is the method of 
choice. In a recent paper, it has been demonstrated that a closely related European species moves 
upward in a different manner. In the breeding colonies, young bats often fall from the rafters into the 
guano. Adult bats, presumably the parents, rescue such fallen bats within a short time, but in the 
meantime, several fleas have found them and are thus carried up to the rafters where they can find 
abundant food. If the bat is not rescued, the fleas will at least be able to feed on it as long as it remains 
alive, which will give them enough nourishment so that they can breed. This process has not been 
observed in our Myotis, but it seems logical that it does occur. [9]
Now comes the unanswered question on which Tracy and Smith disagree. What happens 
between the end of one breeding season and the onset of the next one? Tracy states that adults 
accompany the bats to their wintering quarters and return with them in the spring to start a new 
generation. Smith thinks that they probably survive as pupae, overwintering in the guano and coming 
out when bats return in the spring. He bases this opinion on 2 facts: 1) He found very few fleas on 14
hibernating bats, and 2) a large number of fleas appeared almost at once when bats returned to their 
breeding sites. I suspect that both are wrong, and that some adults overwinter in crevices in the rafters 
and emerge in spring to feed and lay eggs. In my experience, few if any fleas are found on bats in 
hibernating quarters. I and my students have collected hundreds, but have found significant numbers of 
fleas only in the breeding sites. It would seem possible to remove bats from a cave and take them to a 
known summer breeding site, and see if they pick up fleas there and if so how fast. No one to my 
knowledge has done this.
The second Eastern [North American] flea about which we know a good deal is Nycteridopsylla
chapini, a parasite of the big brown bat, Eptesicus fuscus. This flea spends the entire life in the 
wintering caves. Big brown bats in breeding colonies are flealess, at least in my rather extensive 
experience. Adult fleas live in crevices in the cave walls and emerge to feed periodically. Eggs are laid 
in these crevices, or sometimes when the flea is on a host. If the eggs fall to the floor they are probably 
lost. In the crevices, there is abundant blood in the form of flea droppings, and these larvae do not 
require bat guano to develop. When these fleas emerge as adults, if they do so during the hibernating 
season, they will be within inches of a suitable host. Again, we do not know how they over-summer, 
but it is likely to be as either pupa or adult. We owe our knowledge of this flea largely to Nixon Wilson,
of Northern Iowa University, who studied them in caves in Indiana. A Czech scientist, Hurka, has 
studied a species with the same life history pattern as this in Europe, and he was unable to find any 
evidence of the fleas in any stage in summer in the caves. Of course, if pupae were deep in crevices, 
they would be virtually impossible to find, whereas adults would be more likely to be seen, which 
might suggest that the pupa is the more probable over-summering stage. [10]
I have left to the last the most complex situation yet studied, and the one which I have the most 
direct knowledge, since my students and I have been working on it for nearly ten years. It involves four
species of fleas, all of which infest the southern flying squirrel, Glaucomys volans, in the Northeast 
[U.S.A.]. Some ten years ago one of my students trapped a flying squirrel in a forest near the college 
where I teach. Fascinated by these pretty little creatures, he read up on them and found that they will 
readily use nest boxes. So he built a half dozen nest boxes and put them on trees in the area where the 
squirrel had been caught. To his delight, he soon had squirrels using his boxes. His preliminary work 
demonstrated the presence of four species of fleas, and later on a student named Jon Day studied their 
life histories and erected a couple of dozen boxes [11]. After Jon completed his study, Michael Surman 
attempted laboratory rearing studies on these fleas [11]. Since then I have tried to fill in some of the 
gaps which remain in our data. Unfortunately there are still some gaps left.
It is quite easy to begin with collection of eggs, because eggs of each species can be readily 
recognized. Opisodasys pseudarctomys is a fairly large flea - this is a male - and lays large oval eggs 
with little surficial [sic, superficial] character. This egg is not in perfect shape, but may give you some 
idea. Epitedia faceta is a small flea, and lays smaller eggs which are somewhat urn-shaped. 
Conorhinopsylla stanfordi is a rather odd-looking flea, especially the male. Its name means cone-nosed 
flea, which is not entirely inappropriate. Its eggs are beautifully sculptured in a reticulated pattern 
which makes them easily recognizable. The fourth flea is Orchopeas howardi, a parasite of all kinds of 
squirrels - gray, red, fox, chipmunk - as well as the flying squirrel. I have no pictures of its eggs, but 
they are small, oval and very smooth.15
In the laboratory, under 20 degrees Celsius conditions, eggs of three of these species hatch in 
less than a week. Larval periods vary but are about a week or so under these conditions. Pupal periods 
are relatively uniform at about seven or eight days. Thus an average cycle from oviposition to 
emergence of the imago would be about three weeks, give or take a few days.
In nature the situation is not quite so simple. If we collect an occupied nest in January, adults 
will be largely Orchopeas howardi witih small numbers of each of the other species. If, however, we 
keep the nest in the laboratory large numbers of Opisodasys pseudarctomys will emerge in about ten 
days, indicating that they were in the pupal stage when the nest was brought in. In nature, this 
emergence occurs very suddenly and in great numbers about the end of February or early March, after a
few warm days. If we collect a nest in February, practically all adults are Orchopeas howardi, but again
large numbers of Opisodasys will emerge in a few days. If we sift such nest material carefully and 
extract larvae and eggs, most of the larvae will be Conorhinopsylla and the only viable eggs will be 
those of Epitedia faceta. [12]
I construe this to mean that Orchopeas howardi overwinter in the adult form, and reproduce 
near the end of winter to produce an immense new generation in late March or April. Opisodasys 
pseudarctomys overwinter in the pupal form, with a large emergence taking place in very early spring. 
Epitedia faceta overwinter in the egg, while the larvae of Conorhinopsylla stanfordi overwinter. 
Orchopeas has at least four or five generations per year, Opisodasys has three or four. I have taken 
good numbers of adults in late summer in Minnesota and northern New York, but not around western 
New York, so I am not sure if a fourth generation per year occurs here in the summer. [13]
We feel that we have the annual cycles of these two species pretty well in hand. The other two 
present a problem. Conorhinopsylla appears to have but one adult generation per year emerging 
through the fall. I find this rather hard to believe, and it is quite possible that they work in two 
generations in this fall and winter period. However, from then on adults are almost never taken. They 
overwinter as larvae, and I have maintained larvae for up to sixty days in an outdoor box in my 
laboratory window. I was unable to rear any of these larvae to adulthood, however, so I do not know 
what happens to them from then to late September. One might suspect that they pupate in spring, and 
spend the summer as pupae. But I simply don't know.
Epitedia faceta overwinter, as I have said, as eggs. I have been able to collect viable eggs of this
species as late as March, when they were the only viable eggs I could find in the nests. Of course, a few
adults live all or most of the winter, but I think most of the eggs are laid in early winter. If these eggs 
produce a spring generation, we have not been able to detect it. [14]
Just when I left Fredonia, I collected a nest which had many adult fleas. I did not have time to 
look at very many, but among the 15 or so that I collected there was at least 1 Epitedia. Perhaps I will 
find a spring generation of adults in this nest when I return.
Our model is not without flaws, as we fully realize. When we extract nest material from a box, 
removing all parasites in the process, we alter the future events in that box. When we try to rationalize 
data from field collections, data from laboratory studies and data from nests maintained under more or 
less natural outdoor conditions but in the laboratory, we run into difficulties. However, when data 16
secured in al these ways point to the same general conclusions, we think that these conclusions have 
some validity as far as they go.
Just a week or two ago, I read that the incidence of bubonic plague was increasing in the 
western United States. Since fleas are the vectors of this often fatal disease, its increase emphasizes the 
importance of understanding flea life histories. I hope that what I have said today may spark an interest 
in the study of fleas in at least one or two of you, and you will be able to have as much fun and 
satisfaction from that study as I have had over the past 35 years. 
Thank you.
- A.H. Benton
Annotations of R.L. Bossard to A.H. Benton's "Life History Strategies Among the Siphonaptera"
1. Flea larvae species show a variety of diets, feeding behaviors, and mandible shapes of complex 
three-dimensional forms, including chewing with mandibles or sucking fluids with pharynx. Flea larvae
can be detritivores on organic matter, carnivores on mites, ticks, etc., or cannibals on flea eggs, other 
larvae, naked pupae, and adult fleas. Uropsylla tasmanica (Lycopsyllidae) larvae feed on their 
vertebrate hosts (Marshall 1981).
The dietary requirements of flea larvae for  blood of specific hosts, fungi (yeast), organic matter,
etc. appear rather involved in the literature and dependent on the species and their habitat. 
Ctenocephalides larvae do not eat organic matter (Krämer et al. 2001), but eat blood or adult flea feces,
as do Echidnophaga larvae; Xenopsylla eat organic matter but are helped by yeast vitamins (Sharif). 
Tunga monositus larvae do not feed (Elbel 1991).
Hinkle et al. (1991) hypothesized that "fleas may have initially been scavengers... they have 
subsequently evolved nearly complete hematophagy" for both adults and parental care of their larva. 
Silverman and Appel (1994) hypothesized: "host blood excretion [by adult fleas] evolved in response to
larval nutritional requirements.", however, Almeida et al. (2020) showed that blood in tick feces was 
also usable by flea larvae. 
A variety of flea larval mandibles illustrated by Elbel and Pilgrim ranged from broad and 
generalized insect cutting/chewing mandible ( Rhadinopsylla) to specialized, narrow mandibles, some 
with 3 or 5 spatulate teeth ( Hystrichopsylla, Ceratophyllidae). Flea larvae of different species in the 
same nest may have different mandible shapes. Pilgrim (1988) hypothesized that this had to do with 
differences in diet. Specialization on food could minimize interspecific competition among flea species 
(see note 14 below). Also, Notiopsylla (Pygiopsyllidae) mandibles change shape as larvae age. Pilgrim 
(1998) again hypothesized differences in diet. This could minimize intraspecific competition between 
larvae of different ages. In this regard, there are 2 forms of cat flea feces that Hinkle (1991) 
hypothesized fed different instars.

lifestyle within fleas".

9. There seem to be at least 5 ways that bat fleas in guano on the floors, walls, and ceilings of the roost 
could reach bats hanging from the ceiling of the roost. 
i. Bat fleas such as Sternopsylla distincta are slow walkers and weak jumpers, but have long 19
limbs and can climb up a steep incline in the laboratory (negative geotropism). This climbing ability 
may be sufficient to bring them to the ceiling (Elbel & Bossard 2007), however Hutson (1981) noted, 
in regard to bat flea Ischnopsyllus simplex, "There was no evidence of any of these fleas making any 
attempt to climb". In Myodopsylla insignis, jumping depended on whether or not the flea had reached 
the host (Smith and Clay 1988). Climbing and jumping in bat fleas may be plastic behaviors: Unfed 
fleas climb and jump, fed fleas do not. Or these behaviors may differ in different species.
Unknown stimuli of unknown organs of bat fleas likely triggers pupal emergence and host-
locating behaviors (Smith and Clay 1988, Elbel & Bossard 2007).
ii. Bats occasionally brush up or even collide against barriers as they fly, and there are 
"groundings" by young bats learning to fly (Hutson 1981, Orbach and Fenton 2010, Sändig et al. 2014).
When bat fleas Sternopsylla distincta ascend to the highest point they can (such as onto the tip of a 
stalagmite), they quest (Elbel et al. 1999, Elbel & Bossard 2007). If bats brush by, it seems likely the 
flea could latch on. 
iii. As Benton describes, bats often retrieve fallen pups (Kunz & Hood 2000, Bohn et al. 2009), 
presumably along with fleas from the floor of the roost. 
iv. Earwigs (Dermaptera), showing negative geotropism (Hutson 1981), carry bat fleas upward 
in an unusual phoresy in Indo-Malaysian caves (Hastriter et al. 2017). An earwig carrying fleas 
possibly could also grapple onto bats. 
Phoresy is important for fleas in order to balance the conflicting demands on a metapopulation 
between dispersal and host-specificity (Bartlow & Agosta 2021, cf. bat fly: Dick & Patterson 2007, 
beetle: Ohnishi et al. 2021). "Accidental" vertebrate hosts are frequently found with fleas; even if the 
flea is unable to complete its life cycle on them, the flea could be transported to new and improved 
environments, e.g., carnivores transporting rabbit fleas (Iannino et al. 2017), contra Belthoff et al. 2021.
Fleas themselves carry phoretic mites (Houck  & OConnor 1991, Hastriter  & Bush 2014, Bezerra-
Santos et al. 2021).
v. Finally, some eggs may be laid in ceiling crevices so the fleas are already near to the bats. All 
of these behaviors could use further observations.

10. Each of the 4 genera of bat fleas in temperate North America (north of Mexico) - Hormopsylla, 
Myodopsylla, Nycteridopsylla, and Sternopsylla - (Lewis and Lewis 1994) occupy a unique niche 21
which may be determined by whether the host is a migrator (Molassidae) or a hibernator 
(Vespertilionidae), and the thermal niche (cool or warm) (Bossard 2017). For example, Sternopsylla 
distincta overwinters as pupae in temperate caves abandoned by migrating Molassidae (Elbel and 
Bossard 2007), but some fleas might also survive as adults on bats which have migrated to winter 
roosts in the south (Bossard 2017).
Several have commented on bat flea rarity. Lewis (1964) noted: “distribution of bat fleas is one 
of the most enigmatic problems in the entire field… Doubtless the rarity of bat fleas in this area is in 
part attributable to lack of collecting. Even in areas that have been thoroughly investigated, however, 
these fleas are still uncommon", 
Marshall (1981) remarked: Only 4% of bat species in Panama, and 6% in Malaysia have fleas, 
so "conditions in the host's home are presumably critical" [it is unclear if temperate bats are more 
infested].
Chilton (et al. 2000): "The life cycles of most of the 131 named taxa of bat fleas (Siphonaptera: 
Ischnopsyllidae) are unknown, but they seem to have particular affinity for hosts that are gregarious 
and that occupy permanent roosts, such as buildings or caves (Lewis and Lewis, 1994). These sites 
permit the accumulation of bat guano beneath the roost, which is essential for larval development and 
completion of the life cycle (Lewis and Lewis, 1994)", "Frequency of infestation may be related to the 
host’s roosting behaviors. All species of ectoparasitic insects found in this study spend some portion of 
their life cycle off the host (Marshall, 1982). Frequent roost-switching and small colony size may result
in low infestation rates (Lewis, 1996)", and "many M. lucifugus roost in buildings or in deep cavities in
trees (Fenton and Barclay, 1980; Crampton and Barclay, 1998), favoring the accumulation of guano 
necessary for completion of the flea’s life cycle. However, the feces of bats that roost beneath loose 
bark will generally fall far from the roost, and thus these bats will likely experience lower infestation 
prevalences of fleas." (Chilton et al. 2000). 
Different roosts have different advantages for the bat and flea. In addition to physical 
challenges, I wonder if some roosts could have predators or pathogens on fleas such as mites, 
pseudoscorpions, or fungi especially in tropical areas, or lack the unusual phoresy when earwigs carry 
fleas.

12. One of the advantages of working with the flying squirrel flea community is that eggs, larvae (Elbel
and Bossard 2007), and adults are now identifiable to species. Pupae may be identified by letting them 
emerge as adults. Benton did not count immature stages to my knowledge, but these data would 
enlighten the life histories involved.
13. Benton hypothesizes that each species in a flea community overwinters in a different stage. It is 
untested to what extent this describes other flea communities, but nests of diverse rodent species often 
have 4 or 5 dominant flea species, seasonally spaced (Bossard 2022). 
We might predict that Orchopeas howardi adults would occur as broadly temperature tolerant 
including the coldest time of the year, Opisodasys pseudarctomys  in hottest (summer) temperatures, 
Epitedia faceta and Conorhinopsylla stanfordi  intermediate (spring and fall) temperatures. This tests 
the hypothesis that each species is adapted to a different thermal niche (Bossard 2022).  Indeed, 
Orchopeas howardi occurred at coldest or hottest temperatures of the year, but with an absence at 
intermediate temperatures  (Bossard 2022). However, Opisodasys pseudarctomys did not occur much 
during hottest temperatures, falsifying this prediction. Interestingly, Opisodasys keeni in deer mice 
nests was at the hottest. Epitedia faceta and Conorhinopsylla stanfordi were intermediate, thus 
corroborating prediction.
Bossard (2022) also hypothesized that Orchopeas howardi and Opisodasys pseudarctomys  
represented an evolutionarily newer, more abundant Ceratophyllidae community of a host generalist 
and a host specialist that was superimposed over an older, less abundant Ctenophthalmidae community 
of a host generalist and a host specialist ( Epitedia faceta and Conorhinopsylla stanfordi ). Although the 23
players change, the play remains the same?
14. Both Benton and Bossard hypothesized that competition between flea species in nests was 
significant, and that the seemingly different life histories and thermal preferences were adaptations that 
minimized competition. However, this hypothesis has not been rigorously tested. There are multiple 
alternative hypotheses on flea community assembly including dispersal, ecological fitting, 
environmental filtering, neutrality, and phylogenetic constraints (Bossard 2022, Krasnov et al. 2022).

Li, F., Zhao, S., Li, E., Xie, S., Wang, N., Tan, W., & Wang, Y . (2024). Detection of Rickettsia raoultii 
in Vermipsylla alakurt -Like Fleas of Sheep in Northwestern China. Acta Parasitologica, 69(1), 776-784.
Introduction: To date, a total of 2574 validated flea species have been discovered. 
Vermipsyllidae is a family of fleas that comprises at least eight species. Vermipsylla is a genus of the 
family Vermipsyllidae within the order Siphonaptera of fleas. Here a novel Vermipsylla species was 
described, and rickettsial agent was also detected in it.
Methods: A total of 128 fleas were collected directly from 260 pastured sheep in China. Of 
these, eight representative fleas (four males and four females) were identified by key morphological 
features. Meanwhile, 120 flea DNAs, including six flea samples for molecular taxonomy, were 
subjected to Rickettsia spp. DNA detection. The molecular identity of fleas was determined by 
amplification and sequenmce analysis of four genetic markers (the 28S rDNA genes, the 18S rDNA 
genes, the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I and subunit II). In addition, five Rickettsia-
specific gene fragments were used to identify the species of the rickettsial agents. The amplified 
products were sequenced and phylogenetically analyzed.
Results: The morphological characteristics of the flea species identified in this study were 
similar to Vermipsylla alakurt, but presented difference in hair number of the metepimeron, the third 
tergum, the genitals and the tibiae of hind leg. The 18S rDNA, 28S rDNA and COII genetic markers 
from fleas showed the highest identity to those of V . alakurt, shared 98.45% (954/969), 95.81% 
(892/931) and 85.86% (571/665) similarities, respectively. However, the COI sequence showed the 25
highest identity to that of Dorcadia ioffi with 88.48% (576/651) similarity. Rickettsia raoutii tested 
positive in 14.17% (17/120) flea DNA samples.
Conclusion: Our study reports the detection of  R. raoultii in V . alakurt-like fleas infesting sheep 
in China.

Kwak, M. L., Burns, P. A., Hastriter, M. W., Jenkins Shaw, J., & Nakao, R. (2024). The threatened 
Pookila (Pseudomys novaehollandiae) hosts a diverse macrobiome of arthropods at varying risks of co-
extinction. Journal of Insect Conservation, 1-10.
The Pookila (Pseudomys novaehollandiae) is a threatened Australian mammal emblematic of 
the global decline of many vertebrate taxa. While conservationists are concerned with the survival of 
threatened vertebrates, few consider the rich diversity of symbiotic arthropods which often depend on 
these hosts for survival. Using P. novaehollandiae as a case study, we demonstrate that even 
opportunistic sampling can rapidly expand knowledge of the species richness of arthropod symbiont 
communities on poorly studied vertebrate hosts. We also demonstrate how DNA barcoding can be 
integrated to provide rapid and inexpensive identification capabilities for non-specialists. Finally, we 
show how various metrics and methods can be used to quantify and qualify extinction risk of poorly 
known arthropod symbionts to provide the foundations for conservation action. Implications for insect 
conservation: This study highlights how opportunistic sampling coupled with DNA barcoding and 
extinction risk metrics can be used to rapidly and inexpensively characterise the arthropod 
macrobiomes of rare vertebrates and evaluate the risk of decline of their component taxa.
